The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.
authors: Lucas Thil, Jesse Read, Guillaume Doquet, Rim Kaddah
bullets: Removes the need to predefine mechanisms and labels when adapting neural operator libraries.
Infers each candidate operator’s contribution using convex optimization, then assigns mechanisms with a calibrated test.
Detects failures when required physics is missing or mechanisms cannot be sufficiently separated.
Recovers mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and composes them into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations.
Can add previously unseen physics without labels or forgetting; on Navier–Stokes, performance is about as accurate as supervised counterparts.
papers.selection_reason: Learned neural-operator simulators of physical dynamics are directly relevant to environment-dynamics prediction in world models.
papers.title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
papers.tldr: SPLICE discovers and expands libraries of physics-specific neural operators from unlabeled trajectories containing multiple interacting mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Generative policies such as diffusion models provide expressive data-driven priors for robot behavior, yet the situations a robot faces at execution time rarely match its training data and impose constraints and objectives the policy never learned. Existing inference-time guidance methods either rely on gradients that can push samples away from the learned prior, or on sampling procedures that can be inefficient, collapse modes, or average them into out-of-distribution predictions. We introduce MOSAIC, a mode- and support-aware framework for gradient-free inference-time control of robotic diffusion models. MOSAIC treats the initial noise and all stochastic reverse-step perturbations as a joint input to the pretrained denoising process and adapts a distribution over this input using importance weights computed from fully denoised outputs. Physical feasibility and consistency with the learned support are balanced using adaptive penalties, while mode-wise importance-weighted updates preserve modes and avoid destructive averaging. The same formulation can jointly steer multiple independently trained diffusion models through shared coupling costs, enabling coordinated behavior without requiring a joint model. We evaluate MOSAIC on navigation, dexterous grasping, motion planning with unseen geometry, and collaborative box manipulation with independently trained robot priors. Across these settings, MOSAIC adapts and composes frozen diffusion priors under new deployment constraints without retraining.
authors: Sabrina Bodmer, Rahel Rickenbach, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Melanie N. Zeilinger, Colin Jones
bullets: Addresses deployment constraints and objectives not represented during diffusion-policy training.
Adapts the joint distribution of initial noise and reverse-process perturbations using importance weights on fully denoised outputs.
Balances physical feasibility with support consistency through adaptive penalties and preserves modes with mode-wise updates.
Can coordinate independently trained diffusion models using shared coupling costs, without a joint model or retraining.
Evaluated across navigation, dexterous grasping, unseen-geometry planning, and collaborative manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Gradient-free inference-time control of robot diffusion models with mode preservation, directly advancing robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Mode- and Support-Aware Inference-Time Control of Robot Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: MOSAIC enables gradient-free, inference-time adaptation and coordination of frozen robot diffusion policies while preserving feasible, in-distribution behavior and multiple modes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
authors: Yuqi Ye, Caigao Jiang, Zhuonan Wang, Congyuan Pei, Chao Qu, Changhao Peng, Junhong Lin, Qize Yu, Zetian Song, Guangzhao Fu, Chongruo Wu, Shiyu Huang, Shuchang Zhou, Honggou Yang, Wei Gao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but weakly understood vision-action models and accurate but slow autoregressive VLAs.
Uses joint chain-of-thought supervision to preserve spatial understanding and guide trajectory generation.
Generates actions before chain-of-thought during training, so inference outputs only actions for lower latency.
AUGUstus-GRPO jointly optimizes action and reasoning objectives.
Reports strong performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes, with 12 Hz operation in a preliminary real-vehicle deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Autonomous driving VLA model unifying diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive chain-of-thought understanding; directly fits vision-language-action.
papers.title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding
papers.tldr: AUGUstus unifies diffusion-based action generation with autoregressive chain-of-thought understanding to deliver safer, accurate, and low-latency autonomous-driving planning.

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
authors: Shenghua Lu, Zixuan Yang, Rongxu Zhao, Bohao Qu, Jifeng Hu, Hechang Chen
bullets: Targets the cost and weak use of suboptimal trajectories in multi-step generative offline RL.
Encodes trajectory chunks into a structured high-level latent decision space shaped by behavioral data.
Learns shared flow mappings from Gaussian-induced or suboptimal decisions toward positive and high-value decision regions.
Uses hierarchical chunk-level advantages to guide refinement while compressing sequences from T to approximately T/H.
Achieves an average score of 90.91 on D4RL Gym-MuJoCo, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Offline RL policy learning with latent flow generation for robotic control benchmarks; relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: From Suboptimal to Optimal: One-Step Latent Flow Policies for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MF2B learns one-step latent flow policies that refine suboptimal behavioral chunks into higher-value decisions for efficient offline RL.

papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
authors: Shu Zhao, Tan Yu
bullets: Visual ICL depends heavily on selecting effective demonstrations, while prior counterfactual methods require complex multi-stage pipelines.
SMILE offline-mines hard negatives from the target VLM’s own prediction errors to capture model-specific failure modes.
At test time, the model’s prediction guides semantic retrieval of likely recurring mistakes for the current query.
The same mechanism supports both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design.
Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE gains an average of 3.09 task-score points over the SOTA baseline with 5× lower latency.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual in-context learning for VLMs by mining the model's own errors as demonstrations; directly relevant to multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: The Value of Being Wrong: Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors
papers.tldr: SMILE improves visual in-context learning by retrieving a model’s own past mistakes as prediction-conditioned counterfactual demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.
authors: Joshua Sari\~nana
bullets: Defines event boundaries and feature schemas informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation.
Applied to interviews from five participants, producing 256 traceable event-states.
Multidimensional analyses found consecutive event-states were closer than expected under randomized narrative order.
Basin-state similarity aligned with one-step routing profiles, while context, mechanism, and theme differentiated pathway engagement.
Successor-representation analyses linked feature-space distances with modeled multistep occupancy patterns across tested geometries.
papers.selection_reason: LLM framework for event memory and narrative dynamics with hippocampal/navigation-inspired structure, relevant to embodied memory.
papers.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
papers.tldr: A source-traceable LLM framework represents autobiographical narratives as multidimensional event states and models their sequential organization, linking narrative transitions to hippocampal-inspired memory principles.

papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
authors: Zhenhua Yang, Jiafeng Liang, Xingyu Zhou, Yi Jiang, Xiayu Cao, Zui Chen, Luqi Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yufei Xiang, Chang Li, Rongchuan Mu, Bowen Chi, Zihe Tong, Mingyu Li, Huijie Ma, Yiqiao Yang, Baoqi Ren, Zhiming Ma, Zhihao Zhu, Jiahao Ji, Zhuoyao Wang, Qianyu Wang, Xiangyu Liu, Wang Zixiang, Shunliang Zhang, Ming Liu, Xiaocheng Feng, Duyu Tang, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses proactive intervention in changing physical environments, where tasks arise before users specify them.
Combines StreamingJev for deciding whether and when to intervene with a Response Model for generating human or device actions.
Uses an automated video-to-supervision pipeline to support scalable learning of proactive timing.
Experiments show more accurate timing and fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline across explicit objectives and standing roles.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate detection of emerging needs followed by appropriate physical actions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an embodied system that continuously observes the physical world, identifies intervention needs, and executes physical actions; includes real-robot evaluation.
papers.title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
papers.tldr: ProAgent enables Physical AI to continuously detect emerging needs and intervene at the appropriate time without waiting for explicit instructions.

papers.abstract: How do language models reconcile conflicting contextual evidence within a prompt? We study this question using lexical redefinition, where an explicit instruction specifies how a word should be interpreted and a subsequent sentence provides additional evidence through its usage. Across 870 word pairs, we find that lexical redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules. Instead, the behaviour depends systematically on the relationship between the explicit instruction and the intervening sentence: the contextualised usage can preserve, weaken, or completely reverse the instruction. These results suggest that the interpretation of an explicit instruction remains sensitive to subsequent contextual evidence. Lexical redefinition therefore provides a controlled behavioural paradigm for studying how language models integrate multiple sources of information within a prompt.
authors: Roksana Goworek, Haim Dubossarsky
bullets: Studies how models reconcile conflicting evidence within prompts.
Uses lexical redefinition: an instruction assigns a word’s meaning, followed by a sentence using the word.
Evaluates 870 word pairs across different relationships between the instruction and intervening sentence.
Finds that redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules; subsequent context systematically changes their effect.
Proposes lexical redefinition as a controlled paradigm for studying prompt-level information integration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies context-sensitive instruction following in LLMs via lexical redefinition, relevant to LLM reasoning and context.
papers.title: Lexical Redefinition Reveals Context-Sensitive Instruction Following
papers.tldr: Language models interpret lexical redefinitions context-sensitively, with later usage evidence sometimes preserving, weakening, or reversing an explicit instruction.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models, exemplified by GPT-6 Astra, raise the prospect of general-purpose embodied reasoning and planning. Using Internet videos for embodied pretraining calls for reliable physical-scale annotations. Yet visual geometry foundation models often recover scene structure and camera motion without reliable metric scale. We show that uncertain size priors of familiar objects can jointly constrain a reconstruction's shared scale. Building on this insight, we present UniMetric, a universal and training-free metric scale recovery framework for geometry foundation models, without additional sensors or task-specific metric supervision. Specifically, Metric Prior Acquisition elicits object height intervals from a vision-language model. Semantic-Geometric Alignment measures reconstructed object heights along the estimated support-surface normal in each frame and converts the priors into scale intervals. Global Scale Recovery reconciles these intervals through a convex objective, yielding a jointly feasible scale when they overlap and a unique compromise otherwise. The estimated sequence-level scale is applied uniformly to reconstructed points and camera translations. Controlled experiments with real VLM priors show that combining observations improves scale accuracy with exact relative object heights. To evaluate metric accuracy on GFM reconstructions without ground-truth scale alignment, we introduce MetricBench, covering twelve embodied, driving, and roadside subsets with sensor-derived ground truth. Across nine geometry foundation models, UniMetric reduces mean depth Abs Rel, reconstruction Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively, improving every model on all three tasks at the suite level. We release the UniMetric code and MetricBench data.
authors: Lei Yang, Yuner Zhang, Ziyang Liu, Ziying Song, Kai WU, Yiyang Gao, Jiangtao Su, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable physical-scale annotations in geometry foundation model outputs.
Elicits object-height intervals, aligns reconstructed objects with support-surface geometry, and converts them into scale intervals.
Reconciles multiple observations with a convex global objective to estimate one sequence-level scale, applied to points and camera translations.
Introduces MetricBench, a sensor-grounded benchmark spanning 12 embodied, driving, and roadside subsets.

Across nine geometry foundation models, reduces mean depth Abs Rel, Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively. In scope: requires familiar objects with usable size priors and overlapping or reconcilable scale constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free metric scale recovery for visual geometry foundation models using VLM object priors and geometric alignment; directly relevant to spatial/geometric reasoning in multimodal systems.
papers.title: UniMetric: Universal Metric Scale Recovery for Visual Geometry Foundation Models
papers.tldr: UniMetric is a training-free framework that recovers metric scale for visual geometry foundation model reconstructions using uncertain object-size priors from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
authors: Zhe Sun, Liang An, Jiayu Yao, Ronglai Qian, Jianing Cai, Ziwei Huang, Qing Fan, Zhiyuan Yang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Xiaoyan Wang
bullets: Targets underwater signal recognition for vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing.
Contains 375,051 traceable records spanning detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise under modeled propagation conditions.
Provides three-level labels, 13 leaf classes, templated multi-turn dialogues, and source/channel metadata.
On a balanced 2,600-record evaluation, nine open LALMs achieve only 2.0%–13.1% leaf accuracy; waveform input helps source routing more than fine-grained recognition.
Includes a silent-audio control, gated coarse-to-fine evaluation, and a released training partition for future adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks large audio-language models, which are multimodal LLMs with an additional audio modality; relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
papers.tldr: UA-Bench is a large synthetic benchmark showing that open large audio-language models struggle with fine-grained underwater acoustic recognition without task-specific adaptation.

papers.abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.
authors: Iacopo Ghinassi, Hy Nguyen Gia La, Luke Ong
bullets: Targets uncertainty quantification for inputs combining multiple modalities, beyond methods limited to two modalities.
Scores Chain-of-Thought grounding in multimodal inputs and internal coherence using external omni-modal embeddings.
Geometric signals are highly redundant with each other but complementary to answer-dispersion baselines; reliability varies by generator and modality.
On UNO-Bench, results provide small, systematic gains over self-consistency for a closed model and mixed gains for an open model, while remaining competitive with other baselines.
Requires an auxiliary model to segment reasoning traces; aggregated scoring may use a small labelled calibration set, though its benefit is limited.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty quantification for omni-modal LLMs using external embeddings; fits multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.tldr: An external-embedding framework estimates uncertainty in omni-modal LLM reasoning without accessing model internals or rerunning the evaluated model.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Builds a knowledge-dense, token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving, improving planning and achieving 2x speedup via register-guided token compression.
papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ConDenseDrive distills diverse visual knowledge into a token-sparse encoder that improves planning while delivering 2.0× faster inference for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Mona Jaber, Shanxin Yuan, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Mines modality detections for 0.4M objects across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo to characterize when cameras and LiDAR disagree.
Introduces Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution to reveal distance-dependent structure hidden by global attribution.
Finds that modality preference depends on object type and location: cameras favor some objects and peak at 10–30 m, while rear-facing objects are more LiDAR-dominant.
Shows failure drivers are interactive rather than purely additive, with distance–density effects outweighing viewing-direction main effects.
Injecting a Modality Reliability Map into four pretrained fusion detectors improves performance by up to 1.3 mAP while fine-tuning under 4% of parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and corrects camera-LiDAR perception reliability for autonomous driving 3D detection; relevant to embodied perception and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
papers.tldr: A large-scale analysis shows that camera–LiDAR reliability varies by object type, distance, interaction effects, and direction, enabling a lightweight reliability map that improves fusion detection with minimal fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: The rapid spread of face forgeries on the Web challenges the credibility of visual content. In practical Web environments, manipulated media originate from evolving generation pipelines and undergo diverse processing during dissemination, making reliable authenticity assessment under unseen manipulations and visual changes a critical challenge. We observe that a standard LoRA-adapted CLIP detector exhibits uneven patch-level decision dependence, concen trating a disproportionate share of class-specific relevance on a small fraction of visual patches. To improve robustness to variations in such highly dependent evidence, we propose EviStress, a two-stage framework for generalizable face forgery detection with textual explanations. In the first stage, Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation (ETPP) estimates patch dependence from global, relational, and semantic cues and assigns positively correlated perturbation probabilities, explicitly stress-testing highly dependent visual evidence during training. We further introduce Discriminative Variation Preservation (DVP), which constrains the residual between clean and perturbed representations to retain authenticity discriminative information. In the second stage, Intrinsic Evidence Instruction Tuning (IEIT) transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA as its vision tower and performs parameter-efficient multimodal instruction tuning, enabling authenticity prediction and textual explanation directly from the learned forgery-sensitive representation without an external detector. Experiments demonstrate improved cross-dataset and cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with the multimodal model providing authenticity predictions and human-readable explanations.
authors: Jiuyao Jing, Xuanyu Yi, Yu Zheng, Chunlei Peng
bullets: Targets the brittleness of CLIP-based detectors that rely disproportionately on a small number of image patches.
Uses Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation to identify and perturb highly dependent evidence during training.
Applies Discriminative Variation Preservation to retain authenticity-related information in perturbed representations.
Transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA with parameter-efficient instruction tuning for prediction and explanation.
Reports improved cross-dataset, cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with human-readable authenticity explanations.
papers.selection_reason: Uses evidence-targeted patch perturbation and multimodal instruction tuning on CLIP/LLaVA to produce predictions with textual explanations; transferable to robustness and interpretability of multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: EviStress: Evidence Stress Learning for Generalizable Face Forgery Detection with Textual Explanations
papers.tldr: EviStress improves face-forgery detection under unseen manipulations and visual corruption by stress-testing highly influential visual evidence and generating textual explanations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.
authors: Yanfeng Zhao, Haoyang Li, Sheng Lin, Yuming Zhou, Jiawei Jiang, Bin Cui, Fangcheng Fu
bullets: Addresses underutilized resources caused by static allocation across RL post-training roles.
Uses global parameter storage and unified context transfer to support rapid resource shifting.
A shift-aware scheduler migrates sequences, while a planner balances throughput gains against shift overhead.
Evaluated on 128 GPUs across four dense and mixture-of-experts model groups.
Shifts resources within seconds and improves throughput by 1.81–2.05× over colocated and 1.50–1.95× over disaggregated deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a resource-shiftable runtime for RL post-training that dynamically reallocates GPU resources to improve throughput, fitting the broad Efficient AI interest in reducing AI-system resource waste.
papers.title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
papers.tldr: PivotRL dynamically reallocates GPUs among RL rollout, generative reward evaluation, and policy training to improve post-training throughput while preserving convergence.

papers.abstract:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.
authors: Andre Marchildon
bullets: Targets fast training, posterior evaluation, low memory use, and scalability in high-dimensional settings.
Uses one n×n matrix to store multiple symmetric matrices in separate triangular regions, reducing memory requirements.
Improves speed through memory-efficient algorithms, extensive BLAS/LAPACK use, and reuse of expensive kernel calculations.
Outperformed scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT in all reported comparisons on a MacBook Pro and Trillium.
For 10⁴ points in 10 dimensions, it used 9.6–35× less memory and achieved up to 54× faster likelihood-gradient evaluation; posterior mean plus gradient evaluation was over 440× faster.
papers.selection_reason: Gaussian process library focused on faster training and lower memory usage, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
papers.tldr: GpFlash is a memory-efficient Gaussian process library that substantially accelerates training and posterior evaluation, including for high-dimensional problems.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.
authors: Ziye Guo, Ye Yuan
bullets: The study examines how label arrangement patterns interact with model biases in in-context learning.
Five 8–9B autoregressive and discrete diffusion models exhibit label collapse, including under balanced alternating demonstrations.
Some label pairs collapse consistently, while others reverse collapse direction depending on arrangement.
Near-chance accuracy can hide query-independent predictions, so accuracy is not a sufficient diagnostic.
Separation—query-position log-odds between label words—combined with artifact-aware label extraction reveals the collapse.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes in-context learning failure modes in diffusion language models; relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Label collapse causes language models to produce query-independent ICL labels, and accuracy alone may miss this failure, making separation a necessary diagnostic.

papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
authors: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu
bullets: Evaluates 12 controlled configurations, including one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants.
Tests models up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks.
Standard causal attention matches or exceeds structural attention masks without architectural changes and remains compatible with FlashAttention.
At the 1B-parameter scale, the best SLM shows no clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline.
The study covers different tree linearizations and attention masks, addressing an underexplored design space.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of syntactic language model architectures and scaling, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
papers.tldr: A large-scale study finds that syntactic language models with standard causal attention perform as well as or better than structural-mask variants, but lose their relative advantage over non-structural models at 1B parameters.

papers.abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn
bullets: Open-weight deployment creates constraints beyond user-side image defenses.
Protection should balance effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance.
Long-horizon attack simulations are used to improve resistance to protection removal and re-alignment.
Experiments with one protection tool show stronger re-alignment resistance but reduced clean fidelity.
Further research is needed for practical model-side protection.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses image protection in open-weight diffusion models, proposing requirements and resistance to long-horizon attacks.
papers.title: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: The paper frames image protection for open-weight diffusion models around four practical requirements and strengthens tamper resistance through long-horizon attack simulations, though clean-image fidelity declines.

papers.abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.
authors: Amir Mohammad Karimi Mamaghan, Ferdinand Kapl, Andrea Dittadi, Karl Henrik Johansson, Kaitlin Maile, Johannes von Oswald, Stefan Bauer
bullets: Studies progressive depth growth in masked autoencoders (MAE) and self-distilled DINOv3.
Reports 13.9–24.8% lower training FLOPs and up to 3.36 percentage-point higher ImageNet linear-probe accuracy.
Improves performance across global and dense vision tasks, including at intermediate layers.
Finds that growth reshapes computation: MAE develops alternating global/local attention, while DINOv3 reaches global attention earlier.
Scope: focuses on progressive depth growth’s effects on self-supervised vision-transformer representations and internal computation.
papers.selection_reason: Progressive depth growth reduces training FLOPs for self-supervised ViTs, an efficiency-oriented pretraining method.
papers.title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Progressive depth growth makes self-supervised vision-transformer pretraining more compute-efficient while improving representations and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.
authors: Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Abdelrahman Elsayed, Ibrahim Almakky, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Mohammad Yaqub
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of VFMs while avoiding expensive teacher-guided distillation.
Jointly optimizes layer-wise capacity allocation and within-layer pruning based on task sensitivity and recoverability.
Uses iterative closed-form low-rank corrections to reconstruct removed behavior in the surviving weights.
Produces dense encoders in minutes on a single GPU and reduces compute and memory use.
Across 12 benchmarks and 4 models, it reports the best mean accuracy in 7 of 8 evaluated backbone-budget settings; throughput improves 1.3–2.0× over uncompressed models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a structured-pruning framework that jointly selects and recovers task-specific subnetworks from vision foundation models, directly reducing compute and memory.
papers.title: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Carve VFM automatically extracts task-specific, compact subnetworks from vision foundation models using recovery-aware structured pruning, without backbone retraining.

papers.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.
authors: Yi Wang, Zhenlong Yuan, Yuchan Guo, Maolei Huang, Zijian Song, Dapeng Zhang, Rongbin Tan, Jiyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Wang, Fangfang Lin, Shuhan Song, Huawei Cao
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented CXR agents that lack selective evidence-seeking and safeguards against inapplicable measurements.
Uses reinforcement learning to decouple auxiliary-evidence acquisition from validity-gated quantitative measurement use.
Builds Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus, and initializes Qwen3-VL-8B with agentic supervised fine-tuning.
Optimizes with GRPO using accuracy-gated process rewards for measurement consistency and tool cost.
Achieves the strongest results across three CXR benchmarks, including an 8.6-point gain on held-out ChestAgentBench.
papers.selection_reason: Post-trains a multimodal LLM with tool-augmented reinforcement learning and instruction tuning; technically transferable to general multimodal reasoning agents.
papers.title: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning
papers.tldr: X-Ragent improves chest X-ray reasoning by learning when to seek auxiliary evidence and admitting quantitative measurements only when valid.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enables transformers to solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate reasoning steps. Despite strong empirical success, the mechanisms by which such reasoning abilities emerge during training remain poorly understood, particularly from a theoretical perspective. In this work, we study this question in a stylized yet fully analyzable setting: in-context $\mathrm{K}$-nearest-neighbor ($\mathrm{K}$-NN) prediction with a one-layer transformer. Earlier work has demonstrated that one-layer transformers can be trained to perform $1$-NN without CoT (Li et al., 2024a) by having the softmax attention attend to the nearest neighbor in context. However, this result on $1$-NN cannot be extended to $\mathrm{K}$-NN for $K>1$, as softmax attention is much less naturally suited to attending to the 2nd through $K$-th nearest neighbors. We first give a rigorous negative result showing that this limitation already appears on a well-separated class of binary classification tasks for odd $K>1$. We then give an explicit construction of a one-layer transformer, and show that it can solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN via CoT reasoning. We further prove that, under a stylized training setup, gradient descent can recover this construction, thereby showing that transformers can acquire the capability to solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN through training. In addition, we show that the resulting trained model applies to a broader test class than that assumed in the training analysis. Our results shed light on how CoT expands the ability of transformers to learn and solve tasks that are otherwise hard to solve.
authors: Lyumin Wu, Yuan Cao
bullets: Studies how CoT capabilities can emerge in transformers through a provably analyzable in-context K-NN task.
Proves a negative result: direct softmax attention fails on a well-separated binary classification class for odd K>1.
Constructs a one-layer transformer that solves K-NN by generating intermediate reasoning steps.
Shows that gradient descent can recover this CoT-based construction under a stylized training setup.
Demonstrates that the trained model generalizes to a broader test class than the one used in the training analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of chain-of-thought and in-context learning in transformers, relevant to language model reasoning.
papers.title: One-Layer Transformers Provably Learn In-Context K-Nearest Neighbor Prediction with Chain-of-Thought
papers.tldr: A one-layer transformer cannot generally perform K-NN for odd K>1 directly with softmax attention, but can learn it using chain-of-thought reasoning.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.
authors: Futing Wang, Chenxi Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo, Zhi Wang, Yizhuo Li, Runzhe Zhan, Yu Cheng, Tao Lin
bullets: Addresses inaccurate token-level credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards.
Derives a Bayesian decomposition showing that successive prefix values can be updated additively in log-odds space.
Parameterizes values as cumulative sums of position-wise scalar outputs, trained with terminal-outcome supervision.
Improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
Also improves out-of-distribution generalization, advantage estimates, and performance across additional models and countdown and scientific coding tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves PPO-based reasoning for language models via better value tracking, directly relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
papers.tldr: TPPO improves PPO-based language-model reasoning by tracking token-level value evolution through cumulative log-odds updates.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts part articulation and connectivity from images/depth and demonstrates utility for generating robot motion trajectories; view-grounded spatial representation is transferable to embodied manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
papers.tldr: ViewStruct infers object part connectivity and articulation from visual inputs using a view-grounded representation that transfers beyond synthetic training categories and assets.

papers.abstract: Adaptive optimization methods have received considerable attention in recent years due to their strong empirical performance. However, they generally require maintaining a preconditioning matrix, which incurs prohibitive computational overhead in large-scale applications. To address these limitations, we investigate the acceleration of preconditioned optimization methods through frequent directions (FD), a widely used matrix sketching technique. We first propose FTSL by integrating FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework and adding back the cumulative information discarded by FD. FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art results. We then apply a doubling trick that further reduces the time complexity of FTSL, while maintaining the same regret guarantee. We also consider optimization over matrix-valued decision variables and exploit their structural properties to construct sketched preconditioners. We develop FTSL-Shampoo by adapting FD to Shampoo and give a novel analysis under the primal-dual framework. To further mitigate its computational complexity, we design one-sided variants of FTSL-Shampoo under both mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks. Our algorithms not only reduce the computational cost of FTSL-Shampoo, but also achieve tighter regret bounds. We extend our methods to offline stochastic convex optimization and exploit smoothness to achieve faster convergence rates. Finally, we introduce practical variants of our algorithms and empirically demonstrate their efficiency and effectiveness across a broad range of tasks.
authors: Sifan Yang, Yuanyu Wan, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of maintaining full preconditioning matrices in adaptive optimization.
Introduces FTSL, which combines Frequent Directions with adaptive subgradient methods and restores information discarded by sketching.
A doubling trick reduces FTSL’s time complexity without changing its regret guarantee.
Extends the approach to matrix-valued optimization through FTSL-Shampoo and more efficient one-sided variants.
Also develops stochastic convex-optimization extensions and reports empirical efficiency across diverse tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Matrix sketching for preconditioned optimization reduces computational and memory overhead in large-scale ML, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions
papers.tldr: Frequent Directions sketching makes adaptive preconditioned optimization more scalable while preserving or improving theoretical regret guarantees.

papers.abstract: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at identical one- and two-site moments. In the eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes their entire probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment. Along the Bethe branch, this gap varies with anisotropy, changes sign, and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt{3})/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout transfers a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their separate marginals. At $\Delta=1.5$ the deterministic binary token laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation. Exact speculative verification then gives a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and a neighborhood within targets sharing its first-token marginal. This is a mathematical existence result. It does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.
authors: Abraham Chachamovits
bullets: Parallel decoding requires a joint token law, not just accurate marginals.
Coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain are compared with maximum-entropy pairwise projections having identical one- and two-site moments.
For an eight-site, three-excitation sector, the law difference is one-dimensional and controlled by a contiguous three-site moment; it changes with anisotropy and vanishes at a specific value of Δ.
A nonlinear readout transfers this higher-order gap to the first two token positions while preserving their individual marginals.
At Δ=1.5, the constructed binary laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation and yield a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and nearby targets.
papers.selection_reason: Constructs joint laws for parallel token proposals in language-model decoding; relevant to language foundation model decoding, though theoretical.
papers.title: A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals
papers.tldr: A Bethe-ansatz construction shows that parallel token proposals can share one- and two-token marginals yet differ in higher-order dependencies that affect speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
authors: Zheyu Zhang, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Motivation: Relational models usually predict states, but decision making requires predicting state changes under actions whose dynamics may be system-specific.
Method: TabWM uses executions from an unseen world as context, without parameter updates, to predict sparse structured edits for new actions.
WorldRel is introduced as a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining.
Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 increases from 0.016 with no executions to 0.685 with 64 observed executions.
Predicted edits can be recursively composed to imagine futures; broader search over them improves the realized return of selected action sequences.
papers.selection_reason: Learns relational world dynamics from executions and predicts action-induced edits; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
papers.tldr: TabWM learns unseen relational-world dynamics from observed executions and predicts how actions will change database state, enabling better action planning.

papers.abstract: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.
authors: Fan Yang, Yue Song
bullets: Spectral summaries provide prompt-specific information about sink timing beyond current attention, especially two to three layers beforehand.
The predictive signal varies across prompt cohorts, so it is a pre-sink state-change indicator rather than a universal warning statistic.
The effect reflects broader spectral structure, not just a single extreme activation.
Post-attention singular-value interventions alter later sink behavior across Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS, compared with norm-matched random perturbations.
In Qwen2.5, suppression reduces the next-layer query–key preference for position 0; learned spectral directions are stable with substantially less training data.
papers.selection_reason: Studies hidden-state geometry preceding attention-sink formation in LLMs; fits LLM architecture/behavior.
papers.title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
papers.tldr: A short-lived reorganization in hidden-state spectra precedes attention-sink formation, and modifying this geometry can change later sink behavior.

papers.abstract: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead. The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane. A frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting then turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, so no per-clip trajectory optimization is needed. One phase-indexed reward structure, whose only per-behavior freedom is three scalars from a shared sweep, learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. We then measure what omitting the axis costs. In a training-free rigidity test, a video depth model varies the distance between the animal's hips by $40$ to $107\%$ of its own mean and a single-image metric model by $22$ to $58\%$, though that distance cannot move. Motion capture puts the true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at $4.5$ cm peak to peak, a mean deviation near $1.4$ cm against the $3.5$ cm of lateral foot error our policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution. Depth repaired to feasibility never beats the constant, and the unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.
authors: Mohamad H. Danesh, Raina Hu, Mengxue Xu, Hsiu-Chin Lin
bullets: Targets sagittally dominated motion, where limb movement is mostly visible in the image plane.
Uses frozen 2D keypoints and fixed analytic retargeting to produce reachable foot targets without per-clip optimization.
A shared phase-indexed reward structure learns four gaits and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware.
Measurements show true lateral paw motion is smaller than existing policy foot error, while depth-based alternatives are unstable or infeasible.
Scope is limited to motions where the discarded lateral axis is small relative to the pipeline’s resolution.
papers.selection_reason: Quadrupedal skill transfer from a single side-view video to a robot via retargeting and reward learning; directly fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: CopyQuad: Quadrupedal Skill Transfer from a Single Side-View Video Without a Depth Model
papers.tldr: CopyQuad transfers quadrupedal skills from a single side-view video without depth estimation by fixing the unseen axis to the robot’s stance width.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Zhenwei Shao, Zhou Yu, Yan Yang, Haoyi Sun, Qian Wang, Ning Mao, Pan Zhou
bullets: Problem: Sequence-level advantages do not reveal how visual evidence contributes across individual generated tokens.
Method: A frozen old policy compares rollout-token visual attention with attention from teacher-forced correct answers using Jensen–Shannon divergence.
