The resulting signal is trajectory-centered, position-aware, and balanced before correcting the GRPO sequence advantage.
Diagnostics examine token interventions, visual-index permutations, and generation-position effects.
On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, image AVE improves from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50; gains also hold across other reported models and metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Visual-attention-guided policy optimization for multimodal LLMs; fits MLLM training/reasoning.
papers.title: VAttnPO: Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: VAttnPO improves multimodal RL by converting answer-conditioned visual-attention agreement into token-level credit while retaining sequence-level verifier rewards.

papers.abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.
authors: Haonan Zhang, Ting Jin, Wenzhong Tang, Shuai Wang
bullets: Visual contrastive decoding can wrongly eliminate supported abstentions during candidate filtering or reference subtraction.
The proposed method preserves the abstention instruction’s effect on the original-image prediction while keeping contrast strength adjustable.
Two variants use perturbed-image and image-free references: IP-VCD and IP-M3ID.
Both outperform non-instruction-preserving baselines on decision utility across nine models on VizWiz; IP-VCD leads on eight of nine models on Food-101.
Separate measurement of instruction effects and visual contrast supports both correct answers and supported abstentions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces instruction-preserving decoding for VQA to handle abstention tokens correctly, improving decision utility on standard benchmarks.
papers.title: Lost in Contrast: Instruction-Preserving Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
papers.tldr: Instruction-preserving decoding improves visual question answering by retaining valid abstentions while using visual contrast to correct unreliable answers.

papers.abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee, Saekwang Nam, Efi Psomopoulou
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of FEM and the difficulty of collecting large physical datasets for fragile tactile sensors.
Uses 82 camera-tracked real contact configurations to validate FEM, then generates 768 synthetic scenarios for GNN training.
Supports both forward contact localisation from marker deformation and inverse deformation prediction from contact configuration.
Validated FEM has sub-0.5 mm error in over 90% of cases; the GNN achieves 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond-scale inference versus minute-scale FEM simulation.
Demonstrates sub-millimetre sim-to-real performance and integration into a real-time visualisation pipeline for planar tactile structures.
papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient GNN surrogate for tactile deformation modeling with sim-to-real transfer, supporting robotic manipulation.
papers.title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation
papers.tldr: A FEM-validated GNN surrogate enables accurate millisecond-scale prediction of planar soft tactile deformation using limited real-world data and synthetic training scenarios.

papers.abstract: Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Yihan Lin, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: AoE decouples world models from inverse-dynamics models by holding the IDM fixed while swapping future-image sources.
Actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks nearly match replayed demonstrations, but actions from predicted futures fail across benchmarks.
World-model errors concentrate on gripper and interaction geometry, while generation focuses on task-irrelevant backgrounds.
The VITA loss uses frozen AoE-recovered actions to emphasize action-relevant visual details.
Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, VITA raises generated-future execution success from near zero to 47.0% and improves native control.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves cross-task generalization in world action models using a VITA loss, central to world model research.
papers.title: What Limits Cross-Task Generalization in World Action Models?
papers.tldr: Cross-task failure in world action models stems mainly from poor prediction of gripper interaction geometry, and action-based supervision substantially improves control from generated futures.

papers.abstract: State space models provide efficient linear-complexity processing for long sequences, but their performance frequently degrades as context length grows. We propose SuPER-Mamba, a training-free framework that uses Surprisal as a model-intrinsic signal for long-range state routing in pretrained Mamba models. SuPER-Mamba computes position-wise Surprisal from next-token predictions, aggregates neighboring responses through Local Pooling, and uses the resulting scores to prioritize Global-Channel updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training. We evaluate SuPER-Mamba on three state-space models across the LongBench-E benchmark. The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
authors: Zhetong Zhang, Gayan K Kulatilleke
bullets: Addresses performance degradation in state space models as context length increases.
Computes position-wise surprisal from next-token predictions and smooths it with Local Pooling.
Uses surprisal scores to prioritize Global-Channel state updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training.
Evaluated across three state-space models on LongBench-E, improving the average score from 8.06 to 15.69.
Ablation and length-wise analyses support the effectiveness of the routing framework.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free surprisal-based routing improves long-context Mamba performance; fits long-context language model methods.
papers.title: SuPER-Mamba: Surprisal Prioritization for Extended-Context Routing in Mamba
papers.tldr: SuPER-Mamba is a training-free surprisal-based routing method that substantially improves long-context performance in pretrained Mamba models.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. Yet existing closed-loop benchmarks primarily measure route completion, safety, and rule compliance, leaving a fundamental question unresolved: does language actually determine which feasible behavior the vehicle executes? A trajectory may be safe and successful while still violating or even ignoring the passenger's instruction. To address this, we introduce \ltd, a benchmark designed to directly test this capability. Its key evaluation unit, the paired counterfactual unit (PCU), holds the initial driving scene fixed while changing only the instruction. This design enables us to distinguish isolated instruction success from counterfactual paired success across four instruction-following scopes. To test whether this distinction persists across evaluation regimes, we instantiate Language2Drive in complementary closed-loop CARLA simulation, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks, including our released CARLA-Language2Drive simulator with purpose-built maps. Evaluating representative driving VLAs across these settings reveals a striking mismatch between strong driving competence and weak language control: 93.2% of successful rollouts do not have a successful counterpart under the alternative feasible instruction. This failure is dominated by one-sided completion, where a model repeatedly executes one preferred behavior but fails when the same scene requires the counterfactual alternative. These results expose two fundamental limitations of current evaluation: isolated success and driving scores, which are widely used by conventional driving benchmarks, can substantially overstate language-following capability, while current driving VLAs themselves lack reliable instruction following under matched counterfactual tests.
authors: Zihan You, Zehua Fan, Wenqi Lyu, Aoqi Wang, Ni Wang, Yifei Yang, Linge Zhao, Huan Li, Sining Ang, Yuguang Yang, Jueyu Chen, Xiangyu Li, Qianshan Wei, Jieyuan Pei, Yuxin Wang, Zhiwen Chen, Jiaqi Li, Wenxuan Song, Yanyuan Qiao, Benjin Zhu, Haoang Li, Yan Wang
bullets: Introduces paired counterfactual units (PCUs), which keep the scene fixed while varying only the instruction.
Separates isolated instruction success from paired counterfactual success across four instruction-following scopes.
Evaluates VLAs in closed-loop CARLA, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks.
Finds that 93.2% of successful rollouts lack a successful counterpart under an alternative feasible instruction.
Failures are mainly one-sided completion: models repeatedly choose a preferred behavior instead of following the requested alternative.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the instruction-following capability of Vision-Language-Action models in autonomous driving, identifying a critical gap between driving competence and language control.
papers.title: Language2Drive: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Really Follow the Instructions in Autonomous Driving?
papers.tldr: Language2Drive shows that current autonomous-driving VLAs can drive successfully yet often fail to change behavior when instructions change.

papers.abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.
authors: Hang Xu, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Hu Yu, Jie Huang, Jiayin Xiao, Lin Song, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Feng Zhao
bullets: Targets cross-shot visual consistency while preserving user control in long-video generation.
Uses a planner–adapter–generator design: the planner manages memory, while adapters translate plans for different black-box video generators.
Trains with supervised fine-tuning followed by single-shot and multi-shot GRPO, enabling later shots to inform earlier memory decisions.
Evaluated on identity preservation and intended state changes with text requests and timed reference-image uploads.
Improves cross-shot consistency over no-memory baselines on JoyAI-Echo 1.5 and MiniMax-H3, including 15.1% and 20.7% gains on ST-Bench.
papers.selection_reason: Visual memory planner for long-horizon multi-shot video generation; fits video generation and memory-based adaptation.
papers.title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.tldr: REEL learns a general visual-memory policy that retrieves, creates, and updates references to improve consistency and state changes in long-horizon multi-shot video generation.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.selection_reason: Sample-aware visual token reduction for VLMs balancing relevance and diversity at inference time.
papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.tldr: SAVER improves visual token compression by adapting the relevance–diversity trade-off to each input sample at inference time.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.
authors: Haifeng Qian, David Mosallanezhad, Christian Munley, Adithya Renduchintala, Oleksii Kuchaiev
bullets: Verifiable final-answer rewards can misrepresent reasoning quality, creating noisy credit assignment and unstable RL.
For each rollout, the method truncates the reasoning trace and samples multiple continuations from the prefix.
It replaces the original outcome reward with the mean continuation reward as a more robust quality estimate.
The approach adds moderate compute cost and improves math and coding performance across Qwen and Nemotron models.
Combined with length-based rewards, it further improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Double-rollout reward estimation improves RL training of reasoning language models; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
papers.tldr: Double-rollout reinforcement learning improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency by estimating reward from multiple continuations of truncated reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.
authors: Chiheng Lou, Xiangwei Deng, Bangjun Xiao, Xiaodong Ji, Yikai Zhao, Xin Jin, Hailin Zhang
bullets: Agentic RL’s multi-turn rollouts repeatedly mix prefill and decode requests, creating interference and changing workload demands.
Prefill-decode disaggregation improves efficiency through reduced attention-module interference, stage-specific parallelism, and shorter trajectory completion times.
Prorsa forecasts near-term prefill and decode demand from each trajectory’s lifecycle.
It reallocates workers and switches rollout-engine roles to match anticipated workload composition.
Across synchronous and asynchronous settings, Prorsa achieves 1.11×–4.05× rollout speedups over colocated prefill and decode.
papers.selection_reason: Improves LLM serving and agentic RL rollout efficiency via prediction-guided prefill-decode disaggregation, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Prorsa speeds up agentic RL rollouts by dynamically allocating resources between prefill and decode workloads based on predicted demand.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.
authors: Xin Liu, Feng Lu, Wei Li
bullets: Maps variable EEG channels into fixed regional tokens using electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances.
Preserves fine-grained channel information through a channel-evidence injection branch.
Uses a Region-Time Transformer with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals for pretraining.
Outperforms compared methods in average balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets.
On OpenBMI-MI, matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, while using 96.8% fewer parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Uses hyperbolic geometry for self-supervised EEG representation learning. The hyperbolic aggregation method is transferable to spatial reasoning tasks involving hierarchical data.
papers.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
papers.tldr: HyBRA is a self-supervised EEG representation-learning framework that uses hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation to improve robustness across heterogeneous electrode montages and datasets.

papers.abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.
authors: Yu-Tong Jin, Yi-Yang Tian, Qiwei Ye, Peng-Shuai Wang
bullets: Models sparse molecular structure from coarse global shape to fine local geometry.
Uses a hierarchical occupancy flow plus a joint atom flow for atom identities and in-cell offsets.
Cell corruption improves robustness to generated molecular support.
Shows strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality on QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, with efficiency gains over dense 3D generation.
Enables spatial conditioning for shape control, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation without task-specific retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. The hierarchical spatial flow approach is a transferable technique for 3D generation tasks.
papers.title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows
papers.tldr: OctMole generates 3D molecules efficiently by combining hierarchical octree structure modeling with fine-grained atom placement and typing.

papers.abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.
authors: Tanja Bien, Samir Darouich, Llu\'is Pastor-P\'erez, Vinh Tong, Loay Mualem, Mathias Niepert
bullets: Physics constraints may improve residual satisfaction while reducing fidelity to the data distribution.
Residual sensitivity varies across feasible states, creating incentives for avoidance and leakage.
The proposed penalty weights prediction errors using the residual Jacobian at clean training samples and normalizes the magnitude.
Experiments cover a synthetic system, three PDEs, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching.
The method improves anchoring without architectural or sampling-procedure changes.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses distributional bias in physics-informed generative models. The proposed 'data-anchored penalty' is a transferable technical contribution for learning physical dynamics.
papers.title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
papers.tldr: Residual penalties can make physics-informed generative models avoid data-supported states or leak into unsupported feasible states; a data-anchored penalty mitigates both without changing architecture or sampling.

papers.abstract: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput. In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.
authors: Tomasz Gniazdowski, Mohammadreza Momenifar, Nadia Vase, Shahram Khadivi, Wiktor Walentynowicz, Nicola Ueffing, Jan Pawlowski, Piotr Szymanski, Abraham Bagherjeiran
bullets: Addresses the cost, latency, and scalability limits of LLM-based relevance labeling.
Builds a reliable teacher pipeline from a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset and iterative prompt refinement.
Uses the teacher to generate large-scale relevance labels for training compact multimodal student models.
Students perform close to the teacher while improving inference efficiency and deployment practicality.
The abstract does not report specific datasets, metrics, or numerical gains.
papers.selection_reason: Distills a large LLM teacher into compact multimodal students to reduce latency and cost, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction
papers.tldr: A distillation framework turns an expensive LLM-based relevance judge into efficient multimodal students for scalable e-commerce search.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.
authors: Jun Xiao, Rui Ye, Dong Cao, Jinyu Gu, Ying Wang, Zhiliang Zhu
bullets: Evaluates 12 VLAs under a unified protocol spanning six capability suites and paired in-distribution/out-of-distribution tasks.
Combines single-factor sensitivity analysis with screening and evaluation of combinatorial perturbations.
Reports a mean Zero-Shot Score of 22.3% and mean R-Score of 9.3 across representative perturbation settings.
Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves held-out zero-shot generalization and robustness for π₀.₅ by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively.
Scope: findings focus on manipulation-task VLAs and the evaluated task suites and perturbation configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic framework for vision-language-action model generalization and robustness; directly fits VLA topic.
papers.title: VLA-GAUGE: Systematically Evaluating Generalization and Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-GAUGE shows that VLAs’ strong performance on familiar manipulation tasks does not reliably translate to zero-shot generalization or robustness to combined perturbations, while diagnosis-driven refinement can substantially improve both.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.
authors: Ruilin Gong, Hao Gong
bullets: Pixel-optimal codes prioritize high-variance visual information, so short prefixes may contain little caption-relevant content.
The paper formulates captioning and image generation as successive refinement with caption loss early and pixel distortion late.
RUNG supervises code prefixes with a hierarchy of captions, then uses the full code for image reconstruction.
With fixed data and capacity, language-first ordering raises prefix-caption information 2.9× and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83.
The approach costs 2.8 dB PSNR at one-quarter code length but only 0.1 dB at full length; RUNG also supports editing without inversion.
papers.selection_reason: Builds an ordered visual code supervised by captions and reconstructs images; novel multimodal representation with language-vision trade-offs.
papers.title: Making Language the Low-Rate Code of Vision: Successive Refinement from Words to Pixels
papers.tldr: RUNG orders visual codes around language first, improving caption alignment and text-to-image generation while largely preserving full-resolution reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.
authors: John S. H. Baxter
bullets: Motivates richer probabilistic output layers to add spatial regularization without substantially increasing data requirements.
Addresses the challenge of obtaining meaningful derivatives and convergence when pairing graphical models with deep networks.
Introduces two solution approaches for pairwise conditional random fields with convergence guarantees.
Evaluates the approaches through mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, showing differences in their performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces convergent differentiable approaches for CRFs with spatial regularization. This contributes to the class of differentiable probabilistic models for spatial reasoning.
papers.title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
papers.tldr: DeepFlow presents two provably convergent differentiable algorithms for incorporating pairwise CRF-style spatial regularization into deep image and signal classifiers.

papers.abstract: Feature caching has become a mainstream training-free strategy for accelerating video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps. However, existing adaptive methods rely on heuristic difference measures misaligned with actual generation quality, employ a single global threshold that ignores heterogeneous phase dynamics, and never validate their budget estimates against true approximation error, allowing systematic bias to propagate uncorrected. We propose \textbf{AlignCache}, a closed-loop caching framework that directly aligns scheduling decisions with their true influence on the final generated video through three tightly coupled components: (1) phase-adaptive budget routing that partitions the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each governed by an independent threshold and a staleness-aware guard; (2) closed-loop threshold calibration that exploits counterfactual error measurement at the classifier-free guided output level to adjust decision boundaries online via an EMA feedback loop; and (3) momentum-augmented draft synthesis combining direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By transforming scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, AlignCache consistently achieves superior acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/AlignCache.
authors: Jiyue Jiang, Zhiyu Huo, Yuhan Chen, Yanruisheng Shao, Gong Zhang, Lei Deng
bullets: Targets heuristic caching decisions, global thresholds, and uncorrected approximation error in existing methods.
Routes caching budgets across denoising phases with independent thresholds and staleness-aware safeguards.
Calibrates thresholds online using counterfactual classifier-free-guided error measurements and EMA feedback.
Uses momentum-based draft synthesis with gated residual extrapolation and unconditional correction.
Reports consistently better acceleration–quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models; specific gains are not given.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free feature caching for video diffusion acceleration; directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Heuristics are Not Enough: Calibrated and Corrected Caching for Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: AlignCache improves training-free video diffusion acceleration by using phase-aware, calibrated, and self-correcting feature caching.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
bullets: RLVR gradients progressively concentrate energy in a shrinking effective subspace, unlike gradients from supervised fine-tuning or random-reward training.
The rank needed to capture a fixed share of gradient energy decreases during training, indicating that useful update dimensionality evolves over time.
Ares estimates gradient spectral energy, tracks effective rank, and restricts each update to the resulting adaptive low-rank subspace.
Across LLM scales, RLVR algorithms, and tasks, Ares improves accuracy over commonly used optimizers.
The findings suggest RLVR may benefit from optimizers designed for its specific gradient geometry and dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive spectral low-rank optimizer for LLM reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards directly addresses LLM optimization and reasoning training.
papers.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: RLVR creates an evolving low-dimensional gradient structure, motivating Ares, an optimizer that adapts update rank to this spectral geometry and improves accuracy across models, algorithms, and tasks.

papers.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.
authors: Bojan Deraji\'c
bullets: HJ reachability identifies states where collision is unavoidable, but online computation is too expensive for newly observed environments.
Neural implicit models learn the nonnegative dynamics correction to signed-distance constraints, preserving conservative safety under approximation error.
The learned representations support model predictive control and control-barrier-function filters for static environments and moving obstacles.
Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show improved collision avoidance, particularly with short planning horizons and moving obstacles.
A tree-search labeling method avoids grid-based solvers and extends barrier-candidate generation to control-affine systems with up to 13 states.
papers.selection_reason: Learned reachability safety representations for real-time robot navigation in unknown dynamic environments directly fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Learning Reachability-Based Safety Representations for Real-Time Robot Navigation in Unknown and Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: The dissertation learns reachability-based safety representations offline so robots can perform real-time, dynamics-aware collision avoidance in unknown and dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
authors: Wenzhan Li, Yiran Qin, Heng Zhou, Huirui Wang, Yulan Guo, Ruimao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between interaction-heavy model-free refinement and potentially biased model-based refinement.
Couples policy optimization with an online-updated world model and reward proxy, using simulator reliability to adjust imagined-data ratios and rollout horizons.
Uses chunk-level trust for replay selection and optimization weighting, with a residual predictor for recursive imagination without future ground-truth queries.
On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, achieves 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than matched model-free control.
With 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA RL post-training with a trust-calibrated evolving world-model simulator directly fits embodied robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Trust-Calibrated VLA Policy Post-Training with Evolving Imagination
papers.tldr: MERL improves VLA reinforcement-learning post-training by dynamically trusting and weighting imagined experience as its learned simulator evolves.

papers.abstract: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so co-committed tokens cannot see each other, breaking multi-token format units that parsers need. On ECHO, an open-weight one-step chest X-ray (CXR) report generator, 32.7-36.7% of evaluation reports lack a parseable Impression heading and score as empty. We propose intent-triggered anchoring, a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit once the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique, content-free completion; fallbacks write the unit when the model stops or loops without starting it. On three CXR evaluation sets, the rule raises readable rates from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0% with no regressions and a 95th-percentile latency ratio of 0.68-1.28 against official decoding. Broken headings state findings absent from the reference; adding the heading at the end leaves them in 15.5-31.0% of reports, our rule in at most 0.6%. For math answer markers, the rule raises accuracy in the most parallel setting of five diffusion language models by 5.8-20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1-17.1 on GSM-Symbolic, held out from tuning. With lenient answer extraction, gains are 3.3-12.5 and 2.7-6.3 points; the rule adds 1.4-8.6 points over a stop-only fallback for four of the five models.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: Parallel decoding can commit tokens simultaneously, preventing tokens within required format units—such as headings or answer markers—from attending to one another.
The training-free rule completes a format unit after its first token when the completion is unique and content-free, with stop-or-loop fallbacks.
Across three CXR evaluation sets, readable reports increase from 63.3–67.3% to 100.0%, with no regressions and latency ratios of 0.68–1.28 at the 95th percentile.
For math answer markers, accuracy improves by 5.8–20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1–17.1 points on GSM-Symbolic in the most parallel setting.
The approach reduces broken headings that state unsupported findings to at most 0.6% of reports; scope is limited to format units with unique, content-free completions.
papers.selection_reason: Decoding rule for diffusion language models to preserve format units; relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Intent-Triggered Anchoring for Multi-Token Format Units in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Intent-triggered anchoring fixes multi-token format units during parallel diffusion decoding, substantially improving parseability and math-answer accuracy without training.

papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
authors: Xin Xu, Ke Cheng, Hao Wang, Yangru Huang, Yanghao Xiao, Zhichao Chen, Zhisheng Zhong, Xun Liu, Yi Li, Qian Li, Haibin Lv, Jun Zhang, Jie Jiang, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between exploring edit sequences and spending limited budget on evaluating intermediate agents.
Uses Verification-Aware Tree Search to allocate resources between further edits and pending verification based on predicted returns.
Uses Group Verification Optimization to train the improver while keeping the evaluator fixed.
Terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%; SpecRSI wins across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs.
Coding-validation success is 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving agent systems through speculative recursive self-improvement, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
papers.tldr: SpecRSI improves agentic systems by drafting successor agents speculatively while requiring full verification before adoption.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Freezes the pretrained backbone and trains added attention and feed-forward branches at each Transformer layer.
Uses zero-initialized output projections to preserve the original policy at initialization.
Keeps learned pathways explicit, supporting transfer across models and sequential addition of further pathways.
Across five backbones, achieves competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with few trainable parameters.
Transferred pathways provide immediate gains, reaching near-100-update performance after only 10 target-side updates in all tested transfer directions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for RL adaptation of LLMs using structural pathways, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GrowRL makes RL adaptations into compact, transferable Transformer pathways, enabling parameter-efficient reuse across compatible LLMs.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in Mixture-of-Experts models through expert merging in a latent space, relevant to efficient AI and LLMs.
papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.tldr: SLEM compresses Mixture-of-Experts models without calibration data by merging experts in a spectrum-aware latent space.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
authors: Wei Yao, Chuyao Wang, Ziwei Wang, Nabil Aouf
bullets: Addresses severe sim-to-real degradation in vision-based autonomous-driving reinforcement learning.
Uses simulated-observation attribution maps to identify and perturb appearance-sensitive Fourier components while preserving task-relevant structure.
Optimises policies to focus on task-critical features and reduce reliance on irrelevant visual cues.
Simulation and zero-shot real-world experiments show improved travel distance and reward, particularly on unseen cluttered maps.
Attribution analysis indicates more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and reality.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real RL for vision-based autonomous driving; transfers policies to real-world navigation.
papers.title: XAI-Guided Fourier Domain Generalisation for Pure-Simulation Sim-to-Real Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: XFD uses explainability-guided Fourier perturbations and robust policy optimisation to improve zero-shot sim-to-real visual driving without real-world training data.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. The four-condition protocol on three base models, with seeds and component ablations, is in progress and not reported here.
authors: Alfaj Uddin Ahmed, Md. Shaown Miah, Md Arid Hasan, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
bullets: Mirage occurs when models answer questions about unseen or irrelevant images, even if the answer happens to be correct.
The proposed support-completion objective presents valid, blank, same-domain wrong, and out-of-domain image conditions, with decline targets for invalid evidence.
Theory shows image-blind predictors are suboptimal under TIDE and links decision errors to how well representations separate valid from invalid evidence.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a three-condition predecessor reduced invalid-evidence mirages from 0.759 to 0.097 and blank-image responses from 0.700 to 0.003, with a false-abstention cost of 0.126.
The full four-condition evaluation across three base models is still in progress; reported results use a predecessor protocol and two judges.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a core failure mode of vision-language models via a new training objective, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
papers.tldr: TIDE trains vision-language models to decline when an image does not support an answer, substantially reducing unsupported image-question responses while preserving valid-image behavior.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors enable fine-grained perception for dexterous robotic manipulation, but current marker-based designs tightly couple surface texture and contact force signals within a single observation. Existing data-driven decoupling methods rely on serial mask-based inpainting, which suffers from mask-sizing dilemmas caused by physical indentation effects, error retention, and lack of real paired data for supervision. To address these challenges, we propose DeTac, a novel dual-branch generative framework that concurrently extracts clean shading and marker images from a single mixed tactile image. DeTac leverages full-image synthesis to naturally bypass mask dependency and introduces a cross-branch synergistic optimization that enables mutual supervision, effectively preventing error retention. Furthermore, we construct a strictly aligned, real-world paired tactile dataset using custom hardware to provide high-quality supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeTac achieves state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, significantly facilitating downstream surface reconstruction and force estimation tasks while exhibiting cross-sensor generalization.
authors: Zhirui Zhang, Yunkai Tang, Jiahang Li, Fan Fei, Jinnuo Zhang, Kairan Ding, Jieji Ren, Yandong Guo, Boxin Shi
bullets: Addresses signal entanglement in marker-based vision-based tactile sensors and limitations of mask-based inpainting.
Uses full-image synthesis to concurrently generate clean shading and marker images without mask-size dependence.
Applies cross-branch synergistic optimization to reduce error retention through mutual supervision.
Introduces a strictly aligned real-world paired tactile dataset for supervised training.
Reports state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, improved surface reconstruction and force estimation, and cross-sensor generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Tactile signal decoupling framework that improves perception for dexterous manipulation, with cross-sensor generalization.
papers.title: DeTac: Dual-branch Decoupling of Texture and Force Signals in Vision-Based Tactile Sensors
papers.tldr: DeTac decouples texture and force signals from a single mixed tactile image using a dual-branch generative framework with mutual supervision.

papers.abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.
authors: Xiuyuan Qi, Yi Wang, Wenjie Wang
bullets: Survey-based preference data can reveal sensitive political, religious, social, gender, and cultural beliefs.
The study formulates alignment as rating prediction rather than pairwise preference comparison.
It evaluates randomized response, the exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD for privacy protection.
Label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level protection in the reported experiments.
Preprocessing and label aggregation choices substantially affect privacy-preserving alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Privacy-preserving preference alignment of language models with differential privacy directly fits LLM alignment and training.
papers.title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a differential privacy pipeline for aligning language models with sensitive, survey-derived preference data using ordinal labels.

papers.abstract: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
authors: Kota Tsuruhara, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by changes in foot geometry, mass, and friction from added footwear.
Freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes identity-initialized modulation modules for sample-efficient adaptation.
Introduces SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that keeps online adaptation within user-defined limits.
Simulation on a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 substantially recovers locomotion performance and outperforms several adapter and residual-RL baselines under the same adaptation budget.
Real-world experiments with human shoes further assess deployment on a Unitree Go2.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts locomotion policies to morphology changes via lightweight online modules, combining embodied control with test-time adaptation.
papers.title: SHOES: Sim-to-real Hardware-adaptation via On-policy Expansion of Skills for Legged Robots
papers.tldr: SHOES efficiently adapts legged-robot locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes through safe, lightweight on-robot fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling.
