Captioning motion video does not imply that a model has inferred its governing dynamics, estimated quantitative parameters, or can regenerate the observed scene from code. Existing video-physics benchmarks evaluate plausibility, property estimation, or future-state prediction, but offer limited insight into whether models can translate visual dynamics into runnable simulation code. We introduce PhySimCode, a benchmark for physics video-to-code generation: given only a raw video, a model must infer the relevant physics, recover parameter values, and generate runnable Python that reproduces the input video. The dataset contains 160.6K procedurally generated samples spanning 162 physics phenomena across analytic SciPy simulations and PyBullet-rendered rigid-body, articulated, fluid, and contact-rich scenes; each sample bundles the simulation code, physical parameters, rendered video, and a structured chain-of-thought covering observations, laws, ODEs, numerical methods, and validation checks. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art closed- and open-source MLLMs along physical-law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery. Models reliably state physics laws (4.27-4.93/5) yet score only 1.51-2.47/5 on inferring them from video, and the best system (Claude Sonnet 4.6) recovers just 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within $\pm 20\%$, exposing a substantial video-to-simulation gap. The 2,430-video evaluation set is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SourajaKundu123/PhySimCode and the evaluation code at https://github.com/SourajaKundu/PhySimCode
authors: Souraja Kundu, Aditya Gupta, Joel Julin, Yizhou Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Targets video-to-code generation requiring physical-law inference, parameter recovery, and runnable simulation reproduction.
Includes 160.6K procedurally generated samples covering 162 phenomena across analytic and PyBullet-based simulations.
Evaluates law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery across 10 MLLMs.
Models state physics laws well (4.27–4.93/5) but infer them from video poorly (1.51–2.47/5).
The best system recovers only 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within ±20%, highlighting the benchmark’s challenging scope.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM physics video-to-code generation fits video understanding and multimodal large language model evaluation.
papers.title: PhySimCode: A Benchmark and Evaluation Method for Physics Video to Code Generation
papers.tldr: PhySimCode benchmarks whether multimodal models can turn physics videos into executable, quantitatively accurate simulations, revealing a large gap between describing laws and recovering them from visual dynamics.

papers.abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.
authors: Zhiwei Lin, Jiahao Liu, Yan Liu, Chengpeng Wang
bullets: Safety incompatibility varies with the sender–receiver model pair and cache-reuse configuration.
Reusing value tensors causes larger safety deviations than reusing key tensors.
VReparo learns offline per-layer, per-KV-head affine maps to align sender values with receiver-native values.
Across evaluated settings, VReparo lowers average HarmBench ASR from 57.28% to 39.21% and StrongREJECT from 0.4215 to 0.2163.
It retains an average 85.62% reduction in time to first token.
papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-model KV cache reuse and proposes a mitigation for safety incompatibility, relevant to KV-cache-based efficient inference.
papers.title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
papers.tldr: Cross-model KV-cache reuse can substantially alter safety behavior, but VReparo mitigates these deviations while preserving most of the latency benefit.

papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
authors: Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yilan Zhang, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Yimeng Chen, Liangyu Wang, Yifan Xu, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, Wenyi Wang, Yanning Dai, Yuhui Wang, J\"{u}rgen Schmidhuber
bullets: Linear attention’s fixed recurrent state must handle both computation and long-term storage, limiting context retention.
NoteBank archives selected text before queries are known, addresses it using native backbone features, and replays retrieved evidence through the model’s forward computation.
The training-free, plug-and-play method requires no external embedder, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader.
On one-million-token RULER retrieval tasks, Gated DeltaNet’s mean accuracy improves from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens.
The approach adds at most 0.025% analytical FLOPs and uses far less persistent storage than a Transformer KV cache; evaluations cover multiple recurrent backbones and long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse episodic memory and native replay expand long-context capability of linear attention, directly relevant to memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.tldr: NoteBank substantially extends linear-attention models’ long-context memory by sparsely storing and natively replaying past evidence without retraining or external retrieval components.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory for assistants needs a gate that decides when a new utterance retires an old stored claim. Benchmark labels for this step mark a pair as changed or not, so they cannot tell a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. We write a task contract that separates the two (SUPERSEDED vs. NEEDS-CONFIRMATION vs. COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from STALE (change pairs plus same-user controls) with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators (one author and a second annotator; provenance reported), and evaluate Jev, a typed "System One" decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. Of the 179 test pairs STALE marks as changed, 72 meet the contract's bar for an established change. Jev never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes. Its failure is premature retirement: the binary gate retires 39.2% of claims whose change is only suggested. A three-way decision cuts this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost, which misses our pre-registered 10-point budget, and it lands on the binary gate's own threshold frontier; these verdicts hold under three readings of the gold labels. On a held-out vault scored against a second annotator's labels, a cascade that escalated uncertain cases to a reasoning model and looked best on development data was indistinguishable from simply raising the threshold (premature retirement 26.8% vs. 6.5% on dev). Part of the gap comes from the gold labels: relative to that annotator's reading, LLM-majority gold shares most of its errors with a same-family escalation model, and an identity for binary labels says how much such shared errors hide. The rest is small-sample selection on development data. For builders this means a binary score should not be wired to delete: route suggested changes to pending evidence, and do not trust a cascade selected on development data of this size.
authors: Xupeng Chen, Chenqian Le
bullets: The task distinguishes established change (SUPERSEDED), suggested change needing evidence (NEEDS-CONFIRMATION), and compatibility.
Among 179 pairs marked changed by STALE, only 72 met the contract’s bar for established change.
The binary gate prematurely retired 39.2% of claims where change was only suggested; a three-way gate reduced this to 15.5%, missing the pre-registered cost target.
A development-selected reasoning cascade was indistinguishable from simply raising the decision threshold on held-out evaluation.
The practical recommendation is to route suggested changes to pending evidence rather than delete stored claims, and avoid trusting cascades selected from small development sets.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates memory-retirement gates for long-term assistant memory, fitting LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: Suggested Is Not Superseded: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a System-One Model as a Memory-Retirement Gate
papers.tldr: A pre-registered evaluation finds that binary memory-update gates often retire claims on mere suggestions, while three-way decisions reduce but do not eliminate premature retirement.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.
authors: Haotian Li, Liran Dong, Kaicheng Xiao, Guoliang Xing
bullets: Recurrent states are requantized after every update, causing coherent errors that accumulate over time.
Low-Rank Bypass (LRB) stores small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges them into the state.
Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR) rounds reversed state updates toward their intended direction without extra storage.
Evaluated across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, the method outperforms INT4, cuts state memory by up to 5.3×, and speeds decoding by up to 1.9× versus FP32 states.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes low-bit recurrent state quantization with update-preserving techniques, directly targeting memory and decoding efficiency for recurrent/linear-attention models.
papers.title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
papers.tldr: A training-free low-bit recurrent-state quantization method preserves small update directions, substantially improving INT4 state performance while reducing memory and accelerating decoding.

papers.abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.
authors: Xiaotian Ye, Chunyao Yang, Xiaohan Wang, Junkai Chen, Yongqi Duan, Mengqi Zhang, Shu Wu
bullets: Direct generalization—expecting factual edits to reliably change reasoning-task outputs—is theoretically and practically constrained.
In-the-wild chatbot evaluations reveal fluent generalization even with classical editing methods.
Theoretical analysis identifies an identifiability problem in direct generalization.
Attempts to address this face ambiguous constructed biases and interference from factors such as optimization dynamics.
Compositional generalization is supported theoretically and empirically across multiple models and editing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Examines generalization of LLM model editing and proposes compositional generalization, directly relevant to LLM knowledge-update research.
papers.title: Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization
papers.tldr: Model editing may generalize more effectively through compositional reasoning in real chatbot interactions than through the conventional direct input-output update paradigm.

papers.abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.
authors: Haq Nawaz Malik, Nahfid Nissar, Faizan Iqbal
bullets: Addresses uneven parallel data and missing direct bitext, especially for lower-resource Indic languages.
Contains 984,764 English sentences translated into all 22 languages, yielding 21.7M Indic cells.
Row alignment enables 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 pairs when including English.
Adds a confidence layer for controlling pair connectivity and proposes row-keyed human corrections that can improve multiple pairs.
The corpus is machine-generated, unverified, and reported without translation-quality results.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a large-scale translation dataset for Indian languages, relevant to the development and evaluation of Large Language Models.
papers.title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
papers.tldr: BharatSetu provides nearly 1M English-aligned machine translations across all 22 scheduled Indian languages to enable broad pivot-derived translation pairs, while highlighting the need for human correction.

papers.abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) largely focuses on optimizing learning algorithms within a pre-defined task formulation, while applying RL to new tasks still relies heavily on human expertise to design the learning pipeline: what an agent observes, how it is rewarded, which algorithm it uses, and how training is configured. Automating these choices is challenging because they are tightly coupled. We introduce FARL (Fully Automated Reinforcement Learning), a framework that automates RL design by jointly searching observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings. FARL uses training statistics and observed behavior to diagnose failures, propose changes, and test whether they improve learning. Its search preserves diverse candidates and the controls needed for these tests, using a staged budget to screen designs before investing in longer training. Experimental memory records each finding together with its conditions, so an unsuccessful component can be reconsidered in a different combination. Across expert-withheld and expert-available settings, FARL outperforms the evaluated automated baselines on challenging navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks. On Adroit Hand Relocate, FARL achieves 97.1% success at 5M training steps per policy, compared with 0% for Eureka and LiMEN and 1.0% for native Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) under the same policy training budget.
authors: Tianyu Jin, Liuyu Xiang, Chaowen Yang, Xingyang Chang, Pei Pei Li, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Addresses the human expertise required to formulate new RL tasks and configure their training pipelines.
Searches observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings as coupled choices.
Uses training statistics and behavior to diagnose failures, test revisions, preserve diverse candidates, and reuse experimental findings.
Applies staged evaluation to screen designs before allocating longer training budgets.

Outperforms evaluated automated baselines across navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks; on Adroit Hand Relocate, it reaches 97.1% success at 5M steps per policy versus 0% for Eureka and LiMEN and 1.0% for native PPO.
papers.selection_reason: Automates RL interface and solver design, evaluated on navigation, locomotion, and manipulation; relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: FARL: A Fully Automated Pipeline of RL Interface and Solver Design
papers.tldr: FARL automates RL pipeline design by jointly discovering what agents observe, how they are rewarded, which algorithms to use, and how to train them.

papers.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.
authors: Junwen Chen, Hongwei Wang, Zixuan Wang, Jingbing Wang, Gorden Liu, Sheng Siong Ong, Xiaojiao Zang, JuChin Chao, Ze Jin, Kaiwen Men, Yin Li, Jeremy Li, Zhuolin Hao, Hongyu Xiong, Yang Song
bullets: Targets the inefficiency, slow iteration, and expense of manual short-video annotation.
L1 uses a supervised fine-tuned discriminative multimodal large language model (MLLM) for direct label prediction.
L2 applies a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short-video data for zero-shot, flexible labeling.
L3 introduces an agentic workflow with tools to address complex, unfamiliar, or ambiguous cases.
Experiments across content issues show progressive accuracy gains and substantial real-world reductions in manual effort.
papers.selection_reason: Develops MLLM-based autopilot labeling for short video content, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
papers.tldr: A multi-stage autopilot framework progressively automates short-video content labeling, achieving higher accuracy while reducing manual labor costs by up to 85%.

papers.abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. Understanding how these sources interact is essential: conflicts reveal whether new knowledge can override outdated knowledge, while multi-hop reasoning tests whether new knowledge can be composed with existing knowledge to support generalization. We study these interactions in a hypernetwork-based adaptation framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context, allowing a frozen base model to adapt without task-specific updates. We find that, under knowledge conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choices depend more on where knowledge is presented than on its content. We also show that context and adapter knowledge perturb the base model's representations along directions orthogonal to its clean hidden states, enabling us to derive steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, we find that models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown arising from the interaction of the hypernetwork with both the base model and the context. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/missswiftie/Knowledge-Interaction-in-CL
authors: Jiaqi Zheng, Yi Hu, Yadong Mu, Muhan Zhang
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and the need to understand interactions among pretrained knowledge, parameter updates, and input context.
Uses a hypernetwork that generates context-dependent adapters while keeping the base LLM frozen.
Under knowledge conflict, models tend to follow the context, with behavior influenced more by knowledge presentation location than content.
Context and adapter knowledge shift representations in directions orthogonal to clean hidden states, enabling steering vectors to control the preferred knowledge source.
Multi-hop reasoning remains unreliable because the hypernetwork struggles to coordinate with both the base model and context.
papers.selection_reason: Studies knowledge interaction in hypernetwork-based continual learning for LLMs, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
papers.tldr: This study analyzes how base-model, adapter, and context knowledge interact in hypernetwork-based continual learning, revealing context preference in conflicts and unreliable multi-hop composition.

papers.abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $\pi_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $\pi_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model-memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.
authors: Seongmin Park, Jaewon Lee, Yujun Heo, Yoonsik Kim, Seheon Choi, Hyoung-rock Kim, Jungwook Choi
bullets: Quantization reduces VLA deployment costs but can impair long-horizon completion and robustness to visual and semantic shifts.
Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, QAT generally outperforms PTQ yet remains below full precision.
QCRL combines progress-based advantage estimation, FP rollout references, and quantization-aware source conditioning.
Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP mean score with INT4 W4A16 and 100.7% with NVFP4 W4A4 on evaluated settings.
The reported deployments achieve 42.9% model-memory savings or a 1.73× speedup, depending on the quantization format.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses quantization-induced failures in vision-language-action policies via quantization-conditioned offline RL, fitting embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Recovering Low-Bit Failures in Vision-Language-Action Policies via Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: QCRL uses offline reinforcement learning with quantization-aware conditioning to recover much of the task performance lost when deploying low-bit VLA policies.

papers.abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.
authors: Abdollah Pourasghari, Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour, Mohammad Roustaei
bullets: The dataset contains 258 instances from 230 real household and office photographs, with reference plans, ambiguity/infeasibility labels, disambiguation QA pairs, and generated rationales.
Experiments ablate retrieval augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and agentic disambiguation, using LLM judging and the new PGOS-FA metric.
Retrieval augmentation has the strongest and most robust effect; finer-grained additions are directionally positive but inconclusive at this dataset scale.
PGOS-FA incorporates step-order sensitivity, over-generation penalties, and Persian-adapted embeddings, and correlates with human judgments at least as well as the LLM judge.

The benchmark and best configuration outperform an independently reproduced external baseline despite using a weaker backbone; results are limited by the small dataset and single-backbone ablation scale.
papers.selection_reason: Persian vision-language-action dataset and benchmark for instruction-to-plan grounding directly fits vision-language-action.
papers.title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
papers.tldr: This work introduces a Persian vision-language-action benchmark that evaluates whether models can ground ambiguous or infeasible instructions into executable, scene-aware plans.

papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.
authors: Chunyu Luo, Hongyu Zhao, Guangyi Ni, Yue Song, Lingkai Kong
bullets: Targets the efficiency bottleneck of diffusion- and flow-based generative policies for online RL.
Combines critic-guided Drift for value improvement with entropy-induced Spread within a single actor.
Uses action regression and distribution matching, requiring neither Boltzmann-target samples nor policy-density or score estimation.
Proves convergence to the Boltzmann target under exact fitting with a fixed critic in the small-step, long-time limit.
On MuJoCo, achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among evaluated methods and improves training and inference efficiency versus diffusion and flow baselines.
papers.selection_reason: One-step generative policy for online RL with strong relevance to learned robot control and manipulation, evaluated on MuJoCo.
papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: DriftSpread is a one-step generative policy that enables expressive, entropy-aware online RL without costly iterative sampling or explicit policy-density estimation.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.
authors: Wanhao Liu, Rulin Zhou, Liangjing Shao, Zhaocheng Lin, Dongyue Li, Jinsong Lin, Guoheng Ma, Hangheng Yang, Zhiqing Tang, Jing Chen, Panshuo Li, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and planned actions.
Injects skeleton geometry and instrument-specific motion descriptors through complementary conditioning paths.
Uses a four-step causal student to retain both injection paths alongside native action conditioning.
Improves all reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over direct-action baselines on SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei.
Teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3% on the two evaluated datasets; ablations favor combining both paths.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned future skeleton prediction and controllable surgical video generation directly fit interactive world models.
papers.title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
papers.tldr: SurgCast forecasts action-conditioned instrument skeletons to make surgical video generation more controllable and structurally consistent.

papers.abstract: Under a limited context budget, a long-term agent must recall not merely memories that are individually relevant, but evidence that is collectively sufficient for the current query. Conventional memory access retrieves, scores, and truncates memories, often spending multiple context slots on redundant facts while leaving complementary evidence behind. We cast the read phase of long-term memory as query-conditioned evidence composition: each memory is valued by what it adds beyond the evidence already selected. We instantiate this operation with MemPursuit, a training-free mechanism that uses the residual of a sparse convex query reconstruction as a representation-space proxy for what the current memory set is missing. By reusing the query and candidate embeddings already available from retrieval, MemPursuit progressively composes nested evidence contexts without invoking a language model or cross-encoder to score each query--memory pair. The effectiveness of our method is verified on 3 popular benchmarks in comparison to strong baselines. In fixed-budget LoCoMo experiments, MemPursuit improves end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 percentage points at Top-20, with consistent gains across multiple memory frameworks, while achieving a 32.9$\times$ speedup in median reranking latency over fully batched BGE-v2-m3. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/FengQi-HITSZ/MemPursuit.
authors: Qi Feng, Jicong Fan
bullets: Problem: Fixed context budgets can waste slots on redundant facts and omit evidence needed collectively to answer a query.
Method: A training-free residual-based selection mechanism estimates what the current memory set is missing using sparse convex query reconstruction.
Efficiency: It reuses retrieval embeddings and avoids language-model or cross-encoder scoring for every query–memory pair.
Results: Across three benchmarks, it improves LoCoMo end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 at Top-20.
It reports a 32.9× median reranking-latency speedup over fully batched BGE-v2-m3, with gains across multiple memory frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-term agent memory evidence composition, fitting LLM memory research.
papers.title: Recall What Is Missing: Composing Evidence from Long-Term Agent Memory
papers.tldr: MemPursuit improves long-term agent recall by composing complementary evidence rather than retrieving redundant individually relevant memories.

papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Targets on-device SLM agents whose accuracy–latency tradeoff changes as context grows.
Calibrates execution-time costs across precisions and context lengths, then combines them with tensor sensitivities to allocate precision under latency or accuracy budgets.
Accounts for the fact that lower-bit weights are not always faster by predicting latency from measured execution costs rather than weight size alone.
Adjusts weight precision as the KV cache grows or becomes quantized, with schedules prepared before execution and followed while preserving the session cache.
Laptop-GPU and tool-use experiments identify cases where context-aware scheduling helps, while showing that accuracy recovery remains limited.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware mixed-precision scheduling for on-device SLMs, directly targeting KV-cache and inference memory/latency efficiency.
papers.title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A context-aware mixed-precision scheduler adapts SLM weight precision to changing context lengths, balancing latency and accuracy while retaining the KV cache.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation is inherently composed of semantically meaningful sub-tasks. While Movement Primitives (MPs) can model these components, their composition typically relies on manual engineering or sample-inefficient reinforcement learning. Existing supervised methods are limited by the lack of MP labels in standard datasets and often fail to generalize across discrete and rhythmic movements. We propose Neural Dynamic Composition (NDC), a supervised framework to compose Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) using only raw trajectories for supervision, given a single example of each primitive. Our approach exploits parallel combinations of DMPs as a differentiable relaxation of categorical primitive selection, and utilizes a warp-invariant loss formulation to identify primitives despite spatial or temporal variations. A staged training curriculum is employed to learn the selection policy and DMP parameters, unifying discrete and rhythmic movements in one framework. Evaluated on 2D handwriting and 3D robotic tasks, our method outperforms baselines on most tasks and metrics. An ablation study demonstrates how each design choice contributes to the system's performance.
authors: Rafid Saif, Auke Ijspeert, Hsiu-Chin Lin
bullets: Addresses manual, sample-inefficient primitive composition and limited generalization across discrete and rhythmic motions.
Uses parallel DMP combinations as a differentiable relaxation of categorical primitive selection.
Employs warp-invariant losses to handle spatial and temporal variations.
A staged curriculum jointly learns primitive selection policies and DMP parameters from a single example per primitive.
Outperforms baselines on most tasks and metrics in 2D handwriting and 3D robotic evaluations; ablations support the design choices.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Neural Dynamic Composition (NDC) to compose Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) for robotic manipulation using only raw trajectories, addressing discrete and rhythmic movement generalization.
papers.title: Imitation Learning via Discrete and Rhythmic Primitive Composition
papers.tldr: NDC learns to compose discrete and rhythmic Dynamic Movement Primitives from raw trajectories, enabling long-horizon manipulation without primitive labels or reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Serving speed depends on phase, batch size, context length, and the resource that becomes limiting.
The model predicts latency from a configuration and operating point using hardware- and stack-specific calibrated constants.
A dynamic-programming allocator combines modeled latency costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs.
The approach is evaluated across three hardware classes and compared with byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
Scope: performance depends on calibration for the target model, GPU, and serving stack.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses mixed-precision LLM serving efficiency, including KV-cache access and memory/latency trade-offs.
papers.title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
papers.tldr: A calibrated cost model improves mixed-precision LLM serving by accounting for compute, weight loading, and KV-cache bottlenecks instead of relying on bit-width or memory alone.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify visual world modeling and action generation, yet their real-world deployment is heavily bottlenecked by iterative action denoising and the sequential execution of visual prefilling and action prediction. We demonstrate that the action-denoising trajectories in WAMs are approximately straight, rendering the first-step velocity a strong estimate of the final action direction. Building on this observation, we introduce 1Step-WAM, a framework that transforms multi-step action denoising into one single forward. Specifically, we employ a lightweight calibrator to directly correct the first step velocity, and use bandwidth-constrained action decoding to further reduce errors in the calibrated one-step actions. Compressing action generation into a single step enables it to execute in parallel with visual prefilling, completely breaking the sequential bottleneck of the traditional imagination-then-action paradigm. Evaluations on RoboTwin and LIBERO show that 1Step-WAM largely preserves multi-step task success with only about 13.4M trainable parameters, while achieving inference speedups of $7.44\times$, $5.98\times$, and $24.84\times$ for FastWAM, ImageWAM and Kairos, respectively. Furthermore, real-world robotic deployments using the FastWAM backbone confirm a consistent 7.44$\times$ speedup while maintaining close success rate to the multi-step baseline. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/changdong1687/1Step-WAM.
authors: Rundong Su, Pengtao Chen, Haohan Geng, Sha Zhang, Zhihang Yuan, Yicheng Rong, Chong Yu, Hao Huang, Tao Chen
bullets: WAM deployment is slowed by iterative action denoising and sequential visual prefilling followed by action prediction.
The method observes that WAM denoising trajectories are approximately straight, using first-step velocity to estimate final action direction.
A lightweight calibrator corrects the one-step velocity, while bandwidth-constrained decoding reduces residual action errors.
One-step generation can run in parallel with visual prefilling, removing the traditional sequential bottleneck.
Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and real robots report speedups up to 24.84×, with success rates close to multi-step baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Speeds up World Action Models for robotic action generation via one-step denoising; relevant to robot learning and inference efficiency.
papers.title: 1Step-WAM: Your World Action Model but Faster using 1-Step Action Generation
papers.tldr: 1Step-WAM converts multi-step WAM action denoising into a single calibrated forward pass, substantially accelerating inference while largely preserving task success.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. This results in fragmented reasoning and a training-inference reasoning-state gap. To address these limitations, we propose ReState, a unified iterative reasoning framework that reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It comprises two complementary components: Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM unifies reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as reasoning-state transitions within a shared state space, enabling these heterogeneous reasoning behaviors to be learned jointly. CRSL further incorporates self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, thereby mitigating the reasoning-state gap and enabling iterative self-refinement without requiring an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. Furthermore, we construct VersaCoT-10K, a high-quality CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains, which provides diverse supervision for multi-domain reasoning and reasoning-state refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReState exhibits strong adaptability across different MLLM backbones and achieves strong performance on multiple public reasoning benchmarks, supporting the shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/ReState
authors: Chuang Yu, Xuefei Ma, Yuanhao Feng, Wuxiong Zeng, Bo Wang, Minghong Cai, Dongming Wu, Fei Zhou, Chen Tang, Wenwen Tong, Lewei Lu, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Stage-centric MCoT can fragment reasoning and create a gap between training and inference reasoning states.
Unified Reasoning State Modeling jointly represents reasoning construction, preservation, and correction in one state space.
Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning uses historical self-generated states during training and recursive updates during inference.
VersaCoT-10K provides supervision across eight visual reasoning domains for multi-domain reasoning and state refinement.
Experiments show strong adaptability across MLLM backbones and performance across multiple public reasoning benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified state-driven iterative reasoning framework for MLLMs, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
papers.tldr: ReState reframes multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning as iterative state transitions, enabling unified learning and self-refinement across reasoning behaviors and domains.

papers.abstract: In real-world indoor fire environments, visual degradation severely impairs instruction grounding, waypoint prediction, and long-horizon exploration in vision-language navigation (VLN). Although image restoration offers a natural means to mitigate such visual degradation, existing methods primarily optimize reconstruction fidelity, which does not necessarily translate into better navigation decisions and may even corrupt task-critical cues when applied indiscriminately. In this paper, we present FireNav, a decision-oriented reconstruction evidence routing framework that aligns visual restoration with navigation utility in VLN. To advance this task, we first contribute FireVLN-Bench, a paired indoor fire navigation benchmark with clean references preserving task semantics, safety supervision, and matched settings for continuous navigation and robot execution with simulated dynamics. Our FireNav retains native visual tokens and treats latent reconstruction features as auxiliary evidence, where a lightweight router leverages visual features, task context, and prior execution states to determine whether such evidence should be admitted and how strongly it should contribute to the visual tokens. To learn when reconstruction is beneficial, we further introduce decision utility calibration, which compares action prediction losses with and without candidate evidence under the same state, thereby supervising evidence selection according to its contribution to waypoint, heading, and arrival prediction. Experiments demonstrate that FireNav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both navigation success and path efficiency across evaluation settings.
authors: Hongbo Ding, Xiang Chen, Jiangxin Dong, Jinshan Pan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between reconstruction fidelity and navigation utility, where indiscriminate restoration can damage task-critical cues.
Introduces FireVLN-Bench, a paired indoor-fire VLN benchmark with clean semantic references, safety supervision, and continuous robot-execution settings.
Uses a lightweight router to combine native visual tokens with optional latent reconstruction features based on visual context, task context, and prior execution states.
Trains evidence selection with decision utility calibration using action losses for waypoint, heading, and arrival prediction.
Reports consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines in navigation success and path efficiency across evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language navigation in degraded indoor fire environments with decision-oriented reconstruction routing.
papers.title: FireNav: Decision-Oriented Reconstruction Evidence Routing for Vision-Language Navigation in Indoor Fire Environments
papers.tldr: FireNav routes visual reconstruction evidence according to its usefulness for navigation decisions, improving VLN in visually degraded indoor fire environments.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs), often built upon pretrained video-generation world models, have emerged as a promising framework for general-purpose and open-ended robot control. However, their real-world deployment often suffers from discontinuous and jerky execution. Existing methods typically address this issue by either improving inference efficiency or enhancing action continuity across prediction chunks, without jointly addressing both challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamingWAM, a streaming-diffusion framework for WAM-based robot control. StreamingWAM combines a noise ladder for chunk-wise action prediction, a prefix rollout module for cross-chunk continuity, and dense video-history memory for temporally consistent conditioning. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that StreamingWAM improves action continuity across static and dynamic settings, achieving competitive performance while reducing steady-state replanning latency to 72.9 ms in simulation and 57.3 ms on the real robot. The method also produces smoother action transitions, while the streaming staircase reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
authors: Shaojie Ren, Jingwen Sun, Zezhi Liu, Hongjin Chen, Xin Jin, Wei Zou, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses jerky, discontinuous execution in World Action Model-based robot control.
Uses chunk-wise staircase flow matching with a noise ladder for streaming action prediction.
Combines prefix rollouts and dense video-history memory for cross-chunk temporal consistency.
Evaluated in simulation and real-world tasks, with steady-state replanning latency of 72.9 ms and 57.3 ms, respectively.
Produces smoother transitions and reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming world action model for robot control.
papers.title: StreamingWAM: Streaming World Action Modeling via Chunk-Wise Staircase Flow Matching
papers.tldr: StreamingWAM enables smoother, lower-latency robot control by jointly improving streaming inference and continuity between action chunks.

papers.abstract: Post-training expert pruning is a promising deployment technique for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The calibration set is an integral part of the pruning process, however, its correlation with evaluation performance is largely misunderstood and unintuitive. In this work, we present an empirical study of the robustness of calibration perturbations, specifically in MoE models. Showing how calibration size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning for gpt-oss-20b. Our findings reveal that (1) domain-general pruning quality receives minimal benefit from scaling calibration data beyond small sample sizes, (2) cross-lingual calibration transfers effectively, with English-only calibration maintaining strong performance across seven languages of varying typologies and scripts, and (3) a diverse calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can yield comparable or superior performance to test-distribution data. Ultimately, we provide practical insights as a recipe for better understanding calibration for more effective domain-general expert pruning.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Examines how calibration-set size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning in gpt-oss-20b.
Increasing calibration data beyond small sample sizes provides minimal benefit for domain-general pruning quality.
English-only calibration transfers effectively across seven languages with varied typologies and scripts.
Calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can match or outperform test-distribution data.
Provides practical guidance for constructing robust calibration sets for MoE pruning.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient deployment of MoE models via calibration-aware expert pruning.
papers.title: Towards Robust Calibration Dataset for Domain-General Mixture of Experts Pruning
papers.tldr: An empirical study finds that small, diverse, and often English-only calibration sets can robustly guide domain-general MoE expert pruning across languages.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
authors: Zide Fan, Jiahui Yuan, Kaixin Zhang, Junhao Fan, Xiaohe Li, Yiru Wang
bullets: Reconstructs receiver-specific traffic graphs from local ego and peer-state information.
Uses shared graph attention to generate Stop/Go intentions augmented with predicted human-vehicle intent.
Exchanges timestamped CAV intentions and applies local conflict-aware arbitration to produce safe executable actions.
In SUMO evaluation, reports 97.53% completion, 0.10% collision, and 35.28 s mean traversal time.
Remains robust across tested communication delays and packet-loss conditions, but safety margins narrow with compound unpredictable human behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent RL for cooperative driving at intersections.
papers.title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X
papers.tldr: SIGN-MAPPO enables safer, more coordinated CAV navigation at unsignalized intersections despite imperfect V2X and unpredictable human-driver intentions.

papers.abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. We find that instruction-following is the first capability to collapse under pruning, well before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling, and that much of the pruning in-domain loss is likely not knowledge loss but a domain-agnostic failure to respond coherently to the prompt. We find in our setting that in-domain data is the strongest pruning signal, whereas instruction-style data recovers the most. Stage order matters little, but only marginally. We further analyze how the importance ranking drifts before and after pruning. Together these results give practitioners a concrete recipe for composing pruning and recovery.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Instruction-following collapses before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling during pruning.
Much of the in-domain loss appears to reflect incoherent prompt responses rather than knowledge loss.
In-domain data provides the strongest pruning signal in the studied setting.
Instruction-style data delivers the strongest recovery.
Pruning and recovery alter parameter-importance rankings, while reversing their stage order has only a marginal effect.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes interaction of structural pruning and recovery in LLMs, yielding a practical recipe for efficient compression.
papers.title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
papers.tldr: LLM pruning primarily disrupts instruction-following, while instruction-style recovery data most effectively restores behavior, making pruning–recovery design choices important even when stage order has limited impact.

papers.abstract: Open-world mobile manipulation requires a robot to find an object, approach it, and move it to a target receptacle from a language instruction. Training vision-language model (VLM) agents for these tasks requires demonstrations of both action selection and active vision. Existing pipelines often convert planned trajectories into high-level action labels, but shortest-path progress provides limited supervision for deciding where to look. We introduce Agent-Interface Data Alignment (AIDA), a data collection pipeline in which a teacher directly selects and executes actions through the deployed agent's skill interface. For mobile manipulation, we design teachers that maintain target visibility, recover lost targets, and approach for picking or placing. We add template-based spatial reasoning supervision and use a shared harness to organize observations, history, and outputs during training and inference. The resulting agent, AIDA-OWMM, achieves 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out OWMM episodes. Teacher sensitivity analysis shows that active-vision demonstrations improve student success. The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training. Applying AIDA to a navigation subset of EmbodiedBench further demonstrates the pipeline's utility for navigation tasks.
authors: Ronghe Qiu, Teli Ma, Jiaming Zhou, Zeying Gong, Yiting He, Qiang Huang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Targets open-world tasks requiring object search, approach, pickup, and placement from language instructions.
Collects teacher demonstrations through the agent’s actual skill interface, including maintaining and recovering target visibility.
Adds template-based spatial-reasoning supervision and a shared harness for organizing observations, history, and outputs.
AIDA-OWMM reaches 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out simulation episodes; active-vision demonstrations improve performance.
The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based open-world mobile manipulation with aligned supervision.
papers.title: Look Before You Move: Agent-Interface-Aligned Supervision for Open-World Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: AIDA trains mobile-manipulation VLM agents with demonstrations aligned to their deployed action and active-vision interfaces, achieving strong simulated and real-robot task completion.

papers.abstract: Settling one comparison between two truncation samplers has cost six thousand A100-hours, and nothing says in advance how far apart two samplers can be. We observe that almost every deployed truncation rule keeps a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, so any two such rules are nested at every decoding step. Nesting yields a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which both samplers emit identical text until they first disagree. Accumulated over a generation, this gives a separation certificate that bounds the difference between two samplers on any bounded outcome, is computable from logs a comparison already produces, and equals their sequence-level total variation distance exactly when neither rule ever overtakes the other. Two consequences follow without measurement: exactness is fragile, and certifying a small difference requires the two retained masses to agree to very high precision at every step. On six open-weight models over four math and science benchmarks, the certificate for every hyperparameter grid we tested is at least 0.998, so a bound alone rarely settles a comparison, although two members of one family can be far closer. What remains useful is the coupling, which gives an unbiased paired estimator that cuts variance $1.2$-$3.8\times$ against prompt-level pairing. Read against benchmark sizes at the default pair's variance and our point estimate of its between-prompt component, resolving a one-point difference needs 8 to 32 samples per prompt on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond and about 210 on AIME 2025; at that component's upper confidence bound GPQA-Diamond needs more than 32 and AIME 2025 cannot be resolved at any sample count. Choosing a truncation sampler is a measurement problem at least as much as a design one. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/truncation-samplers.
authors: Rasul Khanbayov, Hasan Kurban
bullets: Most deployed truncation rules retain a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, making sampler supports nested at each decoding step.
Nesting provides a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which generated texts match until the first disagreement.
The accumulated certificate bounds differences on bounded outcomes, is computable from comparison logs, and can equal sequence-level total variation under a no-overtaking condition.
Across six open-weight models and four benchmarks, tested certificates were at least 0.998, so bounds rarely resolve comparisons; exactness is also highly fragile.
The coupling enables unbiased paired estimation with 1.2–3.8× lower variance than prompt-level pairing, but resolving small performance gaps may still require many samples.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes nested truncation samplers for LLM decoding and provides a coupling-based measurement framework, directly relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: Truncation Samplers Are Nested: Comparing Decoding Rules Is a Measurement Problem
papers.tldr: Truncation samplers are usually nested, enabling exact coupling-based comparison certificates, but the resulting bounds are often too loose—so reliable sampler comparisons remain a costly measurement problem.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models achieve promising results on visual reasoning tasks, approaching human-level performance on existing STEM benchmarks. However, these capabilities degrade under complex real-world scenes. We identify that chain-of-thought reasoning remains largely confined to the linguistic space, rarely anchoring each step in visual evidence. The main cause is the absence of such data during training. In this work, we introduce a training data augmentation pipeline, \textbf{Visual Augmentation Primitives} (VAP), which leverages state-of-the-art vision generative models to synthesize diverse photorealistic training samples and corresponding reasoning text. VAP introduces some basic operators and applies them to a seed image and gets a variant. It also constructs coherent multimodal reasoning chains throughout the generation process. Such training data force models to perceive visual content and perform logical reasoning according to them at every step. We further introduce multimodal chain-of-thought rubric-based reinforcement learning to enhance this. It rewards not only text reasoning but also visual reasoning by scoring intermediate reasoning steps for logical validity, completeness, and consistency. Moreover, we construct the UNREAL benchmark to systematically evaluate visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes across controllable difficulty levels. Experiments show that a 4B model built on this framework surpasses 8B baselines, with performance improving consistently as the model scales to 32B, validating the scaling law for visual reasoning.
authors: Fan Yang, Lifeng Chen, Yipu Wang, Han Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Zhiyang Chen, Chaoyang Zhao, Lingxiang Wu, Hanqi Jiang, Yibo Chen, Xu Tang, Yao Hu, Ming Tang, Xiaojie Jin, Xiaolong Zheng, Jinqiao Wang
bullets: Addresses the weak visual grounding of chain-of-thought reasoning in complex real-world scenes.
Introduces Visual Augmentation Primitives (VAP), which generate photorealistic image variants and coherent multimodal reasoning chains.
Uses rubric-based reinforcement learning to reward logical validity, completeness, and consistency in both textual and visual reasoning.
Introduces UNREAL, a benchmark for visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes with controllable difficulty.
A 4B model surpasses 8B baselines, with performance improving through 32B scale, supporting a visual-reasoning scaling law.
papers.selection_reason: Training data augmentation and reinforcement learning to ground multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning in visual evidence; relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Genesis: Visual Augmentation Primitives for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.tldr: Genesis improves multimodal visual reasoning by training models to ground every chain-of-thought step in visual evidence through synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Large-scale video generation models are increasingly viewed as a promising path toward world models, yet their ability to capture causally coherent physical dynamics remains poorly understood. Existing evaluations largely emphasize visual quality, prompt adherence, or broad physical plausibility, leaving open whether a model can faithfully realize a complete causal cascade, in which an initiating event propagates through causally dependent interactions to a terminal outcome. We introduce CausalCascade, a simulator-grounded benchmark centered on 50 event-rich Blender scenes with structured event graphs, graph-grounded diagnostic VQA, three levels of future-event specification, and 2,832 controlled counterfactual variants, and use it to evaluate nine image-to-video models with complementary motion-, event-, and counterfactual-level diagnostics. Across the evaluated models, generated motion is more reliably localized spatially than realized with correct spatiotemporal evolution, while richer future-event specification improves event recovery but leaves physical realization limited. Counterfactual evaluation further reveals weak selective responsiveness to physical interventions, while most audited failures are foundational, arising at scene consistency or event occurrence. Together, these results position causal cascade generation as a process-level test of world modeling and highlight the need to jointly recover the intended future, faithfully realize its physical evolution, selectively respond to physical interventions, and maintain a coherent physical world over time. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/SJTU-DeepDeltaLab/CausalCascade .
authors: Jialiang Li, Zhengning Xu, Zongyang Ma, Shaobo Cui
bullets: Introduces a simulator-grounded benchmark with 50 Blender scenes, structured event graphs, diagnostic VQA, three future-specification levels, and 2,832 counterfactual variants.
Evaluates nine image-to-video models using motion-, event-, and counterfactual-level diagnostics.
Models localize motion more reliably than they realize correct spatiotemporal evolution.
More detailed future-event specifications improve event recovery but do not overcome limitations in physical realization.
Many failures originate in scene consistency and event occurrence, while counterfactual tests reveal weak selective responses to interventions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of video models as causal world models; directly relevant to video world models.
papers.title: A Plausible Future Is Not a Causal Future: Can Video Models Generate How the World Unfolds?
papers.tldr: CausalCascade shows that current video models can suggest plausible futures but struggle to generate causally coherent physical event cascades, especially under counterfactual interventions.

papers.abstract: Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of up to 7 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 24.27 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced at https://github.com/Stereo-Planner/Stereo-Planner.
authors: Hongming Shen, Junjie Lu, Xun Chen, Wei Wang, Xinhang Xu, Bailing Tian, Lihua Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of RGB-based trajectory planning and the sim-to-real domain gap without dedicated depth sensors.
Uses a scene representor with pretrained vision-grounding features to extract transferable stereo geometric cues.
A lightweight trajectory decoder conditions predictions on trajectory state, retrieved scene features, and stereo baseline for metric scale.
Trained entirely in simulation with differentiable trajectory costs, then deployed directly in real environments.
Reports 95% simulation success at 8 m/s and real-world autonomous flight up to 7 m/s with 24.27 ms mean onboard inference time.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end stereo-to-trajectory planning for quadrotor navigation.
papers.title: Stereo-Planner: Learning Stereo-to-Trajectory Planning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Quadrotor Navigation
papers.tldr: Stereo-Planner learns to convert stereo RGB images directly into quadrotor trajectories, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real navigation without explicit depth reconstruction or real-world fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Visual self-modelling lets robots learn body models from observations, but such models usually encode kinematics implicitly rather than exposing metric joint parameters for computation and control. Moreover, a good fit to images does not by itself establish accurate kinematics. Here we present an explicit analytic robot self-model that requires neither deformation networks nor URDF/CAD templates. Multi-view images and joint readings establish Gaussian appearance and provide motion evidence for rigid link assignments, whereas sparse end-effector poses independently identify metric screw axes. The resulting closed-form forward kinematics and analytic Jacobian can be evaluated beyond the fitting ranges. We validate the model on a simulated seven-axis arm, a simulated twelve-joint quadruped and a real six-axis arm. In simulation, it achieves millimetre-level reaching and pick-and-place, as well as closed-loop quadruped walking. On the real arm, it renders held-out configurations, predicts end-effector positions with a median error of 6.4 mm, compared with 11.7 mm for a calibrated nominal model, and supports reaching with external marker feedback.
