A controlled comparison shows that image fit alone is not enough: two Panda models differing only in their joint axes are 0.54 dB apart in PSNR, yet their end-effector prediction errors differ 13.7-fold.
authors: Chen Xu, Ning Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible self-models and kinematic models with computable metric joint parameters.
Combines multi-view appearance and joint-motion evidence with sparse end-effector poses to identify rigid links and screw axes.
Produces closed-form forward kinematics and an analytic Jacobian that extrapolate beyond the fitting ranges.
Validated on simulated seven-axis and quadruped robots plus a real six-axis arm, supporting reaching, pick-and-place, and walking.
Shows that image fit alone is insufficient: similar PSNR can hide substantially different end-effector prediction accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Learned analytic robot self-model for control.
papers.title: Analytic Robot Self-Model: Learning Screw-Axis Kinematics for Rendering and Model-Based Control
papers.tldr: An explicit analytic robot self-model learns metric screw-axis kinematics from images, joint readings, and sparse poses, enabling accurate rendering and model-based control without CAD or URDF templates.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.
authors: Yeonseok Lee
bullets: Addresses inference latency that grows with action-sequence length in autoregressive VLA models.
Uses shared vision and frozen text encoders, discrete skill selection, a JEPA latent-state predictor, and flow matching for action-chunk generation.
Analyzes representation-collapse regularization and latent sub-goal thresholding to limit error accumulation across task phases.
On LIBERO-10, a two-camera policy achieved 40.0% success over 200 episodes in a preliminary single-run evaluation.
The model has under 20M trainable parameters; a single-camera decision step took 10–14 ms on an Apple M4.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model replacing autoregressive action decoding with latent predictor and flow-matching action chunks; directly fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors
papers.tldr: VPA replaces slow autoregressive VLA action decoding with a lightweight neuro-symbolic latent predictor that generates full action chunks efficiently for closed-loop robot control.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots deployed for inspection and field missions must cross heterogeneous terrain, from stairs, slopes, and gaps to high platforms, stepping stones, and balance beams, where safe support is sparse or see-through. Existing methods interpose a terrain map or a depth image between sensing and control. Maps are costly to maintain, corrupted by odometry drift and outliers, and misled by see-through gratings, while depth cameras degrade with lighting and surface material. In this paper, we present PointWalker, a mapless framework whose single reinforcement learning policy directly consumes raw point clouds from four light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors. Voxelized points are encoded by linear self-attention and fused with proprioception through cross-attention, so terrain geometry reaches the policy without maps or foothold estimation. One proximal policy optimization (PPO) run, with terrain-aware rewards and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings, yields one policy for all seven terrain classes with a 90.1% mean success rate in simulation. Deployed zero-shot on a Deep Robotics X30 at 50 Hz onboard, it crosses 0.8-m gaps, climbs 0.8-m platforms and 45{\deg} steel-grating stairs, carries a 50-kg payload, and completes a 2.5-km mountain route.
authors: Sicen Li, Zhen Chu, Chao Li, Jun Zheng, Qiuguo Zhu, Jun Wu
bullets: Addresses map maintenance, odometry errors, see-through surfaces, and depth-camera limitations in field locomotion.
Uses one reinforcement-learning policy that combines voxelized LiDAR features via self-attention with proprioception via cross-attention.
Trains with PPO, terrain-aware rewards, and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings across seven terrain classes.
Achieves a 90.1% mean simulation success rate and transfers zero-shot to a quadruped at 50 Hz.
Demonstrates traversal of gaps, high platforms, steel-grating stairs, mountain terrain, and a 50-kg payload.
papers.selection_reason: RL policy for mapless quadruped locomotion from LiDAR.
papers.title: PointWalker: Mapless Quadruped Locomotion Directly From Raw LiDAR Point Clouds
papers.tldr: PointWalker enables a quadruped to traverse diverse and challenging terrain directly from raw LiDAR point clouds, without maps or foothold estimation.

papers.abstract: We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one. We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[ R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,\sigma_m\sqrt{\gamma_m/\lambda_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $\sigma_m$, arrival rate $\lambda_m$, and drift rate $\gamma_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients. A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.
authors: Yuriy Dorn, Dmitrii Vishovan, Kirill Novoselov, Ilya Kuruzov, Darina Dvinskikh, Alexander Gasnikov
bullets: Addresses continuously arriving, client-specific data distributions whose drift rates, noise levels, and sampling rates differ.
Assigns each client its own history length based on its noise, arrival rate, and drift, refreshed using a restarted accelerated method from a common point.
Derives a tracking-error bound scaling as $R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\sigma_m\sqrt{\gamma_m/\lambda_m}\right)^{2/3}$.
The method is never worse than the best common window and is strictly better when client heterogeneity is uneven.
Matching lower bounds show the rate is near-optimal; experiments attribute gains to client-specific memory across several solvers.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning from continuously arriving drifting client data with per-client memory windows; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Beyond Aggregate Drift: Optimal Client-Specific Windows in Federated Learning
papers.tldr: Client-specific memory windows improve federated learning under heterogeneous drift, noise, and data rates, with near-optimal tracking guarantees and empirical gains over shared windows.

papers.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

papers.abstract: 3D editing aims to modify an existing 3D asset according to user intent while preserving geometry and appearance outside the intended edit region. Existing methods often rely on task-specific training, source-3D inversion, or external 3D masks, and lack a unified framework for diverse editing conditions and tasks. We propose UMAS3D, a unified 3D editing framework that is training-free, inversion-free, and free from external 3D masks. UMAS3D converts text, bounding boxes, reference images, and their combinations into common target-view guidance, after which addition, deletion, modification, appearance, and pose editing share the same downstream 3D generation process. Our key insight is to couple online edit-region estimation with region-aware source preservation. Mask-Free Adaptive Region Modeling (MARM) initializes an Edit/Keep prior from source-target visual differences and progressively refines it as the target structure evolves, while Source-Guided Preservation Steering (SGPS) constrains the current Keep-region states to retain source geometry and appearance without suppressing target-driven changes. Experiments show that UMAS3D supports addition, deletion, modification, appearance, and pose editing while effectively preserving unedited source content. These advances make UMAS3D a unified framework for flexible and source-preserving 3D editing across diverse editing conditions.
authors: Xianlin Zeng, Xiaolong Shen, Ruijie Quan, Yi Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of editing 3D assets without task-specific training, source-3D inversion, or external 3D masks.
Converts text, bounding boxes, reference images, or combinations into shared target-view guidance.
Uses one downstream 3D generation process for addition, deletion, modification, appearance, and pose editing.
MARM estimates and refines Edit/Keep regions from source-target visual differences during editing.
SGPS preserves geometry and appearance in Keep regions while allowing target-driven changes elsewhere.
papers.selection_reason: Unified mask-free 3D editing framework for modifying 3D assets, relevant to 3D vision and generation.
papers.title: UMAS3D: Unified Mask-Free 3D Editing with Region-Adaptive Source Preservation
papers.tldr: UMAS3D enables unified, training-free, inversion-free, mask-free 3D editing from diverse user guidance while preserving unedited source content.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models represent an emerging paradigm for language modeling. They generate text in parallel by iteratively refining continuous representations and mapping them back to tokens through a decoder. However, realizing the efficiency advantage of parallel generation requires maintaining generation quality with only a few denoising steps. Even when the number of steps is fixed, their placement along the denoising trajectory remains flexible. In this paper, we demonstrate that changing timestep placement alone can substantially alter the final latent representations and thereby affect the decoded token distributions. Building on these findings, we introduce StepTune, an algorithm that searches for timestep placements that improve generation quality. The search is conducted on a small calibration set and guided by a language-aware objective, with the model and sampling budget fixed. Once calibrated, the timestep placement is fixed and reused across inputs. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in unconditional generation perplexity and conditional task metrics across all evaluated sampling budgets. In particular, StepTune enables 16-step sampling with a frozen model to outperform its native 64-step baseline on both XSum summarization and WMT14 translation and reduces end-to-end latency by approximately $3.8\times$. These results establish timestep placement as a practical means of improving the quality-efficiency trade-off in continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Shutian Zheng, Zhihong Yu, Linye Wei, Zeyang Zhang, Meng Li
bullets: Timestep placement alone can substantially change latent representations and decoded token distributions.
StepTune searches for effective timestep schedules using a small calibration set and a language-aware objective.
The optimized schedule is fixed after calibration and reused across inputs, with the model unchanged.
It consistently improves unconditional perplexity and conditional task metrics across evaluated sampling budgets.
With 16 steps, StepTune surpasses the native 64-step baseline on XSum and WMT14 while reducing latency by approximately 3.8×.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes timestep placement in continuous diffusion language models to improve quality-efficiency trade-off and reduce latency.
papers.title: A Step in the Right Place: Understanding and Optimizing Timestep Placement in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: StepTune improves continuous diffusion language model generation by optimizing where denoising steps occur, enabling faster sampling without changing the model or sampling budget.

papers.abstract: Camera-based occupancy prediction provides geometric and semantic scene understanding for robot perception and has been adopted in autonomous vehicle and UAV perception systems. Gaussian primitives offer a promising alternative by potentially representing only occupied regions, thereby concentrating computation and representational capacity where needed and reducing wasted computation and memory in empty space. However, existing Gaussian-based methods suffer from poor primitive utilization, as ineffective training objectives leave some Gaussians in empty space, while the limited expressiveness of Gaussian functions restricts their ability to model complex shapes. To address these limitations, we propose a novel 3D representation, Gaussian Neural Field (GNF), which can accurately map voxel positions to semantic occupancies. In GNF, Gaussians and a neural network jointly parameterize the field, where the Gaussians define its spatial support and provide features for neural decoding, while the neural network enables more expressive occupancy modeling than Gaussian functions alone. We further develop the Gaussian Neural Field Transformer (GNFormer), a streamlined and flexible method that predicts GNFs for camera-based occupancy prediction. Across Occ-ScanNet, SSCBench-KITTI-360, and nuScenes-SurroundOcc benchmarks, GNFormer achieves the highest IoU and mIoU and the fastest inference among the compared single-frame methods. In the experiments, GNFormer can represent indoor and outdoor scenes with only 256 and 1024 Gaussians, respectively, substantially fewer primitives than prior Gaussian-based methods. The code will be released.
authors: Guangcheng Chen, Li He, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses poor Gaussian utilization and limited shape expressiveness in existing Gaussian-based occupancy methods.
Combines Gaussians for spatial support and feature representation with a neural network for expressive occupancy decoding.
Introduces GNFormer, a streamlined transformer that predicts Gaussian Neural Fields from camera inputs.
Reports the highest IoU and mIoU and fastest inference among compared single-frame methods on three benchmarks.
Represents indoor and outdoor scenes with 256 and 1024 Gaussians, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Gaussian neural field transformer for camera-based 3D occupancy prediction.
papers.title: GNFormer: Gaussian Neural Field Transformer for Efficient Camera-based Occupancy Prediction
papers.tldr: GNFormer uses Gaussian Neural Fields to efficiently predict camera-based 3D semantic occupancy with few Gaussian primitives and fast inference.

papers.abstract: Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs. However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression. The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image's meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content. We introduce GIST (Guided Image Semantic Tokenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity. Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. This joint control enables semantic protection: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts. In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to $30\%$ lower LPIPS and $37\%$ lower DreamSim. On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS $2\times$ faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to $5\times$ in the low-token regime. Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.
authors: Danilo de Goede, Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani, Yuki M. Asano, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Pixel-wise error can discard semantically important content when token budgets are tight.
GIST uses a frozen DINOv3 feature space to measure semantic error alongside reconstruction error.
Fixing the semantic target while relaxing pixel fidelity enables detail removal without losing what the image depicts.
On ImageNet-100, GIST improves over KARL at every token count, with up to 30% lower LPIPS and 37% lower DreamSim.
Semantic targets reduce perceptual error faster per token, especially in low-token settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive image tokenization with semantic-fidelity-controlled token allocation; directly relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Semantically Steerable Image Tokenization
papers.tldr: GIST adaptively allocates image tokens using both pixel and semantic fidelity, preserving image content better under compression than pixel-only control.

papers.abstract: Coherent multi-shot audio-visual video generation requires maintaining consistent identities while depicting evolving states and coordinating sounds across shot boundaries. Although dense captions describe individual shots in detail, they rarely specify which entities persist, how their states change, or which entities and actions produce sounds. To address this limitation, we propose Structured Stateful Relational Scripts (SSRS), a textual supervision representation that separates persistent entity and voice identities from shot-specific visual and auditory states. SSRS explicitly encodes sound-source bindings and temporal relations, while a global audio-visual event sequence connects local actions and sounds, including events that continue across shot boundaries. We further introduce MSAV-Script-100K, a large-scale dataset of curated multi-shot audio-visual videos paired with detailed SSRS annotations, enabling models to learn identity persistence, state transitions, and event continuity from structured supervision. Experiments demonstrate improvements in cross-shot consistency, adherence to specified state changes, and audio-visual alignment, highlighting the effectiveness of our SSRS and MSAV-Script-100K for coherent multi-shot audio-visual generation. Our proposed dataset is available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/shenlehan/MSAV-Script-100K}{MSAV-Script-100K}.
authors: Chen Zhao, Lehan Shen, Qilong Huang, Hongyu Li, Zhuoliang Kang, Xiaoming Wei, Jian Yang, Ying Tai
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining entity identity, state changes, and sound coordination across shot boundaries.
Separates persistent entity and voice identities from shot-specific visual and auditory states.
Encodes sound-source bindings, temporal relations, and global audio-visual events that can continue across shots.
Introduces MSAV-Script-100K, a curated dataset of multi-shot audio-visual videos with SSRS annotations.
Experiments show improved cross-shot consistency, state-change adherence, and audio-visual alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes structured scripts and a large dataset for coherent multi-shot audio-visual video generation, directly relevant to video generation.
papers.title: Structured Stateful Relational Scripts with a High-Quality Dataset for Multi-Shot Audio-Visual Video Generation
papers.tldr: SSRS and the MSAV-Script-100K dataset provide structured supervision for generating coherent multi-shot audio-visual videos with persistent identities, evolving states, and continuous events.

papers.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: LDMs support run-time-specified labels, improving generalization beyond task-specific classifiers.
Diverse Decision Supervision trains the model across varied domains, rules, and decision schemas.
Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation uses teacher-generated, consistency-filtered tasks and label distributions to narrow the reasoning gap.
Across three base models, LDMs improve accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, with up to a 182× latency speedup over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B.
A confidence router recovers a median 92% of reasoning’s accuracy advantage on development sets while using 27–58% as many tokens; reasoning remains stronger on new schemas.
papers.selection_reason: Repurposes LLMs as single-pass decision makers with large latency gains, relevant to LLM methods and efficient inference.
papers.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
papers.tldr: Large Decision Models turn language models into fast, single-pass classifiers that output explicit label probabilities while retaining much of the accuracy of slower reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may lose the ability to invoke an old skill from the raw request, while supplying only the correct canonical skill name substantially restores the learned behavior; with further optimization, this conditional execution also degrades. We call these two stages skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM), which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory. At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples.
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Hongyi Wan, Changfeng Sun, Ziyue Qiao, Miao Zhang
bullets: Identifies two forgetting stages: skill-addressing forgetting first, followed by skill-execution forgetting.
Separates memory into a plastic Address Memory and stable, frozen Execution Memory.
Adds a new LoRA executor per training stage and incrementally maps raw requests to the appropriate executor without replaying historical data.
On a five-stage, 100-skill benchmark, achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders.
Outperforms the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 points and remains within 1.9 points of replay-based training.
papers.selection_reason: Factorized skill memory for continual skill internalization in LLM agents, directly relevant to continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: When Skills Remain But Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
papers.tldr: Factorized Skill Memory prevents continual skill internalization from forgetting both how to address old skills and how to execute them.

papers.abstract: Active debris removal requires a servicer spacecraft to approach a non-cooperative tumbling object, capture it, and arrest its rotation. This sequence is conventionally divided among phase-specific controllers, each depending on knowledge of the target's inertia, a dedicated grappling fixture, or a hand-designed switch at the contact-rich seam where such pipelines are most fragile. We show that a single constrained reinforcement learning policy can execute the entire mission, driving a dual-arm free-flying servicer from free-space closing through friction-based fixture-free capture to full detumbling of a target whose mass and inertia are unknown and whose state is observed only through noisy estimates. The enabling mechanism is a smooth proximity gate applied at three loci of a constrained Markov decision process. In the reward it induces the phase structure rather than imposing it; in the action space it forecloses a degenerate grab-and-pull exploit as a hard guarantee; and in the constraint set it resolves a normalization failure of constraint-based learning, in which a constraint spanning phases that load it unequally is rendered nearly inert in the phase where precision matters most. Both the failure mode and the remedy apply to any multi-phase problem of this kind. Over 1000 randomized trials the policy succeeds in 99.5% while holding its contact-force, actuator, base-reaction and collision limits throughout, transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries and centre-of-mass offsets, and extrapolates across a tenfold range of target mass.
authors: \'Alvaro Belmonte-Baeza, Celia Redondo-Verd\'u, Jos\'e L. Ram\'on, Miguel Cazorla, Leonard Felicetti, Jorge Pomares
bullets: Addresses fragile handoffs between separate approach, capture, and detumbling controllers for non-cooperative targets.
Uses a smooth proximity gate in the reward, action space, and constraints to structure phases, prevent grab-and-pull exploits, and balance constraint enforcement.
Controls a dual-arm free-flying servicer using noisy state estimates despite unknown target mass and inertia.
Achieves 99.5% success over 1000 randomized trials while respecting contact-force, actuator, base-reaction, and collision limits.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries and center-of-mass offsets and across a tenfold target-mass range.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained RL for multi-phase robotic capture and detumbling.
papers.title: Phase-Gated Constrained Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End Capture and Detumbling of Non-Cooperative Targets
papers.tldr: A single phase-gated constrained reinforcement-learning policy robustly performs end-to-end capture and detumbling of unknown, tumbling targets without phase-specific controllers or dedicated fixtures.

papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.
authors: Peiqi Jiang, Fan Zhang, Xin Xu, Tianhao Chen, Can Yang
bullets: Addresses alpha mining by jointly using unstructured market descriptions, financial knowledge, historical data, and quantitative factor evaluation.
Agents propose factor expressions, query a real-data evaluator, and update a retained factor pool over multiple turns.
Performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to changing market regimes.
In rolling out-of-sample backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, it reports the highest mean total return, Sharpe ratio, and RankIC among evaluated methods.
Mean total returns were 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively, across three runs.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-turn tool-using LLM agent with retained factor pool and inference-time pool updates; relevant to LLM memory and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: AlphaPilot trains multi-turn, tool-using LLM agents with reinforcement learning to adaptively discover interpretable alpha factors from market text, data, and evaluator feedback.

papers.abstract: Robotic systems for lunar surface operations must act autonomously and preserve their own integrity in an environment where failures are unrecoverable and continuous supervision is impossible. This paper presents a Constrained Reinforcement Learning framework for quadrupedal mobile manipulators that learns a single whole-body policy for tracking a 6D end-effector pose specified in task space, with operational limits enforced during learning through a constrained learning mechanism. We introduce a reward formulation in which the transition between locomotion and manipulation emerges from the reward geometry rather than from an explicit gating mechanism, a stability term derived from the Gravito-Inertial Inclination Margin and motivated by the reduced-gravity dynamics of the lunar surface, and a design rule for reward regularization that follows from the multiplicative structure of the termination-based objective. The framework is evaluated in a lunar-analog simulation spanning three terrain morphologies at five difficulty levels under lunar gravity, with regolith contact properties calibrated to the JSC-1a simulant and varied from loose to dense. The learned policy attains mean position and orientation errors of 3.22 cm and 6.83 deg. under nominal conditions, retains this precision across regolith densities and over the operationally representative range of terrain difficulty, and reduces soft-constraint violation time by up to an order of magnitude relative to an unconstrained baseline while incurring no hard-constraint violations.
authors: Alvaro Belmonte-Baeza, Miguel Cazorla, Gabriel J. Garc\'ia, Carlos J. P\'erez-Del-Pulgar, Jorge Pomares
bullets: Targets autonomous 6D end-effector pose tracking while enforcing operational safety limits during learning.
Uses a single whole-body policy, with locomotion–manipulation transitions emerging from reward design rather than explicit gating.
Introduces lunar-specific stability shaping based on the Gravito-Inertial Inclination Margin and a reward-regularization rule for termination-based objectives.
In lunar-analog simulation across terrain types, difficulty levels, and regolith densities, it achieves 3.22 cm position and 6.83° orientation error under nominal conditions.
Reduces soft-constraint violation time by up to an order of magnitude versus an unconstrained baseline, with no hard-constraint violations.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained RL for whole-body loco-manipulation.
papers.title: Learning Safety-Constrained Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation for Lunar Surface Operations
papers.tldr: A constrained reinforcement-learning framework learns safe, unified locomotion and manipulation for quadrupedal robots operating on varied lunar terrain.

papers.abstract: Image-computable low-level image saliency has shaped perceptual psychology and computer science, but is limited by its inability to capture human high-level cognitive factors that influence attention and eye movements. Here, we propose a new fully automated method to compute semantic saliency by quantifying each object's contribution to scene comprehension without fitting any parameters to human data: the Automated Scene Understanding Map (AUTO-SUM). AUTO-SUM automatically segments and removes individual objects from a scene, uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to describe the original and modified scenes, and measures the semantic similarity between these descriptions using text embeddings. We show that AUTO-SUM can predict which object is most important in a human-measured scene understanding map (H-SUM) estimated using human scene descriptions. We also show that AUTO-SUM can predict the object most fixated by human observers during free viewing and scene description tasks better than a low-level saliency model (GBVS, Itti-Koch), a saliency model trained based on human meaning ratings (Meaning Map), and comparable to DeepGaze, which is trained on human fixation data. We contend that AUTO-SUM can be used as a semantic saliency model that complements lower-level saliency models. Code are available at https://github.com/starsky77/AUTO-SUM-Source-Code .
authors: Ziqi Wen, Shravan Murlidaran, Jonathan Skaza, William Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein
bullets: Addresses the limits of low-level saliency models, which do not capture high-level semantic factors influencing attention.
Removes objects from scenes, compares MLLM descriptions of the original and altered scenes, and uses text-embedding similarity to quantify object importance.
Predicts the most important object in human scene-understanding maps without fitting parameters to human data.
Predicts human fixations in free viewing and scene-description tasks better than several baseline saliency models and comparably to DeepGaze.
Designed to complement, rather than replace, low-level saliency models; code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Uses MLLMs for semantic saliency via scene understanding, relevant to multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Semantic Saliency from Multi-Modal Large Language Model Scene Understanding Maps
papers.tldr: AUTO-SUM uses multimodal large language models to estimate how much each object contributes to understanding a scene, producing a semantic saliency map that predicts human attention.

papers.abstract: With the rapid proliferation of social media, harmful memes have become a growing threat to online ecosystems. Their harmfulness is often implicitly conveyed through complex interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, making accurate detection challenging. Recent studies have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and external knowledge into harmful meme detection. However, existing methods mainly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary information, limiting their ability to capture reusable harmfulness knowledge and underlying reasoning mechanisms, and thus constraining both detection performance and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose MemeLogos, a knowledge-driven retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for harmful meme detection. MemeLogos abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into reusable knowledge units and organizes them into a dedicated star-shaped knowledge graph. By combining structured knowledge retrieval with an explicit multi-stage reasoning process inspired by cognitive mechanisms, MemeLogos leverages retrieved knowledge to guide harmfulness reasoning, improving both detection reliability and interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemeLogos consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detection methods while generating more coherent and interpretable reasoning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured harmfulness knowledge for multimodal content understanding.
authors: Hexiang Gu, Saihui Hou, Changlan Liu, Min Ren, Huijia Wu, Hongxun Gu, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of detecting implicitly harmful content expressed through visual, textual, and contextual interactions.
Abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures into reusable knowledge units.
Organizes this knowledge in a dedicated star-shaped graph for structured retrieval.
Uses a cognitive-inspired, multi-stage reasoning process to improve detection reliability and interpretability.
Experiments report consistent gains over existing methods and more coherent, interpretable reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal harmful meme detection with knowledge-driven RAG, relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: MemeLogos: Knowledge-Driven Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Harmful Meme Detection
papers.tldr: MemeLogos improves harmful meme detection by retrieving structured, reusable harmfulness knowledge to support explicit multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly used to generate videos with targeted emotional expressions, yet existing evaluation methods mainly rely on holistic video-text alignment and provide limited insight into whether failures arise from target-emotion expression, intensity control, or specific affective cues. We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark that controls emotion intensity and selected affective cues in prompts and evaluates generated videos at multiple levels. EmoTrace-Bench contains 448 controlled prompts covering eight emotions, two intensity levels, and diverse cue conditions. Using 12 T2V models, we generate 5,376 videos and evaluate target-emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual dimensions of emotional expression with an automated evaluator calibrated and validated against human annotations on a subset of the data. Results reveal substantial differences across models and prompt designs. Prompts that explicitly describe a character's emotional reaction are followed more reliably than prompts that describe only events or scenes, whereas adding more affective cues or using more explicit cinematic audiovisual language does not consistently improve emotional generation. These results illustrate how aggregate alignment scores may overlook localized differences in target-emotion expression, intensity control, and cue realization. EmoTrace-Bench provides a traceable and interpretable framework for diagnosing emotional video generation without modifying existing generation pipelines, and we release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules.
authors: Yeheng Wang, Liudan Shi, Yi Zheng, Jingke Li, Shiyuan Liu, Xin Tao, Yuanxing Zhang, Guoyu Sun
bullets: Addresses the limitations of holistic video-text alignment metrics for analyzing emotional-generation failures.
Uses 448 controlled prompts spanning eight emotions, two intensity levels, and varied affective cues to evaluate 12 T2V models.
Measures emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual expression dimensions with an automated evaluator validated against human annotations on a subset.
Explicit descriptions of characters’ emotional reactions are more reliably followed than event- or scene-only descriptions; extra cues and cinematic language do not consistently help.
Releases prompts and evaluation rules for traceable diagnosis without changing existing generation pipelines.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark for emotional expression in text-to-video generation is relevant to video generation research.
papers.title: EmoTrace-Bench: Diagnosing Emotional Expression in Text-to-Video Generation through Controlled Cues and Intensity
papers.tldr: EmoTrace-Bench diagnoses how well text-to-video models express target emotions, control intensity, and realize specific affective cues.

papers.abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. The vulnerability reflects a fundamental cognitive asymmetry between human readers, who integrate contextual, phonetic, and visual cues to decipher the intent behind deliberate obfuscation, and text-based LLMs, which rely primarily on token sequences and have limited exposure to evolving evasions. To bridge this asymmetry, we propose PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which combines multi-perceptual views with adversarial self-play to improve understanding of harmful intent as evasions evolve. Specifically, PASP constructs textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, preserving its original context while exposing pronunciation and glyph cues obscured in token space. During adversarial self-play, an attacker uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, while the defender is trained using an intent-invariance reward to understand harmful intent across changing surface forms. Extensive experiments show that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71% and 74.49% on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, respectively, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce.
authors: Yisong Xiao, Benlei Cui, Shiji Zhao, Zonghao Ying, Yaoyuan Zhang, Longtao Huang, Aishan Liu, Hui Xue, Ting Ma, Haiwen Hong, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Targets harmful content disguised through evolving textual, phonetic, or visual evasions.
Builds multiple perceptual views while preserving the input’s original context.
Uses attacker–defender self-play: attackers create intent-preserving evasions, while defenders learn intent invariance.
Reports up to 73.71% and 74.49% reductions in adaptive attack success on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench.
Maintains model capabilities with minimal degradation and interprets real-world evasive e-commerce expressions.
papers.selection_reason: Extends LLMs with phonetic and visual views for harmful content understanding, fitting multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Advancing Harmful Content Understanding via Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play
papers.tldr: PASP improves LLM detection of obfuscated harmful intent by combining textual, phonetic, and visual cues with adversarial self-play.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to hardware-dependent 3D sensing modalities, yet predicting precise metric depth remains a persistent challenge due to intrinsic scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and limited zero-shot generalization in unseen environments. Recent multi-modal approaches incorporate 1D/3D Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) data to resolve these ambiguities, but they mainly treat SPAD noise as a harmful artifact required for denoising or leave the noise ignored. In this paper, we present an essentially different insight: native SPAD noise is an informative prior that implicitly encodes deterministic environmental characteristics. Driven by this paradigm shift, we introduce a novel, lightweight Test-Time Gated Attention framework by Harnessing SPAD Noise, therefore dubbed HSN. Tailored for indoor scenarios, HSN leverages the synergistic combination of 1D SPAD histograms and Gate Adapters (GAs). Through three complementary optimization phases, it generates channel-wise gated attention vectors to dynamically adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, effectively resolving ambiguous scale and boundary challenges without the heavy computational overhead or dense 3D modalities that other TTA methods suffer from. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks show that HSN achieves state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in in-domain settings, while exhibiting even greater potential under zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, interpretability analysis reveals that the proposed gated attention mechanism adaptively shifts attention toward deeper semantic layers under intensifying SPAD noise. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Yiquan Gao
bullets: Targets scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and weak zero-shot generalization in monocular depth estimation.
Combines 1D SPAD histograms with Gate Adapters that dynamically recalibrate encoder features at inference time.
Uses three optimization phases to produce channel-wise gated attention without dense 3D sensing or heavy computation.
Reports state-of-the-art metric-depth accuracy on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks, with stronger potential in zero-shot settings.
Interpretability analysis shows attention shifts toward deeper semantic layers as SPAD noise increases.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time gated attention for depth estimation is a clear test-time adaptation method.
papers.title: Harnessing SPAD Noise: Test-Time Gated Attention for Indoor Depth Estimation
papers.tldr: HSN treats native SPAD noise as useful environmental information and uses lightweight test-time gated attention to improve indoor monocular metric depth estimation.

papers.abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.
authors: Holger Molin, William Peng, Marco Bagatella, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses how to specify what information a world model should retain for downstream control.
Introduces a JEPA framework that trains representations to match target similarity kernels, including physical-state and temporal self-supervised kernels.
Provides theoretical analysis of global optima, linear recoverability, nuisance invariance, and links between temporal similarity and behavioral successor measures under idealized conditions.
Shows that kernel choice determines which physical quantities are recoverable from the learned representation.
Temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel across OGBench Cube, OGBench Scene, and CALVIN.
papers.selection_reason: Spectral alignment framework for latent world models, improving planning in control tasks.
papers.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
papers.tldr: SpecWM steers world-model representations by aligning embedding geometry with chosen similarity kernels, improving planning performance and controlling which physical information is preserved.

papers.abstract: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning (COMRL) has advanced almost entirely through better task representations, which separate task identity from artifacts of the behavior policy so that the latent reflects the task alone. The implicit expectation has been that a clean representation will transfer to out-of-support (parameter-extrapolation) tasks. On such a task, however, the encoder produces a latent outside the training support, where the policy has never been trained. We address this gap with Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization (PLATO), which exposes the policy to off-support latents during training. PLATO assumes a mild manifold hypothesis: task latents lie on a low-dimensional manifold, and out-of-support tasks lie farther from the training centroid. It exploits this geometry by perturbing inferred latents outward from the centroid to synthesize counterfactual tasks. A learned decoder ensemble then rolls out short trajectories at each perturbed latent, and the policy is updated on the imagined transitions under a pessimism weight that down-weights steps on which the ensemble disagrees. We prove that the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by the same perturbation reach, and we give explicit conditions, verified empirically, under which the epistemic disagreement at the perturbed latent stays bounded away from zero. On eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO consistently improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive on in-distribution tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/deephoony/plato.
authors: Chang-Hoon Jeong, Kisung Shin, Hanwool Sul, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Problem: Clean task representations may encode out-of-support latents where the policy has not been trained, limiting extrapolation to unseen tasks.
Method: Perturb inferred task latents outward from the training centroid to create counterfactual tasks under a low-dimensional manifold assumption.
A learned decoder ensemble generates short imagined trajectories, while ensemble disagreement down-weights uncertain policy updates.
Theory: The perturbation exits the training support by a controllable margin, and the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by this reach.
Results: Across eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive in-distribution.
papers.selection_reason: Offline meta-reinforcement learning with pessimistic latent task-aware optimization for robust control.
papers.title: Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization for Robust Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PLATO improves robust offline meta-reinforcement learning on unseen task parameters by training policies on pessimistically weighted, synthesized off-support task latents.

papers.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboCombine.
authors: Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Full-instruction training appears to memorize seen sequence templates: 40.0% success on covered combinations versus 7.7% on recombinations.
HSE diagnoses failures across planning, triggering, and policy execution through a shared modular interface.
RoboCombine evaluates skill recombination without combined-skill training trajectories using ordered-success and transition-conversion metrics.
Failures cluster at subtask boundaries, revealing a start state gap between canonical starts and handoff states.
PRTI broadens atomic-task initialization and reaches 18.16% ordered success under oracle-timed HSE, outperforming the reported perturbation and reset baselines.
papers.selection_reason: VLA skill recombination and manipulation generalization.
papers.title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: Atomic skill competence does not guarantee long-horizon recombination; robust execution requires skills that handle noncanonical handoff states.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host-to-device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per-layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3-30B-A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE-3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE-3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.
authors: Hongliang Cao, Xiuyu Li, Siqi Wang, Ziming Wang, Jingmin Zhu, Hailong Yang
bullets: Offloaded MoE inference makes host-to-device expert transfers a decoding bottleneck, so longer drafts are not always faster.
SpecFit predicts committed tokens from draft-path probabilities and cycle time from subtree size and the experts activated across layers.
It searches ancestor-closed draft subtrees using a monotone submodular expert-coverage cost and also determines when to stop drafting.
With Qwen3-30B-A3B, it decodes 21.6% faster on CNN/DailyMail and 7.0% faster on a GSM8K subset than EAGLE-3, using the same expert cache.
Scope: results are reported for the stated summarization and math benchmarks with an offloaded MoE model.
papers.selection_reason: Improves MoE inference efficiency via speculative decoding and expert offloading, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SpecFit: Not All Draft Tokens Cost the Same in Offloaded MoE Inference
papers.tldr: SpecFit speeds up speculative decoding for offloaded MoE models by selecting draft subtrees that maximize throughput while accounting for expert-transfer costs.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.
authors: Yixin Yang, Yue Wang, Fandong Meng, Zhifang Sui
bullets: Introduces relative long-horizon candidate value to measure within-prefix differences among plausible next tokens.
Builds the RCTV dataset of mathematical reasoning prefixes, candidate tokens, and empirical long-horizon values.
Uses sparse linear probes on hidden states, MLP outputs, and attention outputs across layers.
Candidate-value signals are linearly decodable and can outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines.
An online intervention suggests decoded signals can improve eventual generation success.
papers.selection_reason: Probes LLM internal representations to decode long-horizon candidate value and improve reasoning token selection.
papers.title: From Candidate Tokens to Final Outcomes: Decoding Relative Long-Horizon Candidate Value from Reasoning Model Representations
papers.tldr: The study finds that reasoning-model representations encode how promising different next-token candidates are for eventual success, and that probing this signal can improve token selection.

papers.abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.
authors: Hao Li, Wenping Yin, Fabian Deuser, Jia Jia, Ziqi Liu, Levente Juh\'asz, Fan Zhang, Filip Biljecki
bullets: PhotoMappers’ archive is geographically and temporally uneven, reflecting changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities.
Cross-view geolocalization integrates volunteered geographic information, street-view imagery, and remote sensing imagery with Sinkhorn re-ranking.
The approach achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, with substantial variation across years.
Qwen3.6-27B shows higher agreement with geographic reasoning evidence than InternVL3-8B, but both struggle with localized, place-specific cues.
The study advocates human-centered GeoAI that scales candidate retrieval without replacing expert or volunteer interpretation.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates VLMs on geolocalization and geospatial reasoning from crowdsourced disaster imagery, directly testing spatial understanding in multimodal models.
papers.title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: A decade-long study shows that combining crowdsourced disaster photos with street-view and remote-sensing imagery can scale geolocalization, while human judgment remains essential for ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.
authors: Xin Liu, Yutong Jiang, Jian Su, Ziheng Wang, Chuang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the annotation burden and poor from-scratch performance of VLM reward regressors.
Uses exploration-augmented key-observation gating to identify judgment-worthy episodes and select a low-confusion observation for VLM evaluation.
Adds trajectory-based exploration incentives to reach more VLM reward-triggering episodes efficiently.
Achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL on 12 challenging MetaWorld reward-free tasks and works in 3 real-world experiments without ground-truth rewards.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based reward design for from-scratch embodied reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Harnessing VLM in Embodied RL: From Reward Regressor to Success Detector via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating
papers.tldr: VLMeg improves from-scratch embodied RL by using VLMs as selective success detectors rather than precise reward regressors.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Targets the difficulty of preserving generative performance under low-rank LLM compression.
Uses Generation-Aware Weight Whitening based on gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation.
Employs evolutionary search to optimize layer-wise rank allocation for a target global compression ratio.
Evaluated on Mistral-7B, Qwen3, and Llama-3.3 across multiple-choice and generative benchmarks.
Reports consistent gains over existing SVD-based baselines and scalability to models up to 70B parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank LLM compression reduces model memory and inference cost.
papers.title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
papers.tldr: GA-SVD improves one-shot SVD-based LLM compression by allocating ranks and whitening weights with generation quality in mind.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Structured pruning performance depends on the coordinate basis used for deletion.
The method selects a basis by minimizing local linear reconstruction loss caused by pruning.
Under positive-definite second moments, WUS jointly diagonalizes and balances activation and weight statistics, making deletion error spectrally separable.
A scalable implementation uses blockwise WUS transforms and compact input projections.
Experiments on 8B–72B Llama and Qwen models report consistent gains over pruning baselines across diverse benchmarks, with reduced latency and memory usage.
papers.selection_reason: Structured pruning of LLMs directly targets memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
papers.tldr: WUSPruner chooses an optimal pruning basis using activation and weight second moments, enabling principled structured pruning with improved quality and lower inference cost.

papers.abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
authors: Binhong Wang, Haidong Kang, Yanfeng Zhang, Hong-Ning Dai, Guo Yu, Shangce Gao
bullets: Focuses on smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems where audio-driven decisions can have consequential effects.
Introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) model spanning acoustic sensing, agent processing, edge-cloud runtime, lifecycle changes, and external execution.
Synthesizes attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across acoustic security, LLM-agent, and edge-system research.
Finds that vulnerabilities arise both within individual components and at transitions between stages, limiting the assurance of isolated protections.
Motivates end-to-end evaluation that tracks acoustic influence across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of security risks in audio LLM agents spanning sensing to action in embodied systems.
papers.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
papers.tldr: A survey presents an end-to-end framework for analyzing how acoustic inputs can create security risks as they flow through edge-deployed Audio LLM agents into persistent state and physical actions.

papers.abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.
authors: Weixin Xu, Yifan Liu, Yi Wang, Mingfei Rong, Zhenyu Yang, Zhisheng Zhong, Shengsheng Qian, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving agent harnesses without annotated video question–answer data or parameter updates.
The Questioner generates questions and reference answers from video memory, using quality assessments and Solver trajectories to revise its question-generation policy.
The Solver evolves skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools; executable code-based workflows reduce repeated interpretation of natural-language instructions.
