Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.
authors: Xingjian Zhang
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse is difficult because cached states depend on the prompt prefix, positions, and preceding documents.
SAFE-KV selects a repair start document using risk-guided K2 selection and re-encodes the causal suffix.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, recovery reached 99.8%/98.4% on HotpotQA-500/2Wiki-500 with donor-copy repair and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding.
Unrepaired composition degraded from exact behavior at four documents to substantially worse behavior at sixteen; document-only and fixed-window repairs were less effective.
Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, and in the reported single-request L40S study full prefill remained the operating choice.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache reuse and memory-efficient inference in RAG, fitting the KV cache and memory efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
papers.tldr: SAFE-KV repairs non-prefix KV-cache compositions by re-encoding a causal suffix, restoring behavior close to exact full-prefill generation.

papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
authors: Todd Morrill, Richard Zemel
bullets: Addresses the lack of test-time sequential memory in predictive coding while avoiding BPTT’s large memory demands.
Treats each per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a slowly learned weight.
Derives a predictive-coding-native update rule from a probabilistic model and connects it to DeltaNet-style linear attention updates.
Evaluates scaling, memory footprint, contextual inference, single- and multi-sequence storage, and key-value associative memory.
Reports perfect recall for the tested sequence and associative-memory tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time memory update for linear attention/LLM-style sequence models, derived from predictive coding without BPTT.
papers.title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
papers.tldr: DeltaNet-PC enables predictive-coding models to memorize and retrieve sequential information at test time without backpropagation through time.

papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma, Francesco Pinto, Chawin Sitawarin, Chulin Xie, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Addresses adaptive prompt-injection attacks that can evade defenses based on detecting malicious instructions.
Projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set at every denoising step.
Evaluated across multiple diffusion language model families under static and adaptive attacks.
Substantially reduces attack success while preserving competitive task utility with practical inference overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Policy-constrained denoising for diffusion language models advances secure and controllable language generation.
papers.title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
papers.tldr: CoDA secures diffusion-based agents against prompt injection by enforcing task-specific policies throughout generation.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.
authors: Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker
bullets: Motivation: Repurpose PDE-forecasting representations for fluid-flow control without fully retraining the model.
Method: Attach Gaussian actor–critic heads to frozen PFM representations and train them with PPO.
Evaluation: Test on 2D Kolmogorov flow across two spatial resolutions and Reynolds numbers, comparing against an MLP PPO policy.
Result: The PFM controller consistently obtains higher reward while using smaller executed action magnitudes.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence for transferring self-supervised next-frame prediction features to control.
papers.selection_reason: Physics foundation model for PDE forecasting used for closed-loop control; directly relevant to learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
papers.tldr: A frozen physics foundation model can be adapted with lightweight policy heads for more effective and less forceful closed-loop control of simulated fluid flows.

papers.abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.
authors: Daniel Sanchez, Djordje Mihajlovic, Federica Valeau, Luka Beni\'c, Raghuwansh Raj, Soutrik Sarangi, Snir Hordan
bullets: Addresses ambiguity and discontinuity problems in existing molecular point-cloud canonicalizations.
Selects a unique geometric representative with provable invariance under either O(3) or SO(3).
Achieves approximately 10⁻⁶ Å rotational invariance on QM9 and QM-sym, while mitigating discontinuity jumps on QM-sym.
Runs orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization.
Improves non-invariant model performance on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification relative to that method.
papers.selection_reason: Provably invariant canonicalization of 3D point clouds is a meaningful contribution to 3D geometry representation.
papers.title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
papers.tldr: LexiCan provides a fast, provably rotation- and permutation-invariant canonicalization for 3D point clouds that reduces discontinuities and improves downstream learning performance.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.
authors: Xinge Peng, Zhen Fang, Ruibing Wang, Yongxuan Lv, Haodong Li, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Yiting Lu, Lin Chen, Zehui Che, Feng Zhao
bullets: Targets the gap between visual reproduction and executable, physically grounded world construction.
Evaluates both world understanding and executable realization in an integrated framework.
Includes three tasks: mechanism realization, compositional multi-stage systems, and intent-driven world synthesis.
Experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in physically grounded and causally coherent world modeling.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for code-based executable 3D world modeling, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling
papers.tldr: ExeWorldBench benchmarks how well AI systems understand and construct code-based 3D worlds whose behavior emerges from physical and causal interactions.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
authors: Muhammad Usama, Yeoreum Jung
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-guided layer fusion compresses LLMs, reducing memory and improving inference throughput.
papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FCM compresses LLM depth by grouping functionally similar non-adjacent layers, achieving strong perplexity and efficiency improvements at up to 3× compression.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
authors: Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
bullets: Studies SpikeGPT-family models with an RWKV backbone across widths 384–1536 and compute budgets of 3×10^17–10^19 FLOPs.
Finds the compute-optimal parameter scaling exponent is 0.56, close to the 0.50 reported for dense Transformers.
Decomposes the loss gap versus non-spiking baselines into a roughly compute-invariant backbone cost of 0.16 nats and a spiking cost that decreases before leveling off near 0.23 nats.
Provides a compute-optimal scaling recipe and quantifies the accuracy cost associated with spiking activations.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-optimal scaling laws for spiking language models inform efficient language model design and scaling.
papers.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
papers.tldr: A large-scale scaling study finds that spiking language models follow dense-model compute-optimal parameter–data tradeoffs while incurring a persistent accuracy penalty from sparsity.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.
authors: Yuhang Jiang
bullets: Quantization errors compound because the recurrent state is rewritten at every decoding step.
Tying the quantizer scale to a full-precision reference eliminates norm explosion but recovers only part of the lost performance, separating instability from resolution limits.
Outlier-aware quantization does not resolve the remaining degradation; persistent scaling performs better in the reported comparisons.
Learned bit allocation helps mainly by protecting the first few layers, and group-wise INT4 provides little value at 32K context.
Quantization claims should report the decode horizon over which a bit-width is validated.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent-state quantization for linear-attention and SSM LLMs directly targets memory-efficient long-decode inference.
papers.title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
papers.tldr: Recurrent-state INT4 quantization in linear-attention and SSM LLMs fails over long decoding because scale feedback causes instability, while preventing scale explosion does not fully restore functionality.

papers.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.
authors: Zonghuan Li, Hayley Hung, Chirag Raman
bullets: Addresses the gap between final-answer benchmarks and humans’ incremental, cue-sensitive social perception.
Uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models stabilize interpretations of speaker intent and social affordance.
Applies human gaze-guided corruption to test whether human-attended regions influence model judgments.
Covers more than 6,000 scripted and unscripted conversational clips, with human annotations on a representative subset.
Finds that humans interpret earlier and revise more, while models often hedge or repeat across clips.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for incremental multimodal social perception in multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
papers.tldr: GesBench evaluates whether multimodal language models form and revise social interpretations at the right moments and from the right visual or auditory cues.

papers.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.
authors: Vasileios Saketos, William Reveillard, Alexandre Proutiere, Sebastian Dalleiger, Ming Xiao
bullets: Models online deferral decisions using LLM confidence, expert congestion, and limited expert capacity.
Learns unknown confidence reliability from feedback observed only for deferred and queue-delayed queries.
Uses KL lower confidence bounds to guide deferral decisions across K confidence levels.
Achieves O(K log T) gap-dependent regret and Õ(√KT) worst-case regret, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
Validated on synthetic settings and GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA using Qwen LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning of deferral policies from delayed expert feedback fits continual/online learning interests.
papers.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
papers.tldr: KL-PBD learns when to defer LLM answers to capacity-limited experts despite selective, delayed feedback, achieving near-optimal regret guarantees and empirical validation on QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Rana Mostafa, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad
bullets: Targets traffic signs degraded by environmental conditions and the slow execution of existing deep-learning methods.
Evaluated on GTSRB, BTSC, and Croatian rMASTIF benchmarks.
Reports accuracies of 99.75%, 99.25%, and 99.55%, respectively.
Combined preprocessing and inference take no more than 1.3 ms per image.
Demonstrates robustness to brightness and contrast variations.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on real-time traffic sign recognition for autonomous cars, a core component of visual navigation and robot navigation in embodied AI.
papers.title: RIECNN: Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN for Traffic Sign Recognition
papers.tldr: RIECNN is a real-time CNN-based traffic sign recognizer that achieves high accuracy and robustness across diverse benchmarks under environmental variations.

papers.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.
authors: Can Jin, Yan Kang, Yifan Gong, Chongjian Ge, Mingze Xu, Yuanjun Xiong, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Hongwu Peng
bullets: Organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells with block lower-triangular matrices.
A single full-width forward pass contains the exact hidden states of all nested sub-networks, keeping computation fixed and scalable.
Introduces μE, extending maximal update parameterization so all sub-networks remain maximally updated simultaneously as the supernet scales.
Hyperparameters tuned on small non-elastic proxies transfer near-optimally to elastic families and larger supernets.
One training run outperforms MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, approaching separately trained models with several-times more total steps.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an elastic transformer training method (ShellElastic) with hyperparameter transfer, which is a significant architectural and training advance for LLMs.
papers.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
papers.tldr: ShellElastic enables one efficiently trained supernet to produce strong models across multiple inference budgets while transferring hyperparameters reliably across sizes.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi-view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed-forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per-scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long-horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk-then-align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block-wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block-wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence-aware re-anchoring further mitigates long-range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re-initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state-of-the-art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT-2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point-cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.
authors: Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses GPU-memory and quadratic-attention limits in continuous multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Uses block-wise causal attention to retain local future context while scaling beyond full bidirectional attention.
Detects unreliable streaming states, re-initializes the KV cache, and stitches refreshed segments with SE(3) alignment to reduce drift and trajectory discontinuities.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo; on nuScenes, it improves AbsRel, point-cloud Accuracy, and ATE over DVGT-2.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming geometric foundation model for multi-view 3D reconstruction, with block-wise attention and KV cache re-anchoring for long-horizon driving.
papers.title: Drive3R: Block-wise Streaming Geometric Foundation Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: Drive3R enables scalable, drift-resistant 3D reconstruction for long-horizon autonomous-driving sequences through block-wise streaming attention and confidence-aware re-anchoring.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs. Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.
authors: Petr Senatorov, Karim Vafin, Elena Tutubalina, Oleg Somov
bullets: Addresses unverifiable, costly, and potentially unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations.
Generates computational graphs whose final answers are obtained by deterministic execution.
Uses graph-based reinforcement learning to reward valid structure, correct answers, and overlap with reference graphs.

Across five benchmarks and four model families, improves accuracy over supervised graph training and cuts generation length by up to 5–6× versus standard GRPO and supervised chain-of-thought training.
Faithfulness tests suggest models derive answers from their graphs rather than merely producing post-hoc rationalizations.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reasoning method generating executable computational graphs, with large generation-length reductions.
papers.title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
papers.tldr: Structural Chain-of-Thought replaces free-form reasoning with executable graphs that improve accuracy, reduce generation length, and make reasoning more verifiable.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models are highly sensitive to prompt specificity, while iterative prompt optimization typically improves generation quality only through repeated video generation and vision-language model evaluation at inference time. We propose TIDE, a framework that distills this costly search process into an interpretable and reusable prompt-rewriting Skill. TIDE formulates prompt rewriting as a set of source-conditioned rule modules, each targeting a distinct semantic dimension. Once distilled, the frozen Skill activates the relevant rules and generates both positive and negative prompts in a single LLM call, followed by only one T2V generation, without test-time visual search or backbone fine-tuning. Evolved using only 100 prompts over 14 hours, TIDE achieves prompt-optimization performance comparable to computationally expensive search-based methods. Moreover, when transferred to previously unseen video-generation models, TIDE outperforms existing approaches specifically designed or trained for those models. Code is available at https://github.com/xiningin/TIDE_T2V.
authors: Chengxing Zhou, Yuliang Huang, Jingwei Song
bullets: Targets the high sensitivity of text-to-video quality to prompt specificity and the cost of test-time visual search.
Uses source-conditioned rule modules for distinct semantic dimensions, producing positive and negative prompts together.
Requires no test-time visual search or text-to-video backbone fine-tuning after distillation.
Evolved from 100 prompts over 14 hours and achieves performance comparable to costly search-based methods.
Transfers to unseen video-generation models and outperforms approaches designed or trained for those models.
papers.selection_reason: Prompt-optimization framework for text-to-video generation, relevant to video generation efficiency.
papers.title: TIDE: Trajectory-Informed Skill Distillation for Efficient Text-to-Video Prompt Optimization
papers.tldr: TIDE distills expensive iterative T2V prompt search into a reusable, interpretable skill that rewrites prompts in one LLM call and one video generation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.
authors: Feiyu Qu, Zheng Huang, Andrea Zanette
bullets: Addresses the challenge of satisfying task constraints without degrading DLM capabilities.
A learned anchor generator produces a short output fragment and its insertion position for each query.
The anchor initializes a frozen DLM, guiding subsequent bidirectional denoising.
Reinforcement learning optimizes anchor content and placement using answer correctness and constraint-satisfaction rewards.
Experiments across five DLM backbones show improvements in controllability and reasoning for code generation and mathematics.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion language model controllability via RL-generated anchors is a meaningful contribution to language model generation and reasoning.
papers.title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: AnchorDLM improves diffusion language models’ controllability and reasoning by learning what short anchor to insert and where to place it before generation.

papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses the bandwidth, redundant-compute, and context limitations of text-only communication between agents.
Transfers KV caches across model families without requiring the receiver to prefill the communicated text.
Combined with KV-cache compaction, it reports 40% higher mean accuracy and 4× faster mean wall-clock time than text-to-text communication.
Evaluated across 17 benchmarks, 12 LLMs, and 6 model families.
Can transfer a sender VLM’s vision capabilities to a text-only receiver, while keeping both models frozen.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-family KV-cache transfer for prefill-free multi-agent LLM communication; directly targets KV-cache efficiency and LLM systems.
papers.title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
papers.tldr: SwaT enables fast, prefill-free KV-cache communication between different LLM families, outperforming text-based agent communication in accuracy and speed.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
authors: Pramod Kumar, Raj Kumar Pandey
bullets: Analyzes 600 coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models.
Median observations are small (118–286 tokens); large build logs are uncommon, appearing near the 99th percentile.
Prefix caching serves 98.6% of input tokens, making flat input pricing overestimate loop cost by about 7× on average.
Turn count explains 84% of variance in log trajectory cost, versus 4% for mean observation size.
Delegation raises cost in half of evaluated settings, and the study does not show that reducing turns preserves task success.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes coding agents and focuses on cache efficiency (prefix cache) and loop engineering, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLM agents.
papers.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: Coding-agent cost is driven far more by the number of turns than by typical observation size, especially when prefix caching is accounted for.

papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad, Amr G. Wassal
bullets: Avoids access to training data and model fine-tuning.
Relaxes fixed-point encoding constraints through variable-length coding.
Evaluated on image classification, segmentation, and object detection.
Per-channel quantization reaches up to 6× FP32 compression and up to 1.7× PWLQ compression, with accuracy sometimes exceeding FP32.
Can reach up to 12.25× FP32 compression with less than 4% performance degradation; per-tensor results are competitive with DFQ.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces variable length coding for post-training quantization, a technique that manipulates tokens/weights to improve efficiency, fitting the token pruning and eviction subtopic.
papers.title: VLCQ: Post-training quantization for deep neural networks using variable length coding
papers.tldr: VLCQ enables data-free, post-training quantization with variable-length encoding to achieve stronger compression at low bit-widths while preserving or improving model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Argument structures represent how individual arguments interact within a discourse. However, leveraging these structures to infer meaningful knowledge remains challenging, as it requires a formal representation of how argumentative influence propagates across the structure. We propose Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (NARS) for performing persuasiveness detection directly from online discussions. The neural component employs retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract bipolar argument structures, while the symbolic component applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate argumentative influence over the structure. Using the Webis-CMV-20 corpus, we construct CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions annotated with LLM-derived bipolar argument structures and labeled with delta events (view change vs.\ no change). We investigate whether gradual argumentation semantics can effectively detect persuasiveness, whether augmenting them with argument quality and graph-based centrality improves performance, and whether symbolic reasoning remains necessary in the presence of modern LLMs. NARS achieves F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56 under its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B. We identify support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains as key failure modes limiting attack influence propagation. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of operationalizing formal gradual argumentation semantics over noisy real-world discourse for scalable macro-level persuasion analysis, while highlighting key challenges and directions for future research in neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning. We release both CMV2BAS dataset and the NARS framework for public use.
authors: Siddharth Bhargava, Sara Tonelli, Patricia Mart\'in-Rodilla
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling how argumentative influence propagates through complex online discussions.
Uses retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract argument structures, then applies gradual argumentation semantics.
Introduces CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded discussions annotated with argument structures and view-change labels.
Best configuration reaches F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56, outperforming the reported zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B baselines.
Support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains limit attack-influence propagation; the dataset and framework are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes LLMs and neuro-symbolic reasoning to analyze online discussions, relevant to LLM capabilities in reasoning and argumentation.
papers.title: Have You Been Convinced? A Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning Approach to Detecting Persuasiveness in ChangeMyView Discussions
papers.tldr: NARS combines LLM-extracted bipolar argument structures with symbolic argumentation semantics to detect view changes in ChangeMyView discussions.

papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.
authors: Wenxi Yang, Yuzhong Zhao, Baochang Zhang, Yunfan Liu, Qixiang Ye
bullets: Addresses the costly reliance on curated question-answer pairs and expert demonstrations for training tool-using visual agents.
Uses a challenger to generate image-based QA pairs and a solver that learns tool invocation through reinforcement learning.
Rewards questions according to the solver’s performance gap with versus without tools, encouraging suitably challenging training examples.
Reports up to 7.1% average accuracy improvement across agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and real-world reasoning benchmarks.
Scope: training relies on unlabeled images, while the approach targets adaptive question complexity without human supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving multimodal agent that learns tool invocation via reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
papers.tldr: Marvo enables visual agents to learn effective tool invocation from unlabeled images by using a margin-based self-evolving curriculum.

papers.abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.
authors: Yihang Zhang, Weicai Yan, Qifei Zhang, Yangyang Wu, Tao Jin
bullets: Targets provenance tracking and security verification for synthesized speech.
Injects a content-adaptive watermark residual into the generated representation before waveform synthesis.
Uses focal modulation and dynamic per-bit weighting for watermark decoding.
On two TTS backbones with a 16-bit payload, decoding accuracy improves over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations.
Retains reliable clean-speech decoding at higher payloads and competitive speech quality.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses watermarking for Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems, which falls under multimodal generation and foundation models.
papers.title: GAMW: Generation-Aware Mel-Domain Watermarking for TTS Traceability
papers.tldr: GAMW embeds adaptive multi-bit watermarks during TTS generation, improving robustness to individual and compound perturbations while preserving speech quality.

papers.abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.
authors: Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Frames decoding as maximizing pass@$k$ under an entropy floor and cross-entropy ceiling to preserve diversity and plausibility.
Derives the closed-form rule q⋆ ∝ (p e^{ηV})^{1/T}, where V estimates a partial generation’s likelihood of eventually passing.
Proves that the optimal temperature increases with sample budget k under a natural diversity-scaling rule.
Introduces J-EOS for online learning from binary pass/fail feedback and CTD, which fits one offline scalar with no extra inference-time overhead.
Reports improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines on code-generation benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP.
papers.selection_reason: Optimal decoder rule for LLM sampling with verifier tilt; relevant to LLM decoding and temperature tuning.
papers.title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
papers.tldr: The paper derives a theoretically optimal decoding rule—verifier-informed tilted temperature sampling—and shows how to estimate it online or reduce it to ordinary temperature sampling when model probabilities are calibrated.

papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.
authors: Shiran Liu, Gaohui Xu, Sergio Burdisso, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Shashi Kumar, Petr Motlicek
bullets: Prompt-only ASR post-editing can over-edit correct top-1 hypotheses, hallucinate when the reference is absent, and require very large models.
The method builds three supervision pools from N-best lists: corrections, regularizers, and hard negatives.
Fine-tuning learns a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy and is more effective than random subset fine-tuning.
The clearest gains appear with models around 3B parameters on a proprietary dataset, while CommonVoice results are less conclusive.
The CommonVoice divergence may reflect overlap between public read-speech text and LLM pretraining data.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a fine-tuning method for LLMs to perform post-editing on ASR N-best hypotheses, a relevant application of LLMs in language processing.
papers.title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
papers.tldr: Oracle-guided fine-tuning teaches language models to select correct ASR hypotheses or rewrite them only when needed, reducing brittle corrections and hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.
authors: Fangfei Li, Chenyang Zhao, Long Wang, Feng Tian, Lv Guo
bullets: Introduces TEB, which distinguishes frozen rescoring from context or weight updates using validation gates and held-out tasks.
Uses three frozen 80/20/40 evaluation packs, with coding scored by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace.
DeepSeek’s no-evolve baseline changed by 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across seeds despite no policy update.
Seven of nine text-update cells exceeded their seed-specific baseline bands, but the pattern did not reproduce for GLM or MiniMax.
Positive excess was not consistent across all seeds and models; office and manufacturing packs showed no comparable robust improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark protocol for evaluating agents that update from their own deployment traces.
papers.title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces
papers.tldr: Trace Evolution Bench separates genuine agent improvement from gains caused by rescoring, showing that apparent evolution can occur without policy changes and that update methods are inconsistent across models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
authors: Christopher Solinas, Radovan Halu\v{s}ka, Martin Schmid, Michael Buro, Nathan R. Sturtevant, Michael Bowling
bullets: POMDP beliefs are continuous posterior distributions, making exact planning generally intractable.
BETS represents each search-tree node’s belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE).
The embedding is propagated through POMDP dynamics and supports sampling for Monte Carlo search.
Belief, policy, and value models are trained jointly from experience using the realized hidden state as the belief target.
Across six RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan configurations, BETS is competitive or leading and performs especially well in high-dimensional beliefs, including without search.
papers.selection_reason: Learned Monte Carlo belief-space planner for POMDP navigation and control benchmarks.
papers.title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
papers.tldr: BETS improves POMDP planning by learning generative belief embeddings that are updated through environment dynamics and jointly trained with policy and value networks.

papers.abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $\Omega(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.
authors: Jin Sima, Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Static temperature, nucleus, and top-k sampling can cause repetitive generation and do not adapt to changing token distributions.
The method maximizes sampling entropy subject to a horizon-wide cross-entropy budget, selecting temperature causally from the observed prefix.
EOS loses only O(R log n) entropy relative to the offline optimum and overshoots the budget by the same order; a tightened variant is exactly feasible.
No exactly feasible online method can avoid an Ω(R) entropy loss, making EOS optimal up to a logarithmic factor.
Experiments show EOS tracks the offline temperature and achieves higher entropy than fixed-temperature sampling.
papers.selection_reason: Online temperature sampling for LLM decoding with entropy guarantees; relevant to LLM generation methods.
papers.title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
papers.tldr: Entropic Online Sampling (EOS) adaptively estimates a globally optimal temperature online, improving diversity while controlling plausibility and achieving near-optimal theoretical guarantees.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
authors: Sagar Ghosh, Huy Nguyen, Alessandro Rinaldo
bullets: Derives fast-rate oracle inequalities for least-squares MoE estimators with Lipschitz experts and gating networks.
Dense MoEs achieve rates of order Õ((K d_pr,e + d_pr,g)/n).
Sparse Top-k and Top-p routing incur an additional cost tied to the selector’s Natarajan dimension because routing is discontinuous.
Shows Lipschitz parameterization alone is insufficient to control sparse-routing complexity; linear softmax gating has routing cost comparable to its gating term.
For linear experts, a matching minimax lower bound establishes optimality up to logarithmic factors.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of sparse MoE routing and estimation rates; directly relevant to MoE-based LLM architectures.
papers.title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.tldr: Sparsity reduces MoE computation but does not eliminate the statistical cost of learning adaptive routing.

papers.abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
authors: Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou
bullets: Addresses partial observability and unreliable foundation-model inferences in multi-target embodied search.
Uses MLLMs as hypothesis generators, then refines semantic zones, target cues, and connectivity with online observations and graph context.
Plans via rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear programming with lexicographic priorities for target reward, shorter travel, fewer uncertain edges, and fewer revisits.
Experiments on 100 Matterport3D test cases report improved target coverage and search efficiency over representative baselines, with more balanced workloads.
Its abstract-graph design supports varying agent and target counts, perception modules, and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Cooperative multi-agent embodied search from uncertain vision-language priors; directly relevant to VLN.
papers.title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
papers.tldr: A training-free framework turns uncertain vision-language hypotheses into cooperative multi-agent search plans for unseen, mapless environments.

papers.abstract: Contrastive learning has become the standard paradigm for multimodal representation learning, aligning semantically matched pairs while separating mismatched ones in a shared embedding space. Although various contrastive training strategies have been proposed across negative selection, batch construction, and gradient modulation, their actual effectiveness under controlled, reproducible conditions remains poorly understood. This motivates a fundamental question: Do sophisticated contrastive strategies consistently bring meaningful downstream gains in multimodal embedding learning? To address this, we systematically evaluate representative strategies under a unified benchmarking framework on MMEB. Surprisingly, direct evaluations reveal that most existing strategies offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, with several even degrading overall performance. To uncover the underlying failure modes, we introduce an MLLM-as-a-Judge diagnostic framework that dissects top-1 retrieval behaviors into labeled positives, false negatives (unlabeled valid matches), and hard/easy negative errors. Our systematic analysis yields three key insights: (1) Gradient distortion: Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently hurts downstream generalization; (2) Distribution illusion: Wider separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily translate to better retrieval performance; and (3) Synergistic training: While false-negative mitigation or hard-batch construction yields limited gains in isolation, integrating hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction achieves optimal performance, delivering an average improvement of 6.0% on MMEB with Qwen2-VL-2B. Overall, our findings demystify popular contrastive strategies and provide actionable recipes for training universal multimodal embedding models.
authors: Duo Li, Haojun Pan, Zuhao Yang, Xintong Wang, Chengfu Huo, Shijian Lu, Liang Ding
bullets: Most existing negative-selection, batch-construction, and gradient-modulation methods offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, and some reduce performance.
An MLLM-as-a-Judge framework diagnoses top-1 retrieval errors as labeled positives, false negatives, or hard/easy negative mistakes.
Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently harms downstream generalization.
Greater separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily yield better retrieval.
The strongest results come from jointly using hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of contrastive training for universal multimodal embeddings fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: What Really Works for Universal Multimodal Embeddings? A Controlled Study of Contrastive Training Strategies
papers.tldr: A controlled MMEB study finds that most sophisticated contrastive strategies provide little benefit alone, while combining hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction improves performance by 6.0% with Qwen2-VL-2B.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.
authors: {\L}ukasz Marcjan, Dorota Wilk-Ko{\l}odziejczyk, Roberto Corizzo
bullets: Frames each industrial component as a task in a task-incremental, semi-supervised setting.
Evaluates learning sequences under random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy orderings.
Includes both single-dataset and cross-dataset continual scenarios involving heterogeneous components.
Measures performance at image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization.
Targets knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial inspection environments.
