papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning in industrial anomaly detection, framing it as a task-incremental problem with sequential exposure to new components, which aligns with the configured research interests in adaptation and memory.
papers.title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
papers.tldr: InCLAD introduces a continual-learning benchmark for semi-supervised industrial anomaly detection as models sequentially learn new components while retaining performance on previously seen ones.

papers.abstract: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density. Finite-camera results expose the distinct role of spatial capacity, and transmission measurements separate otherwise identical RGB fields. Controlled training tests and captured-smoke profiles supply mechanism evidence with explicit observation scopes. The results show why rendering accuracy alone cannot certify density: recovery also depends on appearance capacity, spatial resolution and measurement design.
authors: Jianghong Zhou
bullets: Studies density identifiability in emission–absorption volume rendering with physically bounded, independently parameterized sources.
Characterizes how finite spherical-harmonic appearance capacity limits density recovery, while increasing angular or spatial capacity can hide fixed density errors.
Constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity where central density doubles and relative density error exceeds 14.52% without changing any external RGB ray.
Shows that local identifiability can coexist with no capacity-uniform recovery guarantee.

Finds that transmission measurements and density-sensitive acquisition can distinguish cases that RGB rendering alone cannot; conclusions depend on appearance capacity, spatial resolution, and measurement design.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of density recovery in volume rendering is relevant to 3D scene representation.
papers.title: Appearance Compensation in Volume Rendering
papers.tldr: Rendering can reproduce all observed RGB views while still recovering substantially incorrect density, because flexible appearance fields can compensate for density changes.

papers.abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
authors: Jungwoo Park, Taewhoo Lee, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Encoder performance saturates after a few trillion pretraining tokens, limiting the value of additional compute.
Lower masking ratios favor classification, while higher ratios favor retrieval across model sizes.
Distillation with pruning helps classification at low masking ratios but harms retrieval at high ratios.
UltraBERT uses separate language-modeling heads for low and high masking ratios and applies distillation only to the low ratio.
It reports state-of-the-art results on both GLUE (91.0) and BEIR (47.7).
papers.selection_reason: Advances bidirectional encoder pretraining with masking-ratio-specific heads and distillation; relevant to language foundation model design.
papers.title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
papers.tldr: UltraBERT improves bidirectional encoder pretraining by tailoring masking and distillation to jointly achieve strong classification and retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Reliable individual monitoring is essential for dairy cattle welfare and early heat stress detection in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). However, translating raw multi-camera videos into automated diagnostics remains challenging due to disconnected tracking and recognition pipelines and complex physical environments. Dense mutual occlusions and cross-camera viewpoint variations fragment identities, while environmental noise, including camera vibrations, and limited agricultural data obscure subtle heat stress cues such as rapid breathing and flank undulations. To bridge low-level visual features and high-level behavioral diagnostics, we propose CowCare, a unified framework combining viewpoint-robust tracking with spatiotemporal heat stress recognition. Its tracking module, CowTrack, maintains cross-camera identity consistency through a View-Decoupled Aggregation Network (VDA-Net). Instead of relying on static global representations, VDA-Net aggregates localized textures under heavy occlusion and uses a Viewpoint Decoupling Transformer (VDT) to suppress transient viewpoint variations. CowTrack further incorporates a causal online self-supervision mechanism for continuous adaptation to dynamic farm scenes. The resulting tracklets are subsequently processed by TSDF-Net, a fine-grained video understanding network. Its Temporal Stabilization and Aggregation Module (TSAM) suppresses high-frequency jitter, while a Diffusion Semantic Prior (DSP) uses frozen pre-trained diffusion semantics to enhance subtle behavioral signals and mitigate overfitting. Extensive evaluations on two real-world farm benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness: CowTrack achieves 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 for global multi-object tracking on MVCow, and TSDF-Net achieves 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow. These results establish CowCare as a robust end-to-end framework for automated livestock health monitoring.
authors: Xin Liu, Weiran Li, Minghao Zhu, Mina Han, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Addresses identity fragmentation from occlusion and cross-camera viewpoint changes, plus subtle and noisy heat-stress cues.
CowTrack uses localized feature aggregation, viewpoint decoupling, and causal online self-supervision for adaptive cross-camera identity consistency.
TSDF-Net stabilizes temporal signals and uses frozen diffusion-model semantics to improve recognition of subtle behaviors.
On two real-world farm benchmarks, CowTrack reports 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 on MVCow, while TSDF-Net reaches 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow.
The framework targets robust automated monitoring in dynamic agricultural environments, though its scope is limited to the evaluated farm benchmarks and visual cues.
papers.selection_reason: Spatiotemporal heat-stress recognition from multi-camera video fits video understanding.
papers.title: CowCare: A Unified Visual Framework for Viewpoint-Robust Cattle Tracking and Spatiotemporal Heat-Stress Analysis
papers.tldr: CowCare unifies viewpoint-robust multi-camera cattle tracking with fine-grained video analysis to support automated heat-stress monitoring in complex farm environments.

papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved strong results in natural language processing and computer vision, but their deployment is limited by high computational, memory and storage costs, motivating research into model compression techniques, such as pruning, while preserving performance. Prior work has shown substantial redundancy in large language models (LLMs), and redundancy in vision transformers has also been investigated, but it remains less systematically analyzed than in LLMs. In this work, we extend similarity-based redundancy analysis to vision models by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs to identify transformations with minimal impact. We study redundancy patterns across several transformer architectures and find that deep vision transformers such as DINOv2 and SwinV2, like language models, exhibit significant redundancy. We then evaluate how this redundancy can be exploited to improve efficiency, analyzing the trade-off between inference speed and performance degradation under different pruning strategies. Our results show that moderate pruning can yield substantial acceleration with limited impact on accuracy, and that 20% of the DINOv2 blocks can be removed without any retraining, for a 1.24x throughput gain and a 20% lower energy per image at a relative accuracy loss below 1% on ImageNet-1K. We further propose a model selection pipeline that automatically identifies the best pruned configuration for a given dataset, reducing FLOPs by 13% to 27% on average across architectures with an average accuracy change between -0.3 and +1.0 points.
authors: Alessandro Viespoli, Loris Nanni
bullets: Analyzes redundancy by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs across multiple Vision Transformer architectures.
Finds substantial redundancy in deep models, including DINOv2 and SwinV2.

Moderate pruning provides favorable speed–accuracy trade-offs; 20% of DINOv2 blocks can be removed without retraining for 1.24× throughput and 20% lower energy per image, with under 1% relative accuracy loss on ImageNet-1K.
A model-selection pipeline automatically chooses pruned configurations, reducing FLOPs by 13–27% on average with accuracy changes from −0.3 to +1.0 points.
papers.selection_reason: Layer pruning of vision transformers to reduce compute and memory fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Retraining-Free Depth Pruning of Vision Transformers: A Cross Domain Study of Layer Redundancy
papers.tldr: Vision Transformers contain exploitable layer redundancy: pruning blocks without retraining can improve efficiency while largely preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.
authors: Tejas Vaidhya, Gaurav Sahu, Irina Rish
bullets: Replaces 12 untied ICL blocks with 4 tied blocks repeated multiple times, leaving other components and training matched to the baseline.
At matched compute, uses 10.4M versus 27.6M parameters while achieving comparable or slightly better log loss, TALENT accuracy, and TabArena Elo.
A parameter-matched 4-block untied model performs worse, suggesting recurrence—not merely parameter reduction—drives the gains.
Inference-time loop count controls effective depth; accuracy improves across the trained range and remains robust beyond it.
With further training using deeper loops, the model reaches baseline stage-2 scores at 4–5× the baseline inference compute.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent weight-tied in-context learning blocks reduce parameters by 62% at matched compute; relevant to efficient foundation model design.
papers.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Tab-Loop shows that recurrently reusing a small set of blocks can preserve or improve TabICLv2’s tabular in-context learning performance while reducing parameters by 62%.

papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free alignment of asynchronous VLA action chunks; directly relevant to vision-language-action execution.
papers.title: Barrier-Constrained Guidance For Real-time Asynchronous VLA Execution
papers.tldr: FreeBar is a training-free, low-overhead plugin that improves real-time asynchronous VLA execution by correcting action-chunk misalignment with barrier-guided constraints.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.
authors: ZhiYuan Feng, Zhuoshi Pan, Zhaolu Kang, Zhongxia Chen, Shuo Yang, Sen Ye, Heng Wang, Han Li
bullets: Targets harness-level failures where evidence is missing from context or present but used poorly.
Diagnoses decisions by linking action feedback to the model’s actual input and following action.
Uses structured episode summaries and prompt-level edit operators to revise skills and context construction jointly.
Keeps the underlying models and runtime fixed, with compatibility checks and validation-based candidate retention.
Improves success by approximately 10–27 percentage points across VLABench, ALFWorld, and EAI, including unseen task conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Evolves execution harnesses for embodied foundation-model agents from limited feedback; relevant to embodied adaptation.
papers.title: EnactOpt: Diagnosis-Guided Harness Evolution for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: EnactOpt improves embodied-agent performance without changing model weights by jointly refining textual skills and context-construction code using diagnosis-guided execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Hee Suk Yoon, Tung Minh Luu, Eunseop Yoon, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets hallucinated objects—entities described in captions but absent from images—without human supervision.
Uses an Object Consistency Score to measure object correctness and coverage, plus KL regularization for denser guidance.
Introduces a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters while keeping the LVLM backbone frozen.
Reports hallucination reductions of up to 41% on COCO and 29% on Visual Genome with InstructBLIP.
Can also improve caption quality using complementary metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
papers.tldr: A metric-only reinforcement learning framework reduces object hallucination in LVLM image captions while avoiding costly human feedback.

papers.abstract: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $\Omega = B_1^T\Phi + B_2\Psi + H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.
authors: Kiyotaka Kasubuchi, Kazuo Fukiya
bullets: Represents semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on an oriented simplicial complex.
Uses incidence matrices to obtain a unique orthogonal decomposition into exact, coexact, and harmonic components.
Provides explicit projectors, sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, and a verified numerical example.
Introduces an orientation-consistent attention bias built from the decoder’s visible prefix to preserve causal information boundaries.
Presents a mathematical and architectural proposal; factual-error reductions and other language-performance benefits remain unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Hodge-decomposition-based attention interface for Transformers, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention
papers.tldr: HodgePhaseNet decomposes Transformer semantic relations into globally consistent flow, local circulation, and larger-cycle circulation using discrete Hodge theory.

papers.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
authors: Kounianhua Du, Jianxing Liu, Kangning Zhang, Wenxiang Jiao, Yuan Lu, Jiarui Jin, Jianghao Lin, Weiwen Liu, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Targets personalization with sparse, heterogeneous, evolving user histories and query-dependent preferences.
Generates sample-level interference vectors and injects them into the model’s forward pass.
Combines match contrast, attention/MLP activation steering, and query-conditioned signal aggregation.
Validated across text generation and web function-calling scenarios, with reported gains especially in fast-changing and data-sparse settings.
Designed to avoid training cycles while adding limited storage and inference overhead, though specific quantitative results are not provided.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time personalization via activation steering; fits test-time learning/adaptation.
papers.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
papers.tldr: FleetPilot personalizes LLM behavior by dynamically steering internal activations using query-relevant signals from a user’s interaction history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation dose and scan effort, but remains underconstrained due to limited projection information. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based CBCT reconstruction methods rely on gradient-driven densification, which becomes unstable under sparse acquisition and often leads to over-smoothed structures. We propose AD-GS, an Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation-aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD-GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high-attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero-shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi-view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD-GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS-based approaches under sparse-view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD-GS-BMVC2026.
authors: Zonglin Li, Kexian Xie, Feiran Li, Chu Zhou, Yixing Huang, Ruiyang Chen, Zhanyu Ma, Heng Guo
bullets: Addresses instability and over-smoothing caused by gradient-based Gaussian densification under sparse projections.
Models densification as attenuation-aware MCMC sampling to focus representation capacity on high-attenuation anatomical regions.
Uses zero-shot Segment Anything in Medical Images features for semantic regularization and multi-view consistency.
On the ToothFairy3 dataset, it improves structural fidelity and boundary preservation over existing 3DGS-based methods.
Scope: sparse-view dental and maxillofacial CBCT reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: 3D Gaussian Splatting for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction is a 3D reconstruction method.
papers.title: AD-GS: Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Dental CBCT Reconstruction
papers.tldr: AD-GS improves sparse-view dental CBCT reconstruction by guiding 3D Gaussian allocation with anatomical attenuation and semantic consistency.

papers.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
authors: Samuele Doria, Stefano De Rosa, Ruoyu Wang, Zion Leonahenahe Basque, Eleonora Losiouk, Simone Aonzo
bullets: Nine LLM agents were compared with human analysts on two static-analysis challenges using a shared rubric and recorded IDA Pro interactions.
GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3 achieved statistically human-competitive understanding; weaker models lagged substantially.
Performance depended on code representation and workflow demands: richer representations helped open-weight models but not frontier models.
Humans revisited functions and followed local structure, while strong agents broadly fetched information and rarely returned to prior code—a behavior termed “greedy fetching.”
Across 4,000 real-world binaries, context saturation increased with application size and lower-level representations, highlighting the need for selective retrieval and persistent analysis state.
papers.selection_reason: Examines LLM-agent context-window saturation, greedy fetching, and need for persistent analysis state; informative for LLM memory design.
papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.tldr: Top AI agents can match skilled humans on compact binary reverse-engineering tasks, but their broad, context-heavy workflows limit scalability to larger programs.

papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
authors: Vedant Jumle
bullets: A frozen LLM stores experience effects as late-layer activation shifts keyed by a whitened conversation gist.
The method assumes stored shifts approximate effects that attention would otherwise recompute for each question.
Memory is selective: about 98% of unrelated replies remain unchanged.
Facts are rarely used correctly—up to 15% clean recall versus 96–98% when provided in context—and preferences transfer only within a narrow strength range.
The subtraction reference determines preference behavior; without subtracting the opposite, dislikes can be recalled as likes.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates activation steering as persistent memory for LLMs; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.tldr: Training-free activation memories are highly selective but preserve only limited, question-independent information, often distorting facts and reversing preferences.

papers.abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.
authors: Ziqi Ni, Zhou Fang, Shijian Wang, Rui Li, Yi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the complexity and compatibility issues of methods that require architectural changes or extra conditioning modules.
Uses spatial concatenation to inject structured 3D face guidance into the input space.
Supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation in one framework.
Experiments show competitive or superior performance across both animation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Portrait animation with pretrained video generative models fits video generation and understanding.
papers.title: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
papers.tldr: CatPortrait enables controllable portrait animation by adding 3D facial guidance as in-context input, without modifying the pretrained video-generation backbone.

papers.abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.
authors: Erika Hayashi, Andrew Shin
bullets: Full conversation histories are costly and often unnecessary for personalized assistants.
Retrieval ranks history sentences by similarity to the current request and selects a fixed-size relevant context.
On PersonaMem-v2, retrieval matched full-history accuracy with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 judges.
Retrieval performed comparably to an equal-length LLM summary without requiring an LLM to process the entire history.
Relevant evidence was included for only 61% of questions; an oracle using that evidence exceeded full history by 15.6 points, highlighting context selection as a key opportunity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a relevance-filtered context method to reduce the memory footprint of personalized LLMs by matching full history with only 5% of text, relevant to LLM memory optimization.
papers.title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
papers.tldr: Sentence-level retrieval can preserve full-history personalization accuracy using just 5% of conversation text, reducing judge input costs about 20-fold.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM-enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual-inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor-graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM-enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism to create a full Visual-Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real-time on a consumer-grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori-drs/FoundationVIO.
authors: Jin Rhee, Yuhao Zhang, Frank Dellaert, Maurice Fallon
bullets: Addresses the scale ambiguity inherited by feed-forward geometric foundation models and GFM-based SLAM.
Uses a factor-graph approach to integrate inertial sensing with GFM geometry and camera-pose predictions.
Achieves odometry competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO and denser reconstructions than GFM-based SLAM methods.
Adds a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism for globally accurate visual-inertial SLAM.
Evaluated on three datasets with common camera/IMU systems and runs approximately in real time on a consumer laptop GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates geometric foundation model predictions with inertial sensing for metric-scale VIO/SLAM; relevant to 3D perception and foundation-model-based geometry.
papers.title: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
papers.tldr: FoundationVIO combines geometric foundation-model predictions with IMU measurements to recover metric-scale visual-inertial odometry and dense SLAM reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS-denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo-tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up-to-date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic-perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM-free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation-only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure-Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar-PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG-based DSM-free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM-based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV-AVL/LDVP-SAC.
authors: Yibin Ye, Xichao Teng, Shuo Chen, Xiaokai Song, Yuli Sun, Qifeng Yu, Zhang Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of accurate, up-to-date Digital Surface Models (DSMs) for UAV localization in GNSS-denied environments.
LDVP treats perspective-ray scales as latent depths, eliminates them analytically, and reduces estimation to rotation-only optimization with closed-form horizontal position recovery.
SAC uses monocular depth-derived scene structure to choose LDVP for varied-elevation scenes and Planar-PnP for predominantly planar matches.
Experiments report consistent improvement over existing DSM-free OPG methods, with SAC narrowing the gap to DSM-based localization.
Scope: performance depends on matched scene structure and the quality of inferred relative depth.
papers.selection_reason: UAV visual localization and camera pose estimation from scene geometry fits 3D vision.
papers.title: DSM-Free UAV Visual Localization via Latent-Depth Variable Projection and Structure-Adaptive Coupling
papers.tldr: A DSM-free UAV localization method directly estimates horizontal position from image–map geometry and adapts between nonplanar and planar solvers based on scene structure.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Hwanhee Kim, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets the high training and inference costs of diffusion-based offline RL policies caused by iterative denoising and backpropagation through time.
Uses average-velocity modeling with a compositional formulation to learn a direct noise-to-action mapping across scales.
Combines the generative policy with behavior-regularized actor–critic learning using one policy network, without distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computations.
Generates actions in one forward pass, with optional value-guided candidate selection for refinement.
Experiments on offline RL benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks show performance comparable to or better than diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.
papers.selection_reason: Single-step flow-matching policy for offline RL, evaluated on robotic manipulation, fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: InsQL enables efficient offline RL by replacing multi-step diffusion-policy sampling with a single-step, compositional average-velocity policy that avoids BPTT and reduces computation.

papers.abstract: Lifelong learning enables artificial systems to adapt to changing environments. To achieve this, an effective artificial learner should dynamically reorganize past and new experiences, maintaining stability while enabling flexible knowledge integration. However, existing efforts primarily mitigate catastrophic forgetting, lacking the ability to adaptively update memory akin to biological systems. Here, by integrating the full memory life cycle of engram neurons into artificial learners, we propose a framework that constructs a structured memory from gradient representations, which regulates parameter updates and guides memory management. Through comprehensive evaluations on four benchmarks, our approach shows promising lifelong learning capability, maintaining stability over long task sequences and supporting flexible adaptation. Beyond the performance gains, our approach offers a computational perspective on robust and flexible lifelong learning, echoing mechanisms observed in biological memory systems.
authors: Suiyang Jiang, Bomin Wang, Hangqi Zhou, Jianfeng Feng, Xiahai Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the limited memory adaptability of methods focused mainly on catastrophic forgetting.
Models the full life cycle of biological engram neurons within an artificial learner.
Uses gradient-derived structured memory to regulate parameter updates and manage memories.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, it maintains stability across long task sequences while supporting flexible adaptation.
Provides a computational perspective on biologically inspired robust lifelong learning.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong learning with adaptive memory management directly fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Engram Neuron Inspired Adaptive Memorization for Lifelong Learning
papers.tldr: An engram-inspired lifelong-learning framework builds and manages structured memories from gradient representations to balance stability with flexible adaptation.

papers.abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.
authors: Jiahe Feng
bullets: Addresses weak token-level credit assignment in sequence-level GRPO rewards and uniform weighting in standard OPD.
Uses teacher distributions from the original and counterfactual images to estimate each token’s visual dependence.
Applies mass-preserving normalization to stabilize token-weighted distillation updates.
A teacher-supervised warm start stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts.
Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improved visual reasoning and more effective token-level distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language reasoning distillation with counterfactual grounding; fits multimodal LLM training.
papers.title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: VC-OPD improves grounded vision-language reasoning by emphasizing tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence during on-policy distillation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.
Combines two policies’ score or velocity fields during sampling to control exploration–exploitation trade-offs.
Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion policy framework for RL in robotic control and manipulation, directly fitting embodied AI subtopics.
papers.title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
papers.tldr: CFG-Policy uses classifier-free guidance to combine separate exploration and exploitation diffusion policies, improving RL adaptation while preserving behavioral diversity and pretrained capabilities.

papers.abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.
authors: Yuzhou Ni, Ling Chen
bullets: Addresses throughput limits of unidirectional sequence-level pipeline parallelism.
Co-schedules two opposing V-shaped pipelines at the subsequence level.
Uses basic-unit concatenation to keep activation memory invariant to subsequence count.
Combines topology-aware device mapping and communication-computation overlap to avoid deadlocks and reduce communication costs.
Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 report 1.11×–1.13× average speedups over state-of-the-art sequence-level baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Pipeline parallelism for long-sequence LLM training improves training throughput and fits efficient AI.
papers.title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
papers.tldr: BSIPipe accelerates long-sequence LLM training by co-scheduling bidirectional interleaved pipelines while controlling activation memory and communication overhead.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.
authors: Yujie Chen, Weiyan Zheng, Yiwu Yao, Tianchi Hu, Bo Wang, Jiyu Guo, Wenzhan Li, Jingcai Guo, Michele Magno, Haotong Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining predictive behavior when weights use only a few quantization levels.
Introduces Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC): randomized Hadamard mixing and a symmetric four-level quantizer with lookup-free sign-basis decoding.
Introduces Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC), which selects high-divergence calibration sequences and updates only quantization levels and scales while freezing pretrained weights.

Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen show effectiveness for weight-only and joint quantization; on LLaMA-2-7B, it reports 6.62 WikiText2 perplexity at W2A16 and improves W2A4KV4 perplexity from 8.31 to 6.96.
Reduces linear-layer weight memory by 8× versus FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FidelityQ, a quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity while reducing model memory requirements, directly addressing memory efficiency.
papers.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
papers.tldr: FidelityQ enables accurate 2-bit language-model quantization by combining source-adaptive weight coding with targeted calibration that preserves teacher-like predictions.

papers.abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.
authors: Jiajian Zheng, Bin Zhang, Wen Fan, Yanan Liu
bullets: Addresses asynchronous multi-finger contact without dense tactile hardware, using pre-calibrated actuator-load and joint-angle signals.
Builds a 4×20 contact-evolution window from four samples and first differences.
DualExpert combines a TCN for temporal contact evolution and per-finger Stop prediction with an FGFN for finger-topology-aware object classification.
Fixed probability fusion achieves 93.78% trajectory-level classification accuracy and the TCN Stop path achieves 95.25% F1 on held-out trials.
Flash deployment maintains 93.78% classification accuracy and 94.84% Stop F1 with 2.890 ms inference, 9.172 ms sample-to-stop latency, and approximately 0.80 W board power.
papers.selection_reason: Learned dexterous grasp classification and per-finger stopping from joint/load feedback; relevant to robot manipulation.
papers.title: Edge-Native Temporal--Graph Dual-Expert Inference for Dexterous Grasp Classification
papers.tldr: An edge-deployable dual-expert model uses joint-angle and actuator-load feedback to classify grasped objects and independently stop each finger, achieving high accuracy with low latency and power.

papers.abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.
authors: Hao Wu
bullets: The study compares N-gram memory updates, one continually trained shared LoRA, and per-task LoRAs merged into the backbone under matched conditions.
N-gram updates cause substantially less representation drift on general math and code inputs than either LoRA strategy, with drift plateauing after the first task rather than accumulating.
Generic behavior remains essentially unchanged under memory-only updates, and changes are localized to inspectable, reversible table rows.
Memory-only learning acquires new tasks more weakly and suffers task interference, causing old-task forgetting comparable to shared LoRA.
Forgetting tracks representation drift on learned-task inputs—not generic inputs—and follows an exact frozen-head logit-margin relation.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representation drift in continual LLM updates and compares LoRA with N-gram memory; directly relevant to continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
papers.tldr: Updating only an LLM’s N-gram memory preserves backbone representations far better than LoRA-based continual learning, but shifts forgetting and interference into the memory itself.

papers.abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.
authors: Bernhard Wullt, Christos K. Verginis, Per Mattsson, Mikael Norrl\"of, Thomas B. Sch\"on
bullets: Targets the computational cost and limited expressiveness of Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF).
Uses an nSCDF to efficiently estimate collision-free balls and gradients for planning and control.
Plans nominal trajectories that balance path length and obstacle clearance, then tracks them with a geometry-aware funnel controller.
Numerical experiments report paths computed 2× faster, with 20% shorter length and 5× greater clearance.
The approach also improves motion performance and robustness when the nSCDF is used for funnel control.
papers.selection_reason: Neural signed configuration distance functions for manipulator motion planning and control; relevant to learned robot control.
papers.title: Funnel planning and control for manipulators using neural Signed Configuration Distance Functions
papers.tldr: A neural Signed Configuration Distance Function makes funnel-based manipulator planning and control more efficient while preserving collision-avoidance guarantees.

papers.abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.
authors: Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li
bullets: Targets collaborative manipulation tasks involving sequential actions, role specialization, and multiple agents.
A commander performs joint semantic and geometric planning, then decomposes tasks into role-specific subtasks and shared object-centric plans.
Executors use local observations and the commander’s strategy to learn physics-based coordination through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum.
Experiments across varied manipulation tasks show long-horizon collaboration and scaling from two agents to multiple agents.
The method reports higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods, though specific quantitative results are not provided.
papers.selection_reason: Learned hierarchical control for multi-human cooperative manipulation.
papers.title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
papers.tldr: A hierarchical commander–executor framework enables scalable, role-dependent, long-horizon multi-human cooperative manipulation.

papers.abstract: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+\epsilon)$-moment is bounded by $\theta>0$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $\epsilon=1$ can be suboptimal when $\epsilon<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $\Theta((\theta T)^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}}(\log K)^{\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $\epsilon$ or $\theta$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $\epsilon$ nor $\theta$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.
authors: Yuki Shibukawa, Shinji Ito
bullets: Existing methods for the finite-variance case can be suboptimal when the loss-tail exponent is smaller.
The minimax pseudo-regret scales as Θ((θT)^{1/(1+ε)}(log K)^{ε/(1+ε)}).
Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL uses robust scale adaptation and truncation without requiring ε or θ.
Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD achieves near-optimal guarantees in adversarial and self-bounded environments.
With known ε and θ, Shannon-entropy FTRL attains optimal guarantees; the work also proves gap-dependent lower bounds.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning with expert advice under heavy-tailed losses fits the continual/online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Prediction with Expert Advice under Heavy-Tailed Losses
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal regret under heavy-tailed expert losses and gives adaptive algorithms that achieve it without knowing the tail parameters.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.
authors: Weiji Xie, Junsong Wu, Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Xingyi Wang, Zhenhua Xiong, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses the command-execution gap that limits whole-body accuracy in downstream loco-manipulation.
Introduces TTCO, which uses sampling-based optimization over closed-loop BFM and robot-dynamics simulations to adapt input commands.
Across three BFMs on AMASS, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79–84% in simulation.
Derives an approximate compute-optimal scaling strategy to preserve gains with larger test-time budgets.
Generates BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories, validated in simulation and on a real robot for high-level policy training.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time command optimization improves humanoid behavior foundation model execution; relevant to robot learning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Test-Time Compute for Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Test-time command optimization substantially improves humanoid behavior foundation model execution accuracy without retraining, while enabling compute scaling and reuse of demonstrations across models.

papers.abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.
authors: Zonghao Guo, Dongchen Guan, Yubo Wang, Peng Yang
bullets: Addresses inaccurate manufacturer disturbance-torque estimates and the cost and payload of end-effector force/torque sensors.
Combines recursive Newton–Euler rigid-body dynamics with learning of only the robot-specific residual.
Uses only the URDF model and joint feedback, excluding control commands to decouple estimation from inputs.
Trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute without a dedicated six-axis force/torque sensor.
Reduces free-space error by 69% and contact error by 28%, improving haptic feedback and reducing coupled oscillations.
papers.selection_reason: Physics-guided residual learning for external-torque sensing in teleoperation, relevant to robot physical interaction and manipulation.
papers.title: LETS: Low-Overhead External-Torque Sensing for Force-Feedback Bilateral Teleoperation
papers.tldr: LETS enables low-overhead, real-time external-torque estimation for bilateral teleoperation using robot feedback and a physics-guided residual learner, improving force-feedback accuracy and stability.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution.
