We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Satoshi Yamamori, Jun Morimoto
bullets: Existing TTC improves execution by selecting among candidates but requires recomputing this selection at every execution because the policy remains frozen.

The framework uses a fixed verifier to score flow-matching VLA candidates, executes their weighted aggregate, and distills successful episodes into LoRA parameters using the standard flow-matching loss.
It requires no additional reinforcement learning or teacher-generation rollouts, reusing supervision produced during TTC.
On 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling from 10 episodes per task raises verifier-free single-candidate success from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of eight-candidate aggregation’s improvement.
Applying aggregation after distillation further increases success from 76.4% to 82.3%, with gains also observed on LIBERO-Long and distribution-shifted LIBERO-plus.
papers.selection_reason: Distills test-time compute into VLA adaptation; fits vision-language-action and test-time learning.
papers.title: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Verify, Act, Distill turns test-time candidate verification into a learning signal, enabling VLA models to retain and amplify test-time compute gains after adaptation.

papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
authors: Bingjie Zhang, Yibo Yang, Qiantong Liu, Benshuo Fu, Yi Chang, Dandan Guo
bullets: Existing experience-based learning often uses only task success, overlooking the quality of the execution process.
Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL) combines task completion with process quality to provide process-aware feedback.
Paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience estimate how much each experience improves trajectory quality.
Experiences are selected by outcome and quality, while learned utility is combined with semantic relevance for retrieval.
Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, TQG-Exp improves Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points with two backbone LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Experience-based learning with trajectory-quality feedback for LLM agents; fits agent memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
papers.tldr: TQG-Exp improves LLM agent experience reuse by evaluating and optimizing execution trajectories, not just final outcomes.

papers.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.
authors: Yingdong Gu, Haoyu Wang, Shaocheng Yan, Zhenjun Zhao, Hao Han, Pengcheng Shi, Xianfei Li, Qinghua Tan, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Jiayuan Li, Pai Peng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual features and the compact, motion-conditioned states needed for driving prediction and planning.
Uses a V-JEPA framework that injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and predicts masked patches from only those registers.
Adds blockwise register masking to structure predictive information within the register space.
Reuses the registers as future world-model states and shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring.
On NAVSIM-v2, reports a 1.6 EPDMS improvement over the state of the art and 1/10 DriveLaW’s inference latency.
papers.selection_reason: Learns motion-oriented registers as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning, conditioned on ego motion.
papers.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
papers.tldr: MORE pretrains compact, motion-aware registers as a shared state interface for efficient driving world modeling and planning.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal Thermal Geo-localization (TG) provides an illumination-robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied environments. However, existing thermal geo-localization methods mainly focus on near-nadir observations or depend on map-side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo-referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale-aligned local-to-map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo-localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction--refinement--anchoring--propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track-based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame-level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal-Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day--night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame-level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT-only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame-weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo-localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/FloralHercules/ScalLoc.
authors: Xiaoran Zhang, Yu Liu, Jinyu Liang, Huaxin Xiao
bullets: Addresses the limited applicability of existing thermal geo-localization methods to continuous oblique views in GNSS-denied environments.
Uses a reconstruction–refinement–anchoring–propagation pipeline to recover and globally align frame-level UAV trajectories.
Introduces Thermal-Oblique, a dataset of 216 urban and rural day–night trajectories containing 28,112 annotated thermal frames.
Reduces mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m versus the VGGT-only configuration, a 76.07% reduction.
Demonstrates localization with lightweight geo-referenced 2D satellite maps, without digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps.
papers.selection_reason: Thermal UAV geo-localization with 2D satellite maps, supporting autonomous navigation in GNSS-denied environments.
papers.title: ScalLoc: Continuous Oblique Thermal UAV Geo-Localization with a 2D Satellite Map
papers.tldr: ScalLoc enables continuous oblique thermal UAV localization using only 2D satellite maps, substantially reducing positioning error without 3D map or elevation-prior requirements.

papers.abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.
authors: Chenyang Wang, Yuntian Wang, Jiaying Tang, Chunzheng Li, Yang Liu, Siao Liu
bullets: Addresses the problem of full action-chunk regeneration replacing valid predictions when errors are localized.
Uses a history-conditioned action tape combining executed commands with masked future actions to predict coarse action chunks and per-step uncertainty.
Selects a contiguous high-uncertainty span for local action regeneration using executed history and retained future predictions as context.
Experiments across nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks show superior overall performance over several baselines.
Ablations and held-out trajectory analysis support the complementary components and reduced errors within regenerated spans.
papers.selection_reason: History-conditioned action regeneration for visuomotor imitation learning; fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Predict in Chunks, Revise in Spans: History-conditioned Action Regeneration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: CMAP improves robotic manipulation by regenerating only uncertain action spans while preserving reliable predictions elsewhere.

papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
authors: Mutian Xi, Xinyu Su, Xiaohui Zhong, Hao Li
bullets: Operational NWP states differ from ERA5, causing forecast degradation when directly fed into ERA5-trained models.
A source-conditioned Swin-UNet predicts multiscale residual corrections while keeping the forecasting model unchanged.
Its objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with one-step rollout alignment through a frozen FuXi model.
Across GFS, HRES, and CMA inputs, it reduces FuXi rollout RMSE for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with median and maximum reductions of 10.2% and 46.3%.
The adapter also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either model, supporting cross-model transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Input adaptation for pretrained weather forecasting models; relevant to world models as environment-dynamics predictors.
papers.title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
papers.tldr: WeatherBridge adapts heterogeneous operational NWP inputs to the ERA5 distribution for frozen pretrained forecasting models, improving downstream forecasts across sources and models.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the conflict between vision/proprioception before contact and force sensing during contact.
Uses separate experts: a base vision-dominated expert for non-contact behavior and a force-aware expert for contact stages.
Applies a contact-localized curriculum that progressively restores vision and masks state tokens to reduce shortcut learning.
Real-robot tests cover pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping.
Reports 20–40 percentage-point overall success gains over the strongest baseline on each task, while retaining non-contact performance and robustness to held-out grasp heights.
papers.selection_reason: Force-specialized VLA for contact-rich manipulation; fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: DEFT-VLA: Stage-Localized Force Specialization for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: DEFT-VLA improves contact-rich manipulation by using force feedback only during contact stages while preserving vision-led behavior during approach and localization.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text-to-image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. We propose a curriculum-guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent-harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM-5.3-Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng-tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/
authors: Xiaofeng Tan, Jiaxin Lin, Haobo Yuan, Tiancheng Shen, Zihan Su, Rui Chen, Hongsong Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: SpatialCritic uses reusable verification guidance and specialized vision tools to assess spatial correctness in open-world images.
Counterfactual spatial preference data and agent–harness alignment improve tool selection and evidence integration.
A capability graph organizes basic-to-complex skills for mastery-guided rollouts, review, and targeted remediation.
On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic reaches 95.1% verification accuracy with an 8B backbone.
Average scores improve from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and from 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic spatial reward model for spatial text-to-image generation; directly targets spatial understanding and reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: Getting Space Right: Agentic Rewards for Image Generation
papers.tldr: A curriculum-guided RL framework improves spatial text-to-image generation by combining agentic spatial rewards with mastery-guided rollouts.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.
authors: Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
bullets: Addresses underconstrained grasp synthesis without language, target grasps, or object trajectories.
Predicts a time-indexed contact map and hand poses using conditional flow matching, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation.
Recovers rigid object motion via training-free, contact-guided weighted registration after estimating an attachment frame.
On held-out and in-the-wild objects, motion is smoother than LatentHOI, about 30× faster per frame, and preferred in roughly two thirds of user comparisons.
Precise contact closure on novel geometry remains an open challenge.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based 4D hand-object grasping synthesis; relevant to embodied manipulation and physical interaction.
papers.title: Learning Dynamic Grasping
papers.tldr: A conditional flow-matching framework generates complete, smooth hand-object grasping motions from only an initial hand-object state, with faster inference and strong perceptual quality but imperfect contact closure on novel objects.

papers.abstract: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to $25^\circ$. Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to high-speed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot's natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flat-history MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents high-speed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
authors: Huaxing Huang, Ruidong Li, Jinchao Han, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
bullets: High-speed foot impacts create yaw-rate oscillations that disrupt flat-history policies and make direct yaw-rate tracking counterproductive.
Causal multi-head attention captures high-frequency proprioceptive dynamics in the policy.
A heading-direction reward encourages turning while preserving natural gait oscillations.
Skill-conditioned multi-adversarial motion priors maintain distinct motion styles across sprinting and turning.
Ablations and simulation-to-real deployment demonstrate stable sprinting and aggressive cornering, including trunk lean up to 25°.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based high-speed humanoid locomotion with structured temporal feedback; fits embodied robot control.
papers.title: Push the Limit: Learning High-Speed Sprinting and Aggressive Cornering on a Full-Scale Humanoid
papers.tldr: A learning framework enables a full-scale humanoid to sprint above 7 m/s and execute aggressive, high-speed cornering by modeling temporal feedback and conditioning motion style on the commanded skill.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.
authors: Seung-Bin Joo, Alessandro Albini, Luca Wiehe, Perla Maiolino, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Jo\~ao F. Henriques
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by uncertain object mass, friction, scale, and shape.
Extends Rapid Motor Adaptation to bimanual control using observation-action histories and dual wrist depth images.
Evaluated on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties.
Retained privileged-policy performance for bimanual picking and lifting, while stationary PPO without latent conditioning had low success.
Demonstrated sim-to-real transfer on dual Franka lifting without real-world fine-tuning; stacking remained challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Scales latent motor adaptation to bimanual manipulation; fits robot learning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling Latent Motor Adaptation to Coordinated Bimanual Manipulation
papers.tldr: Latent adaptation enables robust coordinated bimanual manipulation under varied object properties and transfers directly from simulation to real hardware, but struggles with long-horizon stacking.

papers.abstract: Evaluating autonomous agents requires examining whether they can translate goals into coherent action across extended interactions. In persistent environments, this requires coordinating interdependent actions under incomplete observations, accounting for delayed effects, and adapting as earlier decisions shape subsequent opportunities. We introduce ASIWorld, a survival sandbox that combines persistent world and character state with character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface to study sustained goal execution. Agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks through direct actions or agent-authored programs that continue running between model calls. The evaluation assesses task success, the attainment of development achievements, and survival costs, complemented by an analysis of execution behavior. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations using a common harness, eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks. Analyses of execution trajectories and performance across difficulty levels reveal different preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar task outcomes. Incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression, while configurations that complete the tasks differ in survival costs and the fulfillment of additional achievement criteria. These findings illustrate the value of assessing sustained goal execution through both task outcomes and the behaviors and costs associated with achieving them.
authors: Jianfeng Lin, Runze Wang, Haorong Hong, Yuxuan Xie, Zeno Zeng, Zhongyuan Liu
bullets: Agents must coordinate interdependent actions under partial observations, delayed effects, and changing opportunities.
The environment supports persistent world and character state, scoped observations, and asynchronous programs that run between model calls.
Evaluation combines task completion, development achievements, survival costs, and execution-trajectory analysis.
In an exploratory study, 8 of 9 configurations completed the production task and 6 completed both production and exploration tasks.
Similar task outcomes masked differences in preparation, combat, recovery, and survival costs; incomplete preparation was linked to stalled progress.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks autonomous agents acting in a persistent survival sandbox, fitting embodied agent perception, reasoning, and action.
papers.title: ASIWorld: Benchmarking Autonomous Agents in a Persistent Survival Sandbox
papers.tldr: ASIWorld benchmarks whether autonomous agents can sustain coherent, adaptive goal-directed behavior in a persistent survival sandbox.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
authors: Guantian Zheng, Lidong Yu, Tianyu Gao, Jiaxing Chen, Jiashu Li, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the lack of inference-time control over acceleration, braking, and following-distance preferences in end-to-end driving policies.
Distills each teacher’s behavior into a task vector that can be scaled or combined without retraining the planner backbone.
Uses a flow-matching decoder to generate multimodal, kinematically feasible trajectory alternatives.
Introduces Style Alignment Score (SAS) for evaluating human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating.
On NAVSIM navtest, assertiveness changes monotonically across six personas while PDMS stays above 0.90, reaching 0.954; evaluated discrete style labels add limited explanatory power.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end VLA driving planner with composable style control; directly fits vision-language-action.
papers.title: YOUDrive: Driving Style as a Composable Direction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: YOUDrive enables continuous, composable control of autonomous-driving style by combining learned teacher-specific directions with a vision–language–action planner.

papers.abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Hui Liu, Ziyang Ling, Ronald X. Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-domain adaptability of methods trained on subdomain-specific datasets.
Uses RAG to retrieve candidate biomedical entities from a standardized knowledge base.
Uses an LLM to select the best candidate based on the mention’s context.
Achieves performance comparable to existing methods without fine-tuning on gene, disease, or chemical subdomains.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free RAG framework for Bio-NEL, utilizing retrieval to augment LLM context, which is relevant to LLM memory and context management.
papers.title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
papers.tldr: BioNEL-RAG enables biomedical entity linking without domain-specific training by combining candidate retrieval with LLM-based context-aware selection.

papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.
authors: Renjie Cao, Yifei Cheng, Li Shen
bullets: Studies single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives.
Derives explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting.
Shows that per-task data, task similarity, and task ordering affect forgetting, with different effects across objective classes.
Neural-network experiments on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST exhibit trends consistent with the theory.
The theoretical analysis is focused on convex objectives, while experiments assess whether its insights extend beyond that setting.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical analysis of catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
papers.tldr: This work develops a theory explaining how data amount, task similarity, and task order drive forgetting in online continual learning.

papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
authors: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu
bullets: The key bottleneck is timing, not visual recognition or semantic reasoning.
Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) describes targets that appear and disappear before processing finishes.
A Perceptual Deadline Contract separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline.
The proposed architecture combines an always-on bounded fast path, active durable-memory capture, and deferred multimodal deliberation with tools.
Measured frontier-model latency suggests answers may take 1.2–9.3 seconds or longer, while evidence can disappear sooner.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory architecture and perceptual deadlines for camera-first embodied agents acting on ephemeral visual targets.
papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.tldr: Camera-first agents should capture fleeting visual evidence immediately, then reason about it later, because semantic processing may outlast the moment an object is visible.

papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.
authors: Tillmann Rheude, Roland Eils, Benjamin Wild
bullets: Challenges the reliance on manually specified scorers such as cosine similarity in multimodal contrastive learning.
Uses a Transformer as the compatibility scorer and finds frozen random initialization more effective than jointly optimizing the scorer with encoders.
Introduces Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS), pretraining the scorer on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model priors.
The SCM prior represents shared, pairwise, and modality-private information to shape higher-order cross-modal similarity.
Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive with contrastive baselines, while prior-fitting improves over random initialization.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Transformer-based scorer for multimodal contrastive learning, relevant to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning
papers.tldr: Frozen Transformer scorers can replace hand-designed multimodal similarity functions, with synthetic causal pretraining further improving their transfer to real data.

papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
authors: Ajwad Abrar, Md Kamrul Hasan, Hasan Mahmud
bullets: Bengali requires choosing ordinary or respectful register, although English source text does not specify deference.
The benchmark contains 2,016 sentences spanning 72 occupations, seven frames, and four pronoun conditions, including one-word-difference gender counterfactuals.
It reports a 0–100 Honorific Bias Score (HBS), where lower scores indicate more even respect allocation.
Across nine models, HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1; occupation explains 3.2%–51.5% of register-choice variance, versus at most 1.2% for gender.
Occupation-level honorific-rate variability is substantial, while only two models show significant directional gender gaps, favoring opposite genders.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark to measure honorific allocation bias in LLMs for Bengali/English translation.
papers.title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
papers.tldr: A counterfactual benchmark finds that Bengali honorific choices in English–Bengali translation vary substantially by occupation and model, while gender effects are generally small.

papers.abstract: Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in S\~ao Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation. Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
authors: Fabr\'icio Carraro, Rodolfo Joel Zevallos, Rodrigo Gon\c{c}alves de Souza, Caio Henrique Faustino da Silva, John E. Ortega
bullets: Assembles a 14.5k-pair parallel corpus centered on the 2023 Portuguese translation of Brazil’s Federal Constitution, plus the first spontaneous-speech MT evaluation set.
Releases the first open-weight bidirectional Portuguese–Nheengatu MT models, with evaluations on constitutional, near-domain, and speech text.
Glossary training and constrained decoding improve realization of legal terminology, though decoding constraints increase repetitive output.
Adding transcribed conversation improves speech chrF++ by 24–27 points without improving written-domain performance, exposing a register gap.
Larger NLLB models help translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu; remaining errors include inconsistently attested legal terms.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an open MT system and corpus pipeline for the low-resource Amazonian language Nheengatu.
papers.title: The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral
papers.tldr: The paper introduces an open, reproducible Portuguese–Nheengatu MT resource and shows that conversational data and terminology controls substantially improve coverage of this under-resourced language.

papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.
authors: Emebet Bekele, Fekade Getahun
bullets: Addresses the information-access barrier caused by limited Amharic Web content.
Translates user questions with statistical machine translation and processes Amharic text using maximum-entropy NER.
Uses normalization, tokenization, stemming, semantic indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction.
Reports 72% precision and 79% recall for Amharic-to-English retrieval, and 65% precision and 70% recall in the reverse direction.
Demonstrates useful cross-language QA under low-resource conditions; the article also contextualizes the work alongside later multilingual transformer research.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a cross-language QA system for low-resource languages (Amharic/English) using traditional NLP components.
papers.title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
papers.tldr: A bidirectional Amharic–English question-answering system combines translation, named-entity recognition, semantic indexing, and retrieval to improve access to cross-language information for Amharic speakers.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
authors: Junjie Li, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
bullets: GDN prefill signals—write gate, decay, and write magnitude—anticipate future KV-entry utility before attention queries are available.
Lightweight per-head nonlinear predictors estimate utility without using attention scores.
The model’s native attention output gate determines the retention budget separately for each attention layer.
After one post-prefill scoring pass, discarded KV entries are physically released for serving.

At one-tenth of the KV cache, GateSight leads KVzip across all four model-benchmark pairs and is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three; scope covers Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next up to 262K tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes query-agnostic KV eviction for hybrid LLMs to reduce attention cache memory, directly targeting inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
papers.tldr: GateSight uses recurrent Gated DeltaNet signals to predict which attention KV-cache entries will matter, enabling query-agnostic cache eviction with substantially lower memory and little scoring overhead.

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
Proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence dynamically select and fuse the most relevant views.
It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.
papers.selection_reason: Motion-adaptive temporal visual memory for quadruped locomotion; fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Beyond Fixed Visual History: Learning Motion-Adaptive Temporal Receptive Fields for Complex-Terrain Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: TempoLoco dynamically adapts visual-history timescales to a quadruped’s motion state, improving locomotion across complex terrains.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.
authors: Jiaxin Fang, Ruitong Liu, Zeyu Lai, Xingyu Wang, Mingyuan Jia, Pingyue Sheng, Weikang Wan, Mengdi Xu, Yuxiang Gao
bullets: Replaces dense layer-wise video–action coupling with 32 Latent Bridge Queries that aggregate visual, language, and proprioceptive information.
Joint video–action supervision adapts visual representations for action prediction, while cross-attention retrieves task-relevant features.
Decouples expert depths and reuses bridge queries, enabling a deep 30-layer Video Expert with an ultralight two-layer Action Expert.
Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.
papers.selection_reason: VLA-style world action model with latent bridge queries for robot action prediction and real-robot execution.
papers.title: BridgeWAM: Bridging Video and Action Experts via Latent Bridge Queries
papers.tldr: BridgeWAM uses latent bridge queries to selectively connect video and action experts, improving robot-task performance while reducing inference cost and latency.

papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
authors: Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang, Kaicheng Yang, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation in sub-3-bit weight-only quantization, especially on real-world tasks.
Energy-Stratified Grouping mixes channels across energy tiers and uses activation-weighted fitting to protect sensitive channels.
Adaptive Bit Split assigns the fixed bit budget between direction and radius for each weight matrix based on reconstruction error.
Achieves state-of-the-art 2-bit quantization performance across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following, and tool-use benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, retains 95.3% of BF16 average benchmark score and reaches up to 2.55× non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16 with a custom CUDA kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Extreme low-bit weight quantization reduces LLM memory and deployment cost, fitting efficient AI and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
papers.tldr: SAGE improves the accuracy and deployment efficiency of 2-bit vector-quantized LLMs through energy-aware channel grouping and adaptive bit allocation.

papers.abstract: Set-based variational autoencoders (VecSet VAEs) represent 3D shapes as compact sets of latent tokens. Although each token originates from a query at a sampled surface location, whether these latents truly align with geometry remains unclear. We investigate this alignment and identify four issues: (i) attention-sink-like tokens that attract queries from across the shape; (ii) spatially periodic repetitions in decoder attention responses; (iii) mismatched normal information in encoder and decoder query features; and (iv) missing supervision of the intrinsic relation between signed distance fields and surface normals. To address these issues, we introduce Align-VAE with four corresponding modifications: (i) a shared bank of learnable decoder tokens provides a workspace for global computation; (ii) distance-biased cross-attention guides retrieval toward nearby predicted spatial anchors; (iii) normal-free encoder queries align the two stages' access to normal information while retaining normals in the encoder keys and values; and (iv) a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer supervises surface values and normal-direction derivatives. These changes align latent retrieval and field prediction with geometry without enlarging the per-shape code. On the ABO dataset, Align-VAE reduces Chamfer distance by 26.6% compared to the standard VecSet VAE.
authors: Huaizhi Qu, Mingxin Yang, Xintong Han, Fangneng Zhan, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Identifies four geometry-alignment issues: attention-sink tokens, periodic decoder responses, encoder–decoder normal mismatch, and missing signed-distance/normal supervision.
Introduces shared decoder tokens for global computation and distance-biased cross-attention toward nearby spatial anchors.
Uses normal-free encoder queries while retaining normals in keys and values to align information access across stages.
Adds a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer for surface values and normal-direction derivatives.
Improves reconstruction without increasing the per-shape code size; evaluated on the ABO dataset.
papers.selection_reason: Improves set-based VAEs for 3D reconstruction with geometry-aligned attention and regularizers, advancing 3D shape perception.
papers.title: Align-VAE: Aligning Attention and Geometry in VecSet VAEs for 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Align-VAE improves VecSet VAE 3D reconstruction by aligning latent attention and field prediction with shape geometry, reducing Chamfer distance by 26.6% on ABO.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
authors: Muquan Yu, Dihan Hu
bullets: Introduces memory lifecycle evaluation through repeated reviews and full-horizon counterfactuals.
Includes a controlled Diagnostic tier and a naturalistic customer-service-style interaction tier.
Measures adaptive-choice potential, horizon reversals, and diversity of optimal lifecycle actions.
Finds substantial delayed-decision structure across both tiers, with many states changing preferred actions over longer horizons.
A learned delayed lifecycle policy improves joint utility over the best fixed strategy on the Naturalistic tier.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VitaBench, a benchmark for evaluating memory lifecycle decisions (compression, consolidation, deletion) in language agents, addressing the gap between retrieval and persistence management.
papers.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
papers.tldr: VitaBench evaluates whether language-agent memories should be preserved, compressed, consolidated, or deleted based on their delayed future value—not just retrieved.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
authors: Pengcheng Pan, Guoqing Ma, Yuhan Zhang, Yang Chen, Yichen Liu, Ziheng Li, Shan Yu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and rollout drift that limit open-loop planning in autoregressive world models.
Uses a strided high-level context channel to reduce global context update frequency and shorten the effective prediction horizon.
Dynamically routes a low-level mixture of experts using global context and current observations for flexible high-low coordination.
On a 14-game Atari subset with 10% offline data, achieves 0.884 IQM HNS across three seeds, versus 0.529 for matched JOWA-70M.
Matches JOWA-150M numerically while using 77M parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive world-action model for decision making with hierarchical temporal abstraction fits interactive world models.
papers.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
papers.tldr: MHWA reduces drift in autoregressive world-model rollouts through multi-timescale hierarchical context and dynamic expert routing, achieving strong Atari performance with substantially lower compute than a larger baseline.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models enable high-quality video generation, but video VAE encoding and decoding remain computationally expensive. Existing methods use stage-specific lightweight operators, yet either constrain spatial and temporal computation jointly or remove temporal computation altogether, without distinguishing their compression sensitivities in pretrained Conv3D. To address these limitations, we present LightVAE, a compression framework that exploits redundancy in temporal modeling and network depth. LightVAE exactly reparameterizes eligible causal Conv3D layers into an aggregate spatial response and a difference-driven temporal correction. Based on their distinct compression sensitivities, temporal low-rank compression (TLR) keeps the aggregate spatial kernel dense and applies layer-specific low-rank approximation only to the temporal correction. An algebraically equivalent folded implementation converts the arithmetic savings into practical acceleration. LightVAE further uses width-preserving block pruning to reduce depth and probe-guided feature alignment, guided by feedback from a frozen teacher suffix, to recover quality after compression. The framework also extends to video encoders. Across three video VAE backbones and two GPU platforms, LightVAE consistently accelerates decoding. For the Wan VAE family, it achieves up to $2.24\times$ and $1.11\times$ the decoding throughput of state-of-the-art efficient VAE decoders on NVIDIA H100 and RTX~5090, respectively, with higher DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS. On MiniMax-H3, it achieves up to $2.97\times$ the original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51\% of the original model's overall VBench-2.0 score. Our code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightVAE.
authors: Shiqiao Gu, Yang Yong, Fengjun Zhong, Ruihao Gong, Chengtao Lv, Xiangyu Fan, Lei Yang, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video VAE encoding and decoding in latent diffusion pipelines.
Reparameterizes causal Conv3D layers into dense spatial responses plus temporal corrections, then applies layer-specific temporal low-rank compression.
Uses width-preserving block pruning and teacher-guided feature alignment to recover quality after compression.
Provides a folded implementation for practical acceleration and extends the framework to video encoders.

Across three VAE backbones and two GPUs, reports up to 2.97× original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51% of MiniMax-H3’s VBench-2.0 score; Wan VAEs also show improved DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses video autoencoders via low-rank temporal approximation and block pruning, directly reducing compute and memory.
papers.title: LightVAE: Towards Compact and Efficient Video Autoencoders
papers.tldr: LightVAE compresses video VAEs by separately reducing temporal computation and network depth, delivering faster decoding while largely preserving video quality.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni, Minming Gu, Tao Zhou, Fuyuan Hu, Fan Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing TTD methods discover novel classes only with anonymous labels.
Uses an LLM to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space.
At test time, Relational Semantic Grounding compares unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors to propose and rerank candidate concepts.
Applies confidence-guided semantic stabilization to refine discovered concepts over the test stream.
Experiments show improvements over TTD baselines, though the abstract does not report specific numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time discovery and semantic grounding of novel classes after deployment fits test-time learning.
papers.title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
papers.tldr: SEGA makes test-time discovery more interpretable by assigning semantic concepts to novel classes using attribute-based visual-language grounding.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Causal action-gain world action model for robot manipulation; fits robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: CAG-WAM uses causal modeling to separate action-driven effects from environmental changes, improving action evaluation and policy learning for robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time.
