Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
authors: Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Weiqiang Hang, Luqing Wang, Zejian Wang, Zirui Tu, Jingsheng Mao, Shaobo Hu, Yang Luo, Jiale Guo, Jin Zhang, Yudan Liu, Zhaokai Luo, Ren Huan, Yao Hu, Chengyue Jiang, Wenjie Li, Chuan Mu
bullets: Addresses the gap between static or synthetic training data and the evolving behavior needed to infer users’ preferences, intent, and future actions.
Converts anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks across 91 templates, retaining approximately 75,000 tasks with selected trajectories.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Vela trajectories improves user-related task performance by up to 11.5 points and general benchmark performance by an average of 4 points.
Additional user behavior data provides further gains, while reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points.
papers.selection_reason: Uses user behavior data as supervision to improve LLM intelligence, fitting LLM training.
papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.tldr: Vela turns real-world user behavior histories into training tasks and trajectories, improving LLM performance on user-centered and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
authors: Rui Hua, Yu Wei, Ziri Jin, Zhuo Sun, Kai Chang, Jianan Xia, Zixin Shu, Xiaodong Li, Dongmei Jia, Fei Dong, Runshun Zhang, Jian Yu, Hao Xu, Haibin Yu, Jiansheng Li, Baoyan Liu, Wenjia Wang, Xuezhong Zhou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating TCM knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, prescription composition, and dosage.
Uses continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, reasoning supervision, and prescription-level reinforcement learning.
Includes 4B, 8B, and 14B-parameter models evaluated on public TCM tasks and a private spleen-and-stomach prescription dataset.
The 14B reinforcement-aligned model achieved 37.0 prescription-generation F1 on the public benchmark and 52.8 herb-level F1 on the clinical dataset, with improved dosage agreement.
Expert heterogeneity affected reward stability, indicating a limitation for prescription-focused reinforcement learning.
papers.selection_reason: Develops TCM-specific LLM family with clinical alignment and reinforcement learning, fitting LLM research.
papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.tldr: Lingdan-V2 is a family of TCM language models trained with staged clinical alignment and prescription-focused reinforcement learning to support herbal prescription recommendation.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang
bullets: Identifies “Flow-Time Starvation”: standard flow-matching objectives under-supervise decisive moments in precise tasks.
Uses offline precision-demand scores to reweight flow supervision toward consequential, observable action signals.
Internalizes precision demand in the VLM representation so the policy can recognize when finer control is needed.
Simulation and real-robot experiments cover connector insertion, bimanual mating, and screw tightening.
Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.
papers.selection_reason: Precision-forcing strategy for generalist VLA policies, improving precise manipulation, fitting vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: PRISM: Precision Forcing for Generalist Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: PRISM improves the precision of vision-language-action policies by focusing training on context and flow times where small errors critically affect manipulation success.

papers.abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"{\i}ve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"{\i}ve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.
authors: Matteo Spallanzani
bullets: Addresses the problem that naive local codec placement can negate compression benefits by increasing operand traffic.
Colors computational-graph edges into weakly connected subgraphs with a unique absolute dominator for codec placement.
The algorithm runs in linear time with respect to the source graph size.
Modeled operand traffic is reduced by 24%–44% across four models versus naive local placement, including 24% on SigLIP and 34% on SmolLM2.
Scope: results are based on modeled operand traffic and target hardware compatibility, as described in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a linear-time algorithm for codec operator placement to reduce operand traffic, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
papers.tldr: A linear-time graph algorithm places compression codecs at absolute dominators to preserve operand-traffic savings for on-device inference.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search-and-rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross-altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal-dispatching paradigms, ignoring high-altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low-altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC-Nav, a training-free cross-altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high-altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task-conditioned priors, which the low-altitude agent incorporates into decision-making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC-Nav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC-Nav.
authors: Jiuwu Hao, Yueyang Wu, Liguo Sun, Haolin Song, Zao Zhang, Pin Lv
bullets: Addresses outdoor UAV search-and-rescue challenges caused by partial observability and uncertain high-altitude observations.
Uses a Global Belief Memory on the high-altitude UAV to provide task-conditioned priors.
The low-altitude UAV integrates this guidance through Local Exhaustion Memory, Local Attraction Augmentation, and Directional Belief Prior.
Treats high-altitude information as an advisory bias rather than a rigid goal assignment, preserving low-altitude autonomy.
Experiments on ESARBench report consistent improvements over existing single-agent and collaborative methods.ﬁ
papers.selection_reason: Cross-altitude multi-UAV collaborative navigation with belief-guided coupling, fitting aerial VLN and robot navigation.
papers.title: BGC-Nav: Cross-Altitude Multi-UAV Collaborative Navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling
papers.tldr: BGC-Nav enables training-free cross-altitude multi-UAV navigation by using high-altitude beliefs as flexible guidance for low-altitude exploration under partial observability.

papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
authors: Nan Wu, Yee Hung Hong
bullets: Addresses the tension between explicit surface-motion supervision and preserving a pretrained video generator’s appearance prior.
Combines confidence-weighted track/visibility prediction, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad on shared LoRA parameters.
Preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects the primary flow-matching update during adaptation.
Improves aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error by 9.7% versus a matched control, with near-matched performance across six VBench dimensions.
Tracking improvements are heterogeneous across seeds, and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022; video quality is not uniformly improved.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptation of a text-to-video diffusion transformer with point correspondence supervision directly targets video diffusion.
papers.title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
papers.tldr: AcrossVAM2.0 uses conflict-aware point supervision and parameter-efficient adaptation to improve video correspondence consistency while largely preserving pretrained video quality, though FVD worsens and tracking gains vary by seed.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Zihan Gao, Yuhong Zhang, Mengzhe Wang, Kaisheng Liu, Shengpeng Li, Siyao Xiao, Runqing Cheng, Xiao Lin, Zhifang Liu, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the need for expensive, manually teleoperated demonstrations in dexterous imitation learning.
Uses joint 3D hand-object interaction reconstructions from monocular RGB-D videos as learning input.
Introduces the DexHand Motion Perception Module to encode inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies.
Conditions a diffusion policy on these compact motion representations to generate future robot actions.
Real-world experiments show strong performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Learns dexterous robot control from human videos, fitting robot learning and human video learning.
papers.title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
papers.tldr: DexCast learns dexterous robot control directly from monocular RGB-D human videos, avoiding costly teleoperation through joint HOI reconstruction and diffusion-based action generation.

papers.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
authors: Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao
bullets: Targets prefix-heavy workflows where multiple models share long contexts such as schemas, tools, histories, and intermediate results.
Combines partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads to enable accurate cross-model reuse.
Uses block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel to make attention-map reuse practical for long contexts.
Experiments report lower prefilling latency and better end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous models and multi-turn workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents cross-model attention map reuse for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
papers.tldr: MapFlow accelerates heterogeneous LLM serving by reusing transferable attention maps instead of model-specific KV states.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.
authors: Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang
bullets: Addresses cross-trajectory inconsistency in existing novel-view video synthesis methods.
Combines appearance diffusion, memory-consistent depth completion, dual-stream warping, and geometry-aware refinement.
Supports coherent spatiotemporal reconstruction across dense multi-view camera trajectories.
Handles large-parallax motion, including 180° rotations without input-view overlap.
Produces geometry-faithful videos that can be optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive video rerendering with 4D memory for navigable worlds; fits world models, video generation, and 3D vision.
papers.title: Demiurge: Forging Navigable 4D Worlds via Autoregressive Video Rerendering
papers.tldr: Demiurge builds coherent, navigable 4D worlds from a single video by autoregressively rerendering novel views with a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.
authors: Hieu D. Pham, Quoc-An Luong, Dung D. Le
bullets: Introduces VLN-Safe, a benchmark comparing sliding evaluation with blocking evaluation that prevents motion after collisions.
Across six agents on R2R-CE, 38.5–56.8% of successful sliding episodes involve contact; blocking lowers success by 11.7–36.1 percentage points.
Depth geometry and recent movement history better predict imminent collisions than policy-derived signals, while nearby safe alternatives are uncommon.
The training-free guard vetoes risky forward actions, performs an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy.

Across five agents, it reduces collision steps by 62–98% and improves blocking success by 6.9–29.3 points; under sliding, collision-free successes increase by 4.1–12.4 points without changing success rate.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes collision safety in VLN and proposes a training-free collision guard, directly fitting vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Successful but Unsafe: An Analytical Benchmark for Revealing Collisions in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: VLN agents can succeed while frequently colliding, but a lightweight collision guard substantially improves safety and often navigation success.

papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.
authors: Pushp Garg, Himangshu Sarma, Mrinmoy Ghorai
bullets: Addresses variable signing speeds, complex spatial structure, and limited large-vocabulary ISL benchmarks.
Uses entropy-driven SVD sampling to retain informative keyframes and reduce computational redundancy.
Models irregular temporal gaps with Continuous Dual Positional Encoding and a distance-aware Elastic Transformer.
Captures bimanual geometry through a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN with unified bone-joint features.
Introduces a 9,453-video, 120-class native ISL dataset and reports 89.8% accuracy, with scope focused on gloss recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Sign language recognition from video with temporal and kinematic modeling fits video understanding.
papers.title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
papers.tldr: A structurally aware hybrid model efficiently recognizes 120-class Indian Sign Language by combining informative keyframe sampling, irregular-time modeling, and bimanual kinematic graph reasoning.

papers.abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers six dimensions: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose.
Questions target quantities such as depth, interpersonal distance, gaze angle, velocity, trajectories, blink count, and contact-deformation strength.
Labels are generated programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state rather than human annotation or model estimation.
The benchmark includes a training corpus produced by the same pipeline and evaluates both open- and closed-source MLLMs.
Results indicate that all six dimensions remain challenging and are only partially dissociable for current MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for human-centric physical and spatial perception in MLLMs; fits spatial intelligence and video understanding.
papers.title: HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: HumanPhys benchmarks whether multimodal models can infer physically grounded human- and camera-related quantities from real-world visual inputs.

papers.abstract: We present CAST-ASD (Causal Attention over Speakers and Time), a causal joint model for active speaker detection (ASD). Recent ASD models improve performance by jointly processing all faces in a scene, but operate offline, with the full clip available before any frame is labelled. Low-latency causal detectors instead process each face independently. CAST-ASD combines joint face reasoning with fully causal inference. It applies scene-level attention across faces within the current frame and causal temporal attention over each face's history, enabling information sharing across speakers with zero lookahead. Its parameter count does not grow with the number of faces. On MSDWild, where most negative face-frames contain a visible competing speaker, CAST-ASD reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% relative to the causal per-face detector it extends, with larger gains as scene occupancy increases. It outperforms all causal baselines on both validation splits while using only one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a three-block fixed-roster convolution. Code and models are available at https://github.com/prathamg007/CAST-ASD.
authors: Pratham Gupta, Haotian Qi, Tushar Sandhan, Gabriel Skantze
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between offline joint models and causal per-face detectors.
Uses scene-level attention across faces in the current frame and causal temporal attention for each face.
Keeps parameter count independent of the number of faces.
On MSDWild, reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% versus its causal per-face baseline, with larger gains in more crowded scenes.
Outperforms causal baselines on both validation splits while using one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a fixed-roster convolution model.
papers.selection_reason: Causal joint attention for online active speaker detection; fits video understanding.
papers.title: CAST-ASD: Causal Attention over Speakers and Time for Online Active Speaker Detection
papers.tldr: CAST-ASD enables low-latency active speaker detection by jointly reasoning across faces and causal temporal histories without looking ahead.

papers.abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.
authors: Tiantian Liu, Meng Wan, Zhiqiang Liang, Jue Wang, Ningming Nie, Yangang Wang
bullets: Existing methods use a fixed competition domain for every attention head, despite head heterogeneity.
EG-Sparse routes low-entropy heads to grouped cross-head selection while keeping high-entropy heads on per-row local selection.
A controlled diagnostic found grouped selection reduced low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, while global pooling increased high-entropy-head error by 7.9%.
Across four configurations, the method improved video quality while lowering attention density and GPU denoising latency versus strong training-free baselines.
Ablations favored selective domain adaptation over uniform, random, and fixed assignment policies.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for video diffusion transformers; fits efficient attention and video diffusion.
papers.title: Competition Domains Matter: Selective Head Globalization for Training-Free Sparse Attention in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: EG-Sparse improves training-free sparse attention for video diffusion by adapting the token-selection competition domain to each head’s entropy.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.
authors: Senbin Xu, Zijun Zhang, Xinhua Wu, Li He, Jubo Feng, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Yan Zhang, Jixiang Luo, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses the challenge of balancing recent observations with potentially useful—but distracting—historical context.
Uses a lightweight gate to determine whether additional evidence is needed, then retrieves relevant past clips with a multimodal embedding model.
Trains the model to jointly use current and retrieved evidence and abstain when evidence remains insufficient.
Shares a visual encoder across understanding and retrieval branches, with separate language backbones and distillation-based adapters.
With visual-only inputs, reaches 77.78% on evaluated OVO-Bench tasks and 73.31% on StreamingBench; the abstract reports gains over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 2 fps.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video QA with adaptive historical retrieval; fits video understanding.
papers.title: SPARE: Shared Perception and Adaptive Retrieval of Evidence for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: SPARE improves streaming video question answering by adaptively retrieving historical clips only when recent frames are insufficient, while sharing visual features between perception and retrieval.

papers.abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.
authors: Chengzhen Wu, Kelei Liu, Sicheng Li, Lu Yu, Yiyi Liao
bullets: Addresses 4DGS storage overhead and the slow, scene-specific nature of prior compression methods.
Uses importance-based adaptive quantization to allocate bitrate according to Gaussian importance.
Introduces motion- and importance-aware packing that reorganizes attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps.
Leverages existing image and video codecs for post-training compression without per-scene optimization.
Compresses 4DGS in seconds while maintaining high quality, supporting practical deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training compression of 4D Gaussian splatting; relevant to 3D scene representation and efficient storage.
papers.title: TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: TETRIS-4DGS enables fast, generalized compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting with over 40× storage reduction while preserving high rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.
authors: Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
bullets: Addresses feature-caching failures caused by large changes between the few remaining denoising steps.
Uses an Anchor-Transport-Correct predictor combining the current chunk’s preceding-step features with the previous chunk’s same-timestep features.
Applies spatial retrieval and adaptive correction to improve velocity prediction across large denoising gaps.
Trains on its own autoregressive rollouts to reduce error accumulation across denoising steps and video chunks.
Evaluated on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay; on Self Forcing, it generates 333-frame videos from 81-frame training videos while exceeding the original model’s VBench score.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates autoregressive video diffusion via historical trajectory guidance; fits video diffusion, autoregressive video, and efficiency.
papers.title: TGuide: Faster Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Historical Trajectory Guidance
papers.tldr: TGuide accelerates 4-step autoregressive video diffusion by guiding feature prediction with historical trajectories, achieving up to 1.89× denoising speedups while preserving or improving quality.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts. To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.
authors: Yifan Shen, Yewei Xia, Gongxu Luo, Peiyuan Zhu, Boyang Sun, Zhenhao Chen, Guangyi Liu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation in long video rollouts caused by training only on the immediate next chunk.
Uses lightweight, offset-specific prediction heads sharing the rolling-window generator’s conditioning information.
Extends supervision to multiple future offsets so representations retain longer-range predictive information.
Accelerates inference by accepting verified future predictions, while falling back to standard generation when candidates are rejected.
Supports multiple next-chunk candidates via learnable embeddings and a learned verifier.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses autoregressive long video diffusion with multi-head future prediction and sampling acceleration.
papers.title: Prospective Forcing: Learning to Look Ahead for Autoregressive Long Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: Prospective Forcing trains autoregressive video generators to anticipate multiple future chunks, improving long-horizon consistency while enabling faster inference through candidate verification and skipping.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.
authors: Yaoxiang Wang, Kai Zhang, Ruobing Xie, Lanrui Wang, Guoliang Zhao, Junhui Li, Jinsong Su
bullets: MoE expert geometry is made explicit by computing expert transformations in a lower-dimensional latent space.
An expert’s local Jacobian rank is bounded by its input dimension and intermediate width; balancing these dimensions maximizes the rank ceiling for a fixed parameter budget.
Controlled experiments across model scales and routing granularities favor near-square expert shapes.

Intrinsic-dimension-guided layerwise allocation, while holding per-layer parameters, activated FLOPs, and communication constant, improves validation loss and downstream performance over homogeneous baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation in MoE LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentMoE shows that expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation are key design choices for improving mixture-of-experts models.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.
authors: Xinhao Wang, Junbo Cui, Zhenghao Liu, Yuan Yao, Xiaohua Li, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Introduces Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH), a failure mode combining false textual premises with visually confusable evidence.
Provides PVFH-Bench, which automatically constructs absent but visually plausible target objects and diagnostic subsets.
Evaluates 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs and finds all are highly vulnerable to PVFH.
Reports that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can worsen the problem by amplifying weak visual cues.
Targets reliability concerns in visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and analysis of hallucination in LVLMs, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reliability.
papers.title: PVFH-Bench: Benchmarking Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PVFH-Bench reveals that vision-language models can be anchored by false premises and weakly confusable visual cues, causing them to hallucinate absent objects—especially when using explicit chain-of-thought reasoning.

papers.abstract: Continuous indoor-outdoor navigation connects destination-level reasoning with motion decisions that must respond to current observations. We present VbotNav-0, a cloud-edge dual-policy framework that links these processes through asynchronous policy-to-policy conditioning. The cloud policy produces subgoal guidance from visual history, navigation instructions, and route tokens; the edge policy combines available guidance with current RGB and LiDAR observations to generate local trajectories. This formulation allows the local perception-action loop to continue between cloud updates. A common route representation connects indoor paths and outdoor map routes, and the training recipe combines navigation demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded visual question answering (VQA). In the reported closed-loop evaluation of 258 episodes across 145 scenes, VbotNav-0 achieves 55.04% success rate and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
authors: Shiqi Tan, Yujun Zhang, Keyu Li, Shuaixi Pan, Siyu Zhou, Hailong Qin, Yinan Yu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking destination-level reasoning with observation-driven motion across indoor and outdoor environments.
Uses a cloud policy for subgoal guidance from visual history, instructions, and route tokens, while an edge policy generates trajectories from guidance, RGB, and LiDAR.
Asynchronous policy conditioning lets local perception and action continue between cloud updates.
A shared route representation connects indoor paths with outdoor map routes; training combines demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded VQA.
In closed-loop evaluation across 258 episodes and 145 scenes, it reports 55.04% success and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
papers.selection_reason: Cloud-edge dual-policy navigation using visual history and instructions, fitting vision-language navigation and robot navigation.
papers.title: VbotNav-0: Asynchronous Cloud-Edge Dual-Policy Navigation across Indoor and Outdoor Environments
papers.tldr: VbotNav-0 enables continuous indoor–outdoor navigation by asynchronously combining cloud-based subgoal planning with edge-based local control.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a route to AI systems that participate in their own continued development. Recent methods allow language agents to retain changes to their parameters, memory, skills, and code for subsequent execution and improvement. We examine how these methods can inform new research ideas through two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy with nine design dimensions organized into four groups: update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, feedback and selection. This taxonomy places existing methods in a shared design space, where examining individual dimensions and their interactions can inspire new research ideas. Second, we examine how existing RSI methods draw on traditional deep learning, for example through optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. We develop further ideas by examining more specific learning mechanisms and drawing on evolutionary computation. We also review how existing benchmarks assess self-improvement under online, offline, and offline-to-online settings. Together, these perspectives help researchers develop new RSI research ideas from existing designs and learning mechanisms. RSI papers and resources are available at https://prism-shadow.github.io/awesome-rsi/.
authors: Leijun Zhou, Yanke Yu, Zhihao Liu, Qu Xiang, Tiancheng Hu, Yiru Dong, Yihan Wu, Yangxi Xiang, Xuejun Wu, Xi Chen, Buyue Qian, Yaowei Zheng, Junhao Hu
bullets: Introduces a taxonomy spanning nine RSI design dimensions across update targets, organization, scheduling/scope, and feedback/selection.
Uses the taxonomy to position existing methods in a shared design space and identify promising combinations.
Relates RSI techniques to deep-learning ideas such as optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning.
Draws additional research ideas from specific learning mechanisms and evolutionary computation.
Reviews benchmarks for online, offline, and offline-to-online self-improvement settings.
papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and analysis of recursive self-improvement spanning continual learning and agent memory; relevant to adaptation and memory.
papers.title: From Existing Methods to New Research Ideas: Two Perspectives on Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: The paper organizes recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods into a unified design framework and connects them to established learning mechanisms to generate new research directions.

papers.abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.
authors: Haodong Chen, Shengtao Wen, Dong Liang, Lingbing Guo, Xiang Chen
bullets: Addresses confabulation and hidden knowledge that surface-level refusal evaluations can miss.
Uses a behavior channel to distill refusals from an ignorance-prompted model copy, masking target tokens to prevent reteaching.
Uses a knowledge channel to directly suppress ground-truth answer spans independently of generated responses.
Experiments show reduced target-information leakage, effective unlearning, and preserved performance on retained data.
Scope: targets honest ignorance rather than refusal behavior alone; code and data are planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM unlearning separating knowledge forgetting from refusal behavior; relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
papers.tldr: FASD decouples knowledge erasure from refusal learning to make multimodal models genuinely forget target information while honestly acknowledging what they do not know.

papers.abstract: In this work, we aim to develop an embodied MLLM agent that understands and solves embodied tasks by learning, abstracting, and reusing transferrable and generalizable behavioral patterns. To this end, we propose StateSkill, a new skill representation for embodied agents, which introduces the concept of "finite-state machines" into skill modeling for effective and efficient skill construction and learning. The core idea of StateSkill is to model embodied interaction experiences as a finite-state machine, where a skill is organized around a set of task-progress states, state transitions, and state-conditioned guidance, enabling embodied agents to dynamically adjust their skills as the task progresses while keeping skill contexts compact and stage-relevant. We further develop StateSkill-Evolve, an experience-driven evolution mechanism that iteratively refines StateSkill through retrospective analysis of new successful and failed state-guided trajectories. Upon this, we introduce StateGRPO, which integrates StateSkill evolution and model optimization via state-conditioned GRPO into a unified iterative learning loop, enabling state-conditioned skills and model capabilities to co-evolve and reinforce each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods and trained model (i.e., StateSkill-Agent) across various embodied tasks.
authors: Changxu Wei, Jingyi Zhang, Zhiyu Zheng, Tianyi Lin, Yixian Zhang, Yunpeng Qing, Jingyuan Liu, Zhi Hou, Jiaxing Huang
bullets: Motivation: Embodied agents need transferable, generalizable behavioral patterns while keeping skill context efficient.
StateSkill represents skills with task-progress states, transitions, and state-conditioned guidance for dynamic, stage-relevant behavior.
StateSkill-Evolve refines skills by retrospectively analyzing successful and failed state-guided trajectories.
StateGRPO combines skill evolution with state-conditioned policy optimization in an iterative co-evolution loop.
Experiments report effectiveness across various embodied tasks, though specific results and scope details are not provided.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a state-conditioned skill representation and evolution for embodied MLLM agents, fitting vision-language-action.
papers.title: StateSkill-Agent: An Effective and Efficient Embodied Agent via State-conditioned Skill
papers.tldr: StateSkill-Agent improves embodied MLLM agents by organizing reusable skills as finite-state, task-progress-aware structures that evolve through experience and jointly optimize the model.

papers.abstract: Navigating cluttered environments while carrying objects remains a challenging problem for quadruped robots. Compared with works that focused on load-aware locomotion adaptation to maintain gait stability, existing autonomous navigation systems generally ignore the influence of carried objects' geometries and use fixed footprint inflation, leading to overly conservative navigation. To fill this knowledge gap, we propose a two-phase load-aware navigation learning framework. In Phase 1, we train LOADNav, a load-aware navigation policy via reinforcement learning, enabling the robot to adapt its trajectory and clearance behavior according to the geometric size of the carried object. In Phase 2, we train CoGE, an online geometry predictor via imitation learning, which estimates unknown payload geometry from occasional contact events. We evaluate the framework in cluttered environments with loads of varying sizes and shapes. The results show that our navigation policy exhibits clear load-aware behaviors, and the online geometry predictor estimates object geometry from occasional contact events, refining its estimate and adapting the navigation behavior accordingly. Without requiring any prior knowledge of the payload, it narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.
authors: Qi Yin, XiaoLi Zhang, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets overly conservative navigation caused by fixed footprint inflation and ignored payload geometry.
LOADNav uses reinforcement learning to adapt trajectory and clearance behavior to the carried object's size.
CoGE uses imitation learning to infer unknown payload geometry from occasional robot–object contacts.
Experiments with varied load sizes and shapes show adaptive navigation and progressively refined geometry estimates.
Without prior payload knowledge, the method narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.
papers.selection_reason: Load-aware quadruped navigation with RL and online geometry estimation, directly fitting learning-based robot navigation.
papers.title: Load-Aware Quadruped Navigation with Online Contact-based Geometry Estimation
papers.tldr: A two-phase system lets quadruped robots navigate clutter while carrying unknown-shaped objects by learning load-aware motion and estimating payload geometry from contact events.

papers.abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Haitao Shen, Guanlin Li, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Problem: Fine-tuned VLA flow-matching policies contract around dominant demonstrated actions, producing redundant test-time candidates.
Method: Sample additional policy trajectories, weight them by flow support estimated with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and apply a detached finite-set KL correction.
Contribution: A training-time proposal-diversification method that increases candidate spread while avoiding the success degradation of Gaussian perturbations.
Results: Oracle best-of-8 RoboCasa success rises from 57.6% to 63.0%; fixed verifiers improve by 2.4–4.9 points in simulation and TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on physical-robot tasks.
Scope: ADS increases training cost, while deployment cost remains unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Improves test-time verified VLA policies for manipulation; directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Flow-Support-Weighted Proposals for Test-Time Verified VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Action Dynamic Sampling reduces redundant action proposals during training, improving verifier-based test-time scaling for VLA policies without increasing deployment cost.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.
authors: Hao Wu, Tianyu Shao, Shengju Qian, Yizhou Zhao, Fan Zhang, Penghao Zhao, Weiyan Wang, Yufei Huang, Fan Xu, Kun Wang, Xin Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Yuxuan Liang
bullets: Full-context decoding can make persistent scene information, recent states, and stale generated history compete for attention.
ReCAP is a training-free context schedule that freezes the tokenizer, world model, and decoder.
It preserves temporal order and complete recent visual-action blocks while bounding active context growth independently of rollout length.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN, it improves visual fidelity, action consistency, and robot-structure preservation over Full Context.
On BridgeV2, LPIPS falls 63.3%; at H=64, logical KV footprint falls 73.3% and p50 latency falls 6.51%. The memory-conflict explanation remains confounded by context-length and positional effects.
papers.selection_reason: Context scheduling for long-horizon robot video world models; fits video world models and inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: ReCAP improves long-horizon robot video prediction by retaining the initial scene and recent visual-action context while evicting stale history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS-SUSTech/UIDPO.
authors: Yongyuan Li, Yang Xu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of simplistic linguistic assumptions in preference optimization, given the complexity of human preferences.
Combines global information-rate variability with local second-order differences into an information-uniformity metric.
Integrates this metric into a preference-optimization objective based on chosen and rejected outputs.
Achieves comparable and sometimes better performance than SimPO on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench.
Linguistic analysis suggests UIDPO better captures human tendencies toward uniform information distribution, though its scope is tied to this psycholinguistic assumption.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a preference optimization algorithm (UIDPO) based on psycholinguistic theory to improve human alignment.
papers.title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: UIDPO uses Uniform Information Density to improve LLM preference optimization by favoring outputs with more uniformly distributed information.

papers.abstract: During human-robot interaction, sight plays an important role. When the human sees a robot, they can observe the robot's actions and better predict the robot's future behaviors. Conversely, when the human cannot see the robot, they become uncertain about the robot's intent and plans. In this paper, we focus on the human's field of view. Existing human-aware planners either ignore this field of view and assume the human can observe the entire scene, or intentionally design their interactions so the robot is always visible to the human. By contrast, we enable robots to infer what the human has and has not seen during interaction, i.e., the human's field of view. We then apply this estimate as a vision-aware filter on the robot's actions. Given a nominal robot policy and a model of the interaction, we roll out the policy over a short horizon to see how the robot's state updates. We then reweight the actions based on how those actions impact the robot's predicted visibility: higher weights are assigned to actions that bring the robot into (or away from) the human's line of sight. In practice, our framework provides an online estimation and filtering process that repeatedly updates its understanding of the human's field of view and then locally perturbs robot actions based on the human's vision. We evaluate our vision-aware filter on robots that assist humans in collaborative cooking and coordinate with them in driving environments. Across simulations and a 12-participant user study, we find that our vision-aware filter changes both performance and preference: participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance while cooking, and had fewer collisions with cars that purposely stayed out of their view while driving.
authors: Mengxue Fu, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Yinlong Dai, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Addresses human–robot interaction settings where existing planners ignore the human’s field of view or keep the robot constantly visible.
Uses short-horizon rollouts of a nominal policy to estimate how candidate actions affect the robot’s predicted visibility.
Reweights and locally perturbs actions to bring the robot into or move it away from the human’s line of sight as appropriate.
Evaluated in collaborative cooking and driving simulations plus a 12-participant user study.
In cooking, participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance; in driving, out-of-view behavior led to fewer collisions with cars.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a vision-aware filter for human-robot interaction, inferring the human's field of view to reweight robot actions, fitting embodied AI.
papers.title: In View or Out of View? A Vision-Aware Filter that Infers and Reacts to the Human's Field of View
papers.tldr: A vision-aware robot filter infers what a human can see and adjusts actions to improve assistance and coordination when the robot is in or out of view.

papers.abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.
authors: Keegan Wang
bullets: Frontier LLMs enable rapid prompt-based iteration, while SLMs offer substantially cheaper inference for narrow, repetitive agent subtasks.
The proposed lifecycle records converged production behavior and uses it—not synthetic examples—for supervised fine-tuning of an SLM.
In a home-care scheduling safety task, a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B achieved 0.913 agreement with recorded GPT-5.4-nano decisions.
The SLM was more consistent than the teacher on replayed prompts, and a blinded professional scheduler preferred it in disagreements.
The SLM also had approximately 2.5× lower median latency and a fraction of the cost.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-to-SLM distillation for low-cost, low-latency production agents; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
papers.tldr: Develop behavior quickly with a frontier LLM, then distill real production decisions into a cheaper, faster SLM for deployment.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best carbon-SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.
authors: Burak Topcu, Musa Cim, Zuhal Ozturk, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
bullets: Modern inference dynamics—including queueing and continuous batching—create a key tension between carbon reduction and latency guarantees.
The study builds a hardware-calibrated simulator that models latency, power, queueing, and continuous batching across datacenters.
It evaluates schedulers ranging from per-request heuristics to batch-level ILP and facility-level MILP optimization.
The MILP scheduler reduces carbon emissions by up to 60% versus round-robin, with an average SLO violation of 3%.
Carbon savings increase with cross-datacenter carbon-intensity differences and decrease at higher system loads; SLOs also depend on load-update frequency.
papers.selection_reason: Carbon-aware scheduling for geo-distributed LLM serving directly targets energy/carbon efficiency of AI systems, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
papers.tldr: A latency-aware geo-distributed simulator and carbon-conscious schedulers show that batched MILP scheduling can substantially reduce LLM serving emissions while largely respecting strict latency SLOs.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence.
